docs.title: django-spec-agents
docs.text:
Pydantic-AI agents for Django, in two halves under one import path, django_spec_agents:

  • The agent host takes an AgentConfig and a tool registry and returns a built pydantic_ai.Agent, with composed toolsets, audit, an approval gate, a failure policy and user resolution, and reads no Django settings of its own. Each transport (django-ag-ui for AG-UI over SSE, django-a2a for agent-to-agent) owns its settings namespace, builds an AgentConfig, and hands it down.
  • spec_tools, behind the [specs] extra, serves django-service-specs specs to an agent as tools, in process, with each spec's own validation, permissions and rendering.
pip install django-spec-agents            # the agent host
pip install "django-spec-agents[specs]"   # and specs as agent tools

The host was published as django-pydantic-agent and spec_tools as djangorestframework-pydantic-ai; moving from them maps each old name and seam to its new one. The package root never imports spec_tools, so the host installs and runs without the extra.

docs.title: Is this the package you want?
docs.text:
Often not directly: most projects install a transport and get this as a dependency. Reach for it on its own when you are:

  • building a transport, a new wire protocol over the same agent host;
  • sharing agent construction between transports, so one project's AG-UI endpoint and its A2A endpoint expose the same tools, audit trail and policy;
  • embedding an agent with no HTTP surface at all, a management command or a background task, where you want the registry, audit and guard machinery without a view;
  • giving an agent your specs as tools, the same services and selectors your API serves, without standing up an MCP server.

If you want an agent in a browser, start with django-ag-ui.

docs.title: The agent host
docs.text:
• Agent construction: AgentConfig → build_agent, model and provider resolution, and an escape hatch to replace construction entirely.
  • A tool registry: @tool with destructive / category / confirm / summary metadata, and JSON Schema derived from the signature.
  • Storage contracts: ConversationStore / AttachmentStore protocols, reference implementations, and the opt-in store app, django_spec_agents.contrib.store, whose label is django_spec_agents_store.
  • Policy: an audit trail over every tool call, a server-side approval gate for destructive tools, and the failure policy.
  • Integrations: the [specs] and [mcp] bridges that compose specs or a django-spec-mcp registry into an agent the host builds.

docs.title: Specs as tools
docs.text:
SpecToolset turns a name -> spec mapping, or a spec registry, into Pydantic-AI tools, and SpecCapability wraps it as a capability. django_spec_agents.spec_tools exports those two, AgentConventions and the string AGENT_TRANSPORT, and nothing else; the deps a run passes are the host's AgentDeps.

  • Specs as tools: what the toolset routes through, and how it compares with an MCP server.
  • Quickstart: specs, a toolset, an agent run.
  • Reference: SpecToolset, SpecCapability, AgentConventions and AGENT_TRANSPORT.

docs.title: The rule that shapes everything
docs.text:
The package reads no Django settings of its own. There is no DJANGO_* lookup anywhere in it. Its public input is an AgentConfig dataclass; each transport owns its own settings namespace, resolves its config, and hands the record down. What it does read is Django's own configuration: STORAGES, for the store app's optional attachment storage alias.

That is what keeps transports independent: django-ag-ui reads DJANGO_AG_UI, django-a2a reads its own, and neither fights the other for keys. A settings read added here would turn every consumer's upgrade into a key migration. It is also why collaborators are always passed as live objects rather than dotted paths: there is no import_string in this package.

docs.title: Where next
docs.text:
• Concepts: how a config becomes an agent, and what belongs here versus in a transport.
  • Tools: registering tools and what the metadata does.
  • Storage: the store contracts and the store app.
  • Policy: audit, the destructive-tool gate and the failure policy.
  • Integrations: specs and MCP tools as agent tools.
  • Spec tools: SpecToolset and SpecCapability in depth.
  • Reference: the host's public API.

docs.title: Child sessions
docs.text:
A child session is a whole conversation that one agent starts on another agent. It gets its own thread, runs headless, and can outlive the run that started it. The parent can message it, answer it and cancel it. The user opens it like any other thread. ChildSessionsToolset gives the parent's model the tools to do this. Child sessions need the [harness] extra, and building the toolset without it raises ImportError.

This page covers starting a child, the limits on it, its report, and how a report, question, answer or steer reaches the model of the thread it was sent to.

docs.title: Mounting the toolset
docs.text:
from decimal import Decimal

from django_spec_agents.child_sessions.child_sessions_toolset import ChildSessionsToolset
from django_spec_agents.child_sessions.types.child_session_limits import ChildSessionLimits
from django_spec_agents.child_sessions.types.child_session_spend import ChildSessionSpend

children = ChildSessionsToolset(
    "support",  # this mount's agent id, its thread scope
    agents={"research": "Reads the docs and answers one question."},
    runner=headless_runner,  # a HeadlessRunner over your mounts
    index=child_index,  # a ChildSessionIndex
    queue=inbound_queue,  # an InboundQueue
    limits=ChildSessionLimits(timeout=300.0),
    spend=ChildSessionSpend(shared_spend_store, tree_usd=Decimal("2"), day_usd=Decimal("10")),
)

Pass children among the mount's toolsets. A tool finds the run's thread through pydantic-ai's conversation_id, which an AG-UI run sets to its thread id. It finds the run's request in ctx.deps.call_context["request"], where the default deps put it. A project with its own deps_factory must put the request there too, or every tool raises.

docs.title: The tools
docs.text:
Tool What it does start_session(agent, prompt) Starts a child on one of agents and returns a receipt list_tasks() Lists this thread's children and their status check_task(thread_id) Shows where one child stands now, and why its last run ended early, without waiting for its report message_task(thread_id, message) Sends a child more instructions, through its inbound queue answer_task(thread_id, answer) Answers a child's question, through its inbound queue cancel_task(thread_id) Cancels a child and every session under it ask_parent(question) Offered to a child only: queues a question to its parent and parks

start_session returns a ChildSessionReceipt, and that receipt becomes the tool's result. It names the child's agent_id and thread_id. A client looks for the child's thread in the tool result, because the result is the one part of the parent's transcript that persists.

The other names are the ones upstream's TaskControl uses, and pydantic-ai refuses two tools with the same name. So a mount that carries both ChildSessionsToolset and SubAgents(task_control=TaskControl()) fails on its first run. Inline delegation through SubAgents' delegate_task still works beside child sessions.

A tool that cannot act returns a ChildSessionRefusal rather than raising. Its refused field names the rule that refused, and the model reads the reason. The tools refuse:

  • an agent id that is not in agents;
  • a thread_id that is not one of this thread's own children.

docs.title: The child's principal and tools
docs.text:
A child runs as the parent's user, so a run with no signed-in user cannot start one: it is refused as principal. The child sees only the tools its parent had when it started, plus the child-session tools, and never any others. A tool that needed approval in the parent needs approval in the child too, and the child's own mount guards each call as well. When a call needs approval, the child parks as waiting, and the parent is not asked to approve it. ask_parent parks the child the same way, on a deferred call of kind question.

The parent passes these tool names to the child, along with the child's place in the tree, as a ChildLineageRecord. The runner composes a ChildLineage capability from it on every run of the child's thread, the first included, as Every run of a child's thread describes.

docs.title: Limits
docs.text:
ChildSessionLimits holds the owner's defaults:

Limit Default Refused as Depth below the root thread max_depth=2, so a child and a grandchild max_depth Live children of one thread max_running_per_thread=3 max_running_per_thread Live children of one user, under any thread max_running_per_user=10 max_running_per_user Each child run's deadline timeout, required, in seconds the run ends timed_out

A child counts as live while it is running and while it waits. A parked child keeps its slot until someone answers it or cancels it. When the model asks for several children in one response, the starts run one at a time, so each start counts the children before it. Starts in two processes at once are not serialised: each reads the index before the other's child is listed, so the per-thread and per-user counts can overshoot by the number of processes starting at that moment. The limits bound the common case, not a race between workers.

ChildSessionSpend adds two pydantic-ai-harness SpendLimits to every child:

  • tree_usd caps the whole tree under the root thread, for all time;
  • day_usd caps one user's children for each day.

A start that finds either budget exhausted is refused, as child_sessions_tree_spend or child_sessions_day_spend. The parent's own spend counts toward the tree budget only if the parent's mount carries the same budget. The store has to be one that every worker shares, such as DefaultSpendStore. An in-memory store counts each process on its own. This needs the [harness] extra.

docs.title: Finding children
docs.text:
No store can say which threads a thread started, or how many of one user's children are live. A ChildSessionIndex answers those two questions, reading the parent link each child's conversation stores and the run status kept beside it. A child must be listed from the moment HeadlessRunner.start returns, or the per-thread limit cannot count it. The limits use it, and so does cancel_task, which walks the tree from the child down.

DefaultChildSessionIndex(run_store), in the store app, is the one to use with DefaultConversationStore. It lists a parent's children, oldest first and in any scope, reading a scoped store's scope:thread_id column back into a ThreadRef, and takes each child's status from the RunStore, idle where it holds none. The run store is keyed by the client's thread id, not its scope, so two children with one thread id in two scopes share one status, and wake_thread, which reads that status, waits on either's run. An inbound queue is not keyed that way: its claim names the scope, so two threads with one thread id in two scopes each have their own inbox, held by their own run.

docs.title: Every run of a child's thread
docs.text:
start_session hands the runner a ChildLineageRecord (the root, the depth, the parent's tools and the ones it gated) beside parent, and no capabilities, since capabilities cannot cross a queue to a worker. The runner saves both on the child's conversation. DefaultConversationStore keeps the record in a JSON column and, as with parent, leaves it alone on a save that names none. A child started through the run_headless spec carries the record too: HeadlessFiring.lineage crosses the queue as JSON, with tools and gated as sorted lists, and the runner saves it the same way.

Every run of that thread (its first, the user typing into it, a resume after an approval, a wake) has to carry the same bounds, or it runs with the child mount's full tools. The runner composes them on each run of a thread that has a parent:

capabilities = child_lineage_for(
    conversation, agent_id="research", owner=str(user.pk), queue=queue, spend=spend
)

It returns nothing for a thread with no stored lineage, so a runner can call it on every run. Until 0.21.0 start_session passed these capabilities to the first run itself; a runner that composes only on later runs leaves a child's first run unbounded.

The runner is also told which run started the child: start_session passes the parent run's id as parent_run_id, and a runner reports it as the child's first RUN_STARTED.parentRunId. A wake that resumes a parked child passes the parked run's id the same way; any other wake passes None. Every caller passes both parent_run_id and routine_id on every start, so a HeadlessRunner must accept them.

docs.title: Deleting a parent
docs.text:
A transport that deletes a parent thread should cancel its running children, with their descendants, and keep them as ordinary threads with the link cleared, as django-ag-ui does from 0.86.0. This package does neither on its own; a store clears the link with unlink_parent, on the optional UnlinkableConversationStore protocol:

from django_spec_agents import UnlinkableConversationStore

if isinstance(children, UnlinkableConversationStore):
    await children.unlink_parent("c1", request=request)

The child then loads with parent=None and lineage=None, so no run of its thread is bounded as a child's, and DefaultChildSessionIndex.children no longer lists it. Call it through the child's own scoped store; unlinking a missing thread, or another owner's, does nothing. Unlink once the child's run has ended or been cancelled: a save that names a parent writes the link again.

docs.title: Reports
docs.text:
ChildReport is composed into every child run, by child_lineage_for. When the run settles it enqueues a REPORT on the parent's queue, with the body {"text": ..., "outcome": ...}, sent from the child's thread:

The run Outcome ends with output ok stops at a usage or spend limit budget passes its deadline timeout raises failed parks, on a gated call or ask_parent no report is cancelled before its deadline no report, since whoever cancelled it knows

The report needs the run's request in call_context["request"], as the toolset does. A report that cannot be sent is logged, and the run's own result or error stands.

When the user joins a child's session, typing into its thread in a browser, the result may follow the user's direction rather than the parent's instructions. The transport says so by passing user_joined=True to child_lineage_for for that run, which hands it to ChildReport: the report's framed body then ends with a line telling the parent that the user joined the session, so its result may reflect their direction. A run nobody joined reports without it.

report_frame(child, agent_id=..., output=..., outcome=...) builds the text: a settled child's output as <task_output> data, with the tag and attributes of upstream's DelegationTask.report(), rendered by pydantic_ai.framing.wrap. The escaping is in the text itself, since the report crosses a queue before any model sees it: the output stays in the user channel, never in system voice, and it cannot close its own frame or forge a <task_question>.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
Reports, questions, answers and steering all travel through the receiving thread's inbound queue. DrainInbound hands them to that thread's model. Compose it into every run of each mount whose threads receive them, the parent's and the child's alike:

from django_spec_agents.child_sessions.drain_inbound import DrainInbound

drain = DrainInbound(inbound_queue, "support")  # the mount's agent id, its thread scope

lease (a keyword, five minutes by default) is how long the run's claim on the thread's inbox lasts without a model request to renew it.

At each model request it reads the run's thread's queue and adds what it finds to the request, oldest first:

Kind Sent by The model reads REPORT ChildReport, when a child settles the <task_output> text the child framed QUESTION ask_parent <task_question task_id="..." agent_name="..."> data naming the child ANSWER answer_task the parent's answer, as plain words STEER message_task the parent's instructions, as plain words

A question is framed when it is read, with pydantic_ai.framing.wrap, so the child's text cannot close its frame or speak in system voice. The parent answers it with answer_task, naming the task_id.

A message that lands after the run's last model request still reaches the model: the run makes one more request before it ends. A message that lands as the run parks on a deferred call waits in the queue for the resume. A message is acked once the model request that carries it is answered, so it is in the run's history.

One run holds a thread's inbox at a time. The run takes it with InboundQueue.take under its pydantic-ai run_id, at each model request, which renews its claim for lease; a second run on the thread meanwhile takes nothing, and a run sees each message once. The claim is the queue's own, so a queued run that a worker picks up later holds it as any other run does, and takes what arrived while it waited. When the run ends, parks or fails, it releases the inbox, and what it took but never acked goes to the thread's next run. A run whose process died cannot release: its messages wait until its lease lapses, and the next run takes them over. A run that starts before then takes nothing from the inbox, so keep lease no longer than the lease your transport gives its RunStore claim. A run with no signed-in user in call_context["request"] reads nothing.

docs.title: Marking what no user wrote
docs.text:
The wake line, a child's report and a child's question all reach the thread in the user channel. Each carries metadata under the key origin (MESSAGE_ORIGIN_KEY), so a transport can keep it and a client can tell it from the user's words:

What origin (MessageOrigin) Where it rides the wake line wake (WAKE) prompt_metadata, passed to HeadlessRunner.start of a runner that opted in a child's report task_output (TASK_OUTPUT) TextContent.metadata on the delivered part a child's question task_question (TASK_QUESTION) TextContent.metadata on the delivered part

A report and a question also carry task (MESSAGE_TASK_KEY), what the frame says as fields, so a client can show them without reading the frame:

task field Holds On taskId, threadId the child's thread id, which is its task id both agentName the child's agent id both outcome ok, failed, budget or timeout a report questionId the tool_call_id of the child's ask_parent call a question body the child's words as plain text, with no frame tags and no escaping both

A field the queued message does not hold is left out, never sent empty: one queued before 0.28.0 has no body on a report and no questionId on a question. body is the child's own text, so a client shows it as data, never as markup. With user_joined, a report's body ends with the same joined line the frame does.

from django_spec_agents.child_sessions.types.message_origin import MessageOrigin
from django_spec_agents.child_sessions.types.message_origin_key import MESSAGE_ORIGIN_KEY
from django_spec_agents.child_sessions.types.message_task_key import MESSAGE_TASK_KEY

An answer, steering and a user's own prompt carry no mark, and the model is never sent one.

A runner opts in to the wake line's mark by setting accepts_prompt_metadata = True (the PromptMetadataRunner protocol), once its start and run_to_first_stop take prompt_metadata. A runner that has not opted in is woken as before, without the keyword, and its wake line is stored unmarked. A runner that hands wake_thread a wrapper of itself sets the attribute on the wrapper.

A runner keeps prompt_metadata as the metadata of the user message it stores for the prompt. Only a wake of an idle thread passes it, and a queued start carries it across in HeadlessFiring.prompt_metadata, which run_headless passes on when set.

A delivered part keeps its mark in the run's message history, through ModelMessagesTypeAdapter, and on the EnqueuedMessagesEvent that reports the delivery. The AG-UI messages Pydantic-AI dumps from those messages leave TextContent.metadata out, so a transport reads the metadata off the event and adds it to what it sends and stores.

docs.title: Waking a thread
docs.text:
A message for a thread with no run would wait until someone opened it. wake_thread starts that run:

from django_spec_agents.child_sessions.wake_thread import wake_thread

started = await wake_thread(
    parent_thread,  # a ThreadRef: the thread id and its mount's agent id
    request=request,  # the owner's request; the run is started as request.user
    runner=headless_runner,
    runs=run_store,
    queue=inbound_queue,
    timeout=300.0,
    conversations=conversation_store,  # optional: the store the thread's mount reads
)

Call it after enqueueing for a thread. What it does depends on where the thread's runs stand in the RunStore:

The thread wake_thread The message is read running starts nothing at the run's next model request; after its last one, by the wake its runner makes once it ends waiting on questions only, with an ANSWER pending for each resumes the parked calls with those answers each answer as its call's result; the rest by the resumed run waiting on any approval, or on more questions than there are answers pending starts nothing by the resumed run, at its first request idle, failed or never run, with messages starts one headless run at that run's first request idle, with nothing pending, or only messages a run took and has not released starts nothing the holder hands them on when it releases; a dead holder's, to the next run once its lease lapses

A child parked on ask_parent resumes when its parent answers. wake_thread takes the oldest ANSWERs in the child's queue, one for each waiting call, and starts the run with answers={tool_call_id: text, ...}, each waiting call's id from the RunStore, in the order the run deferred them, mapped to the next answer's text. An answer names no call, so a child parked on two questions takes its parent's answers in the order they were sent; with fewer answers than questions it waits for the rest. The runner resumes the child's stored history with DeferredToolResults(calls=answers) and sends no new prompt, so the answer reaches the model as ask_parent's result. The wake pairs the answers while it holds a claim on the child's inbox (take, then release), and holds it until the start returns, so when two wakes race on one park, as a parent answering both questions in one response makes them, only one pairs the answers and starts the run; a wake that finds the inbox claimed starts nothing. The ANSWERs are acked once the start returns, still under the claim, so the resumed run's drain, which takes nothing while the wake holds the inbox, does not read them a second time as plain text. A start that fails, or is cancelled or dies with its process before the runner claims the thread, acks nothing: the answers stay pending, in order, for the next wake, once the wake's claim is released or its lease lapses. Once the run has started, a wake cancelled or killed before its ack leaves the answers unacked, and the resumed run's drain delivers them a second time, as plain text, as the queue's at-least-once delivery allows. The claim covers every message the wake took, so the resumed run reads whatever else is queued from its first read after the wake releases the inbox, which can be its second model request rather than its first. An answer can also arrive while the child's run is still going, before it parks on the question; the runner calls wake_thread once after recording such a park, so that answer resumes it too.

So a thread has one run at a time. Two wakes in a row start one run, which reads every message queued by its first request. Two wakes that race in two processes start one too: the runner's claim lets one through, and the other's refusal is absorbed once the thread reads as running. Any other failure to start is raised.

The woken run's new message is a line saying that messages arrived; pass prompt= to change it. No user wrote that line, so the start is marked: see Marking what no user wrote.

A child's thread wakes the same way, when its parent steers or answers it while it is idle. Pass conversations, the store the child's mount reads (a ScopedConversationStore where the mount scopes its threads), and wake_thread starts the run with the parent and lineage the child's conversation stores. The runner composes the child's bounds from them, as Every run of a child's thread describes. wake_thread never passes capabilities. A thread with no stored conversation, or a call with no conversations, is started with neither.

docs.title: Waking on every message
docs.text:
WakingInboundQueue wraps a queue and calls wake_thread after each enqueue. Pass it wherever the toolset and child_lineage_for take a queue, and every message wakes its thread: a child's report or question wakes an idle parent, message_task or answer_task wakes a settled child, whose new run starts with the wake line as its prompt and the message delivered beside it by DrainInbound, and answer_task resumes a child parked on ask_parent with the answer. A message that lands on a running thread after its run's last read is not woken by the enqueue, since the thread still reads as running; the runner's wake after RunStore.finish starts the next run for it.

from django_spec_agents import WakingInboundQueue

queue = WakingInboundQueue(
    DefaultInboundQueue(),
    headless_runner,
    run_store,
    300.0,  # each woken run's timeout
    conversations={"research": research_store},  # agent id to the store its mount reads
)

A thread whose agent id is not in conversations wakes with no parent or lineage, as a root thread does. A wake that fails is logged, and the message stays queued for the thread's next run.

docs.title: Config in, agent out
docs.text:
The whole package is one shape: a ToolRegistry and an AgentConfig go in, a pydantic_ai.Agent comes out.

from django_spec_agents import AgentConfig, ToolRegistry, build_agent, tool

registry = ToolRegistry()


@tool(registry)
def list_orders(status: str) -> list[dict]:
    """List orders with the given status."""
    ...


agent = build_agent(
    registry,
    AgentConfig(
        model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5",
        instructions="You help staff manage orders.",
    ),
)

AgentConfig is a frozen dataclass carrying the model, instructions, model_settings, retries, extra toolsets and capabilities, an audit_logger, and a tool_guard policy. Everything is optional except model.

A transport resolves those values from its settings namespace and hands the record down. This package never reads them itself.

docs.title: What gets composed into the agent
docs.text:
build_agent registers each registry tool as a plain Pydantic-AI tool, then composes capabilities:

  • AuditCapability, when audit_logger is set and isn't the null logger. It hooks pydantic-ai's tool execution, so it times and records every tool the agent runs — registry tools and composed toolsets alike, not just the ones registered here — with one record per execution describing the tool's own.
  • ToolGuard, when tool_guard is set and enabled. It flips destructive tools to require approval.
  • ToolFailurePolicy, unless tool_failure turns it off. A raising tool fails its own call rather than the whole run.
  • Anything in config.capabilities, verbatim.

Each declares its position via get_ordering() and pydantic-ai's CombinedCapability sorts them topologically, so a transport appending its own capability to config.capabilities doesn't have to think about where. Audit is innermost, closest to the tool, and the failure policy outermost, so it converts a failure only after every other capability has seen it; the guard is orthogonal. Within a tier list order breaks ties, which is why build_agent appends audit after config.capabilities and places the policy before them. Ordering says what each position buys.

The agent's output_type includes DeferredToolRequests, which turns on the tool-approval interrupt loop for server-side tools. That is deliberate and not merely a default: the AG-UI adapter only augments output_type when a run carries frontend tools, so a run whose only gated tool is server-side would otherwise never defer. Setting it here makes the approval path independent of whether the client declared any tools of its own.

docs.title: Per-run dependencies
docs.text:
The agent is typed Agent[AgentDeps, ...], so every run is given an AgentDeps — pydantic-ai's own seam for request-scoped values. Tools, toolsets and capabilities read them off RunContext.deps:

deps = AgentDeps(user=request.user, ip_address=request.META.get("REMOTE_ADDR"))

This is what a transport passes as deps= when it starts a run, rather than closing over the request. The difference matters beyond tidiness:

  • The acting user binds natively. The SpecToolset in django_spec_agents.spec_tools already defaults to reading ctx.deps.user, so spec tools act as the right user with nothing passed at the call site.
  • The agent stops being request-shaped. A capability that closes over a request can only serve that request, which forces a rebuild — schemas and all — per call. Request-independent collaborators are the precondition for reusing a built agent across runs. ip_address is the worked example: AuditCapability reads it off the run's deps, falling back to its constructor argument, so one audited agent can serve requests from many clients. Taken only from the constructor, building once would silently stamp every audit record with the IP of whoever arrived first.
  • The request a run arrived on travels as data. deps.call_context is a plain dict of values every tool call may read; a transport puts the request there under request, and each spec tool call is handed its own copy with the tool's name under action and "agent" under transport, so a callable or a permission check reads the request without the agent ever holding it, and can tell it was an agent that called (see per-call seeds and the run's context).
  • AG-UI state has somewhere to land. AgentDeps satisfies pydantic-ai's StateHandler protocol, so a run's RunAgentInput.state is validated into deps.state instead of being dropped with a warning.

AgentDeps is deliberately not frozen, unlike every other record here: the UI adapter assigns deps.state = ... directly. Deps are per-run and never shared, so the mutability is contained.

  • A spec's progress reports have somewhere to go. SpecToolset reads its reporter off ctx.deps.progress exactly as it reads the user off ctx.deps.user. Pass a callable and a long-running spec's progress(...) calls reach it; leave it None and the kernel substitutes its no-op. Where the reports go is a transport's decision, so nothing here constructs a sink.

user has no default: an unauthenticated run says user=None rather than leaving it out. Pydantic-AI types deps as AgentDepsT = None and never validates it, so a run built without deps at all is otherwise silently constructible — spec tools fail closed there, but registry tools run with no user context and the answer reads like any other.

Projects needing more per-run context subclass it — user, ip_address, state and progress are the four fields the framework itself reads. Build the subclass in your transport's deps_factory (django-ag-ui: AGUIServer(deps_factory=...)), which is where per-request construction belongs; AgentConfig is built once and reused.

Inbound state only

Nothing emits STATE_SNAPSHOT / STATE_DELTA back to the client yet. A run receives client state; a tool returning those events as ToolReturn metadata is a separate piece of work.

docs.title: Model resolution
docs.text:
AgentConfig.model takes whatever Pydantic-AI takes — a "provider:model" string or a Model instance.

pydantic-ai-slim ships no providers, so a provider string needs its library installed. The extras exist for exactly that:

pip install django-spec-agents[anthropic]   # or [openai], [google]

docs.title: Falling back to another model
docs.text:
build_model_fallback returns Pydantic-AI's ModelFallback capability, passed in AgentConfig.capabilities. When the agent's model fails, refuses, or is cut off at max_tokens, the next model serves the same request step, and the answer's ModelResponse.model_id names the model that gave it:

from django_spec_agents import AgentConfig, build_model_fallback

config = AgentConfig(
    model="anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5",
    capabilities=[build_model_fallback("openai:gpt-5", sticky=True)],
)

Each name is built when the capability is, so a typo or a provider with no key in its environment variable raises ImproperlyConfigured at startup rather than on the first outage. A fallback never borrows the agent's api_key; pass a built Model for one that needs its own key or provider. With sticky=True a conversation that fell back stays on the answering model across later runs, as long as the history those runs continue carries model_id (the step store's does). A project building agents from a Pydantic-AI agent spec lists ModelFallback in its capabilities directly; ModelFallback.from_spec needs nothing from this package.

docs.title: Replacing construction entirely
docs.text:
When build_agent's composition isn't what a project wants — a custom output type, an unusual toolset arrangement, bespoke instrumentation — a transport can accept an AgentFactoryFn instead. It receives the tool registry and that transport's resolved config object, and fully replaces build_agent.

The config argument is deliberately untyped: this substrate reads no settings and owns no settings namespace, so the second argument is whatever configuration record the calling transport passes down.

docs.title: Core versus transport
docs.text:
The litmus test: if it maps agent output to a specific wire format, or serves a specific frontend, it is a transport; everything upstream of "how do I speak to the peer" is core.

Concern Lands in AgentConfig, model / settings / retries resolution, the factory escape hatch core ToolRegistry + @tool + typed schema derivation core External toolsets and capabilities; the [mcp] and [specs] bridges core (optional extras) The AuditLogger protocol and the tool guard core ConversationStore / AttachmentStore protocols, contrib.store models core An HTTP view, an SSE encoder, a wire adapter, .urls a transport Browser-facing sub-views (thread drawer, attachments, transcription) a transport

The stores are the non-obvious call: they are contracts, which are core, while the HTTP views over them are per-transport. A thread drawer is a browser REST surface; an agent-to-agent peer models the same history as tasks and contexts entirely differently, so the view can't be shared even though the storage can.

Reasoning is the mirror image — it is produced here (a model-settings thinking config) but mapped to wire events by the transport.

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text:
Three optional extras, all lazily imported — the base install stays slim and none of these dependencies is pulled unless configured.

Two of them are bridges: [specs] and [mcp] expose specs you have already declared as agent tools, so you don't re-declare your API as @tool functions. Both make the agent act as the logged-in user — the request is carried into every call, so your existing permission checks apply exactly as they would over HTTP.

The third, [harness], is a different shape: it brings in ready-made capabilities (compaction, agent skills, step persistence and more) that plug into the same AgentConfig.capabilities seam this package's own audit and tool-guard capabilities use.

docs.title: Which bridge?
docs.text:
[specs] [mcp] Path django-service-specs spec → tool, in process django-spec-mcp registry → toolset, in process Needs an MCP server No Yes (but no network hop) Use when The agent is the consumer, and you have specs You already run an MCP server and want the same tools in the agent

If you have ServiceSpec / SelectorSpec objects and no MCP server, take [specs]. If you already run an MCP server for external clients, take [mcp] and get the identical tool surface without standing up a second one.

docs.title: [specs] — specs as tools
docs.text:
pip install django-spec-agents[specs]

build_spec_capability(specs, exclude_names=…) returns a SpecCapability over the specs. It takes no request: the acting user is read at run time from ctx.deps.user, so an agent built once serves every caller. Each call runs through the kernel's transport-neutral dispatch and enforces the spec's own permissions.

Every spec passed here must declare permissions. A spec with permissions=None makes build_spec_capability raise ImproperlyConfigured, rather than exposing a tool anyone can call, because off HTTP there is no view or project default to inherit. This function has no switch for that. A project migrating a large registry builds SpecCapability itself with require_permissions=False, which turns the refusal into an UnguardedSpecWarning, and until a spec declares permissions the model can call it ungated.

Choosing the capability over a bare toolset is deliberate. The tool-set conventions (list-tool page / limit / ordering, and the error contract) live on SpecToolset.get_instructions(), so they reach the model either way and the capability delegates rather than re-emitting them. What wrapping buys is the capability seam itself — defer_loading, and a uniform place to compose spec tools alongside audit and guard.

A tool's input schema asks for what a call needs. A selector parameter with no default, which the toolset does not fill, is listed in required, and a single-item service advertises the lookup its target is resolved through, so a tool changing one row names the pk that picks it. A call that leaves such an argument out is a ModelRetry naming it, Missing required argument(s): `pk`., so the model supplies it on the next turn rather than the run ending on the selector's TypeError. The [specs] route does both, and the [mcp] route asks for the same arguments and retries the same omission. The extra is floored where a parameter a kwargs= provider declines, and the model left out, is retried the same way rather than reaching the selector, and where a selector parameter the toolset takes out of every call, a list selector's page or limit, makes build_spec_capability raise ImproperlyConfigured rather than advertising an argument whose value never arrives, and where a spec's kwargs= key named like a Validator field, or a target selector's named like a Validator field or a read, is served as a namesake, the field or read asked of the caller unless input_data fills it and the provider's value passed to its own seat, rather than the spec refused.

docs.title: Declaring specs once
docs.text:
specs takes either a name -> spec mapping or a spec registry — the kernel's SpecRegistry, the single declaration site for a project exposing the same specs over more than one transport:

from django_spec_agents.integrations.build_spec_capability import build_spec_capability

capability = build_spec_capability(registry)

The registry is matched structurally, through a SpecSource Protocol declaring only specs() -> dict. The package root names no kernel type and depends on pydantic-ai-slim alone; the kernel arrives only with the extra.

If you are writing a transport, normalise with resolve_spec_mapping() before you touch the argument. Iterating a registry yields RegisteredSpec records, not names — so a transport that reserves tool names by iterating the raw argument fills its collision set with dataclasses and silently stops detecting duplicates:

from django_spec_agents.integrations.resolve_spec_mapping import resolve_spec_mapping

specs = resolve_spec_mapping(source)  # mapping or registry -> mapping
seen.update(specs)  # names, as intended

docs.title: [mcp] — an MCP registry as a toolset
docs.text:
pip install django-spec-agents[mcp]

MCPToolset bridges a django-spec-mcp server's registry through its public in-process surface (list_tools / acall_tool), so the kernel's argument validation and the spec's permissions apply as they would over HTTP — without the network hop and without reaching into handler internals. The extra installs django-spec-mcp, which brings the kernel; it brings no Django REST Framework, and the bridge imports none.

from django_spec_agents.integrations.mcp import MCPToolset

toolset = MCPToolset(server, request, exclude_names=frozenset(registry_names))

Import it where the agent is built, never at a module a host import reaches: django-spec-mcp needs a ready app registry to import.

Tool schemas come from the server's own tools/list rather than being re-derived locally, so the bridge advertises the same inputSchema the HTTP transport would — including a paged list tool's pagination arguments and the additionalProperties policy.

That schema asks for what a call needs. A read the spec declares required=True is listed in required, and a service tool also advertises the target lookup its row is resolved through, so a tool changing one row names the pk that picks it. [specs] builds its schemas the same way, so one spec asks a model for the same arguments by either route. A paginated list selector reading page is refused at registration, as [specs] refuses it when the toolset is built, so one spec is served by both routes or refused by both.

A call hands the model the result's structuredContent, which django-spec-mcp sends as an object: a list result as {"items": [...]}, as [specs] hands the same spec's rows. A result carrying none is read from its one text block, parsed as JSON: a scalar, which has no object form, so a tool counting rows hands the model 3, and any result of a tool registered with include_structured_content=False. Text that is not JSON is handed on as it is, and content that is not one text block, such as an image, as its blocks.

A call's call_context is built by django-spec-mcp, not by this package, so the transport a spec reads off it (call_transport(call_context)) is whatever the installed django-spec-mcp stamps. A bridged call reads "mcp", the MCP_TRANSPORT django-spec-mcp stamps from 0.10.0. It is never "agent": that value, AGENT_TRANSPORT, is what [specs] stamps on a call it serves in process, so a spec written to branch on the transport sees a different one on each route.

docs.title: Interactive views (MCP Apps)
docs.text:
A tool registered with ui=UIToolMeta(...) links to a ui:// view. The bridge keeps the tool's _meta and acts on _meta.ui:

  • A tool whose visibility is a list without "model" (["app"]) is not offered to the model: the view's own page calls it.
  • A call to a tool with a resourceUri returns the value as before, wrapped in a ToolReturn whose metadata holds an mcp_app record (resource_uri, tool_input, result in wire form, toolset_id "mcp"). pydantic-ai's AG-UI adapter turns it into the mcp-apps activity; the record is never sent to the model.
  • call_tool_for_app(name, arguments) and read_resource_for_app(uri) are what the endpoint your frontend relays the page's requests to calls, with pydantic-ai's signatures. The first answers -32602 for a tool whose visibility omits "app". Both run as the request's user and return the wire result, or a JsonRpcError for a protocol fault.

docs.title: A tool that cannot run now
docs.text:
A service's affordances can say when the operation is possible at all: a condition written as a callable reads only the user and the request, never the call's arguments, so while it is unmet every call is refused. django-spec-mcp leaves such a tool out of tools/list, and whether one is unmet can change mid-run. So the bridge lists definitions once per request, every tool the user may see included, and on every step:

  • offers only the tools the server would list right now, asking it through MCPServer.aunavailable_tools, so a tool that becomes available mid-run is offered from the next step without listing again;
  • names each tool it left out in the toolset's instructions, with the reason its condition gives, so a model asked for one says why rather than guessing or denying the operation exists:
- These operations exist but cannot be performed right now, so they are not among your tools. If the user asks for one, say it is unavailable at the moment and give the reason listed for it, rather than guessing why:
  - `close_books`: The books are closed.

That is word for word what [specs] says for the same spec, so the model is taught one sentence whichever way a spec is exposed. A server declaring no such condition adds nothing to the instructions and no thread hop per step. Nothing here is an authorization decision: the call enforces every condition, so a tool whose condition flips between the step offering it and the call is refused with its code, as below.

docs.title: Error semantics
docs.text:
The bridge follows MCP's protocol-vs-tool boundary, which decides whether the model gets to recover:

  • a fault in the request the model produced → ModelRetry, so the model retries with the field errors fixed, or with a real name (the retry lists the tools this toolset advertises), instead of the run dying. django-spec-mcp answers arguments it refuses with a tool-level validation_error result, and an unknown tool name on JSON-RPC -32602; the bridge retries both. The retry is the server's message, then its field detail as JSON, unless the message already names every field in the detail, nested ones included, in which case the detail is left off rather than read twice. A detail is sent whole or not at all, so Invalid arguments: {"a": ["Expected an integer."]} keeps it, since that message names nothing. A reason under no field, which the server writes under the kernel's NON_FIELD_ERRORS key (a bare DispatchError, say), is kept unless the message quotes it. Refused arguments include a required read the call left out, which the model reads as Missing required argument(s): `pk`., word for word what [specs] raises for the same call. They also include a shapes value (a fields selection, say) the spec's presenter refuses while rendering, which the server answers as a validation_error naming the argument and quoting the presenter's reason; on a paged tool the likeliest one is a selection written against the page envelope rather than one item;
  • a tool-level input_required result → ModelRetry naming the arguments to add on the next call. In process the server has no client to ask, so a service's AdditionalInputRequired for inputs its spec declares arrives this way;
  • every other tool-level failure (service_error, not_found, a timeout, an oversized result) → ToolFailed, so the model reads the sentence and adapts, no retry budget is spent, and the call is recorded outcome="failed" for anything streaming the run;
  • a permission refusing the user (-32006) → Django's PermissionDenied, which the tool-failure policy passes through by default, so the run ends. Converted, a refusal would leave the model free to try the next id;
  • every other protocol fault → RuntimeError: nothing the model can rewrite its way out of. These are auth, rate limits, and an internal error (-32603). The last is also the answer to a service asking, through AdditionalInputRequired, for an input its spec does not declare in reads=: no answer could reach the service, so declare every input a service may ask for. The tool-failure policy converts a RuntimeError into a failed call, so the run goes on.

A refusal keeps what names it. ToolFailed carries a single string, so when the server serves an affordance refusal's code, it rides as a suffix on the sentence:

The books are closed. (code: books_closed)

That is word for word what [specs] produces for the same refusal raised in process, so a spec reads the same to the model whichever way it is exposed, and the code matches the one a row's affordances answer advertised. The suffix is written for the model and for a person reading the tool call; a program that needs the code reads it from the server's result, or on the [specs] route off the exception through translate_exception, rather than parsing it out of the sentence.

Bridged tools also carry destructiveness into the tool guard: the bridge maps each tool's annotations onto DESTRUCTIVE_METADATA_KEY the way MCP reads them, where destructiveHint defaults to true and means something only on a tool that is not read-only. A tool is marked unless readOnlyHint is true or destructiveHint is false, so a service tool is destructive, a selector tool is not, and a mutation registered with annotations={"destructiveHint": False} is not either. A tool listed with no annotations says nothing and is not marked.

A service's own confirmation (AdditionalInputRequired) is the input_required retry above, which the model can answer itself, on this route and on [specs] alike. A selector's request does not agree: django-spec-mcp builds no input round for a selector, so it arrives as a service error, and so as ToolFailed here, where [specs] raises ModelRetry. It is not an approval gate: see what is gated, and what is not.

docs.title: [harness] — upstream capabilities
docs.text:
pip install django-spec-agents[harness]

The other two extras bridge your API into the agent. This one is different: it pulls in pydantic-ai-harness, a library of ready-made capabilities — the same seam this package's own audit and tool-guard capabilities use. Nothing here wraps or re-implements them; you construct one and hand it to AgentConfig:

from pydantic_ai_harness.compaction import SlidingWindow

config = AgentConfig(model=..., capabilities=[SlidingWindow(max_messages=80)])
agent = build_agent(registry, config)

That is the whole integration. capabilities takes live instances (never dotted paths), so a harness capability, a first-party one, and your own all compose the same way, and pydantic-ai orders them by their own get_ordering().

Version-sensitive

pydantic-ai-harness is 0.x and its minors may break, the StepStore protocol among them. Even so, the [harness] extra declares a floor and no upper bound (the number is in pyproject.toml). A one-minor ceiling over an upstream that releases this often made the package unresolvable on every harness release, whether or not anything broke. Three checks stand in for it instead:

  • The lock pins the harness and pydantic-ai every CI job runs against, and is moved to the newest deliberately rather than left to drift.
  • The lowest declared versions job runs the suite on every pull request against the oldest harness the extra allows, so the floor stays true.
  • The weekly upstream drift run ignores the lock, resolves the newest harness and pydantic-ai the extras allow, and runs the suite, so a breaking release is found by a scheduled job rather than by you.

Recent harness releases pin pydantic-ai-slim to one exact release, so with [harness] installed the harness version you resolve also decides your pydantic-ai version.

docs.title: Long runs: compaction
docs.text:
A tool-heavy run grows its message history until it crowds the context window. The compaction module trims it, and the choice is mostly about cost:

Strategy Cost What it does SlidingWindow(max_messages=80, keep_messages=40) free Drops the oldest messages once a threshold is crossed, preserving tool-call / tool-return pairs. No model calls. ClearToolResults(max_messages=60, keep_pairs=3) free Keeps the conversation shape but blanks old tool results, which are usually the bulk of the tokens. SummarizingCompaction(max_messages=60, keep_messages=20) a model call Replaces the trimmed span with an LLM-written summary, so older context survives in compressed form. TieredCompaction(tiers=[...], target_tokens=…) varies Applies cheaper strategies first, escalating only if still over target.

Start with SlidingWindow — it is free and transparent. Reach for SummarizingCompaction only when losing the old turns outright actually hurts, since it spends a model call on every compaction.

Trimming happens inside before_model_request and is deliberately invisible to the rest of the run: nothing is emitted when a compaction fires. A transport that wants to tell the user "earlier turns were condensed" has to observe it itself — CompactionStrategy is a one-method protocol (compact(messages, ctx) -> messages), so a thin wrapper that compares its input to its output is the seam for that.

docs.title: Progressive disclosure: agent skills
docs.text:
A skill is a folder with a SKILL.md — a name, a description, and a body of instructions. Skills discovers them and exposes each as a deferred capability: the model sees only the name and description up front, and the body loads into context if it selects that skill. A dozen skills therefore cost a dozen one-line descriptions, not a dozen instruction blocks.

from pydantic_ai_harness.skills import Skills

config = AgentConfig(
    model=...,
    capabilities=[Skills("/srv/app/skills")],
)

directories takes one path or several. Discovery scans immediate child directories for a SKILL.md, so /srv/app/skills/summarise/SKILL.md registers a skill named summarise (the frontmatter name wins over the directory name when both are present).

include / exclude select by exact skill name — and are validated against what was actually discovered, so exclude={"draft-only"} raises ValueError when no such skill exists rather than silently excluding nothing. That is the behaviour you want (a typo'd name fails loudly), but it does mean a selection list and a skills directory have to be kept in step.

Instructions only, in v1

Upstream loads the SKILL.md body and nothing else — bundled scripts and resources are deferred to a future sandbox integration. A skill that assumes it can execute its own files will not work yet.

Each skill becomes one capability whose id is the skill name, which is what a client needs to show "using skill X". Enumerate them with skills.apply(visitor).

docs.title: Also available
docs.text: step_persistence (used by DefaultStepStore), subagents, code_mode, overflowing_tool_output, guardrails, filesystem, shell and ManagedPrompt all compose the same way. None of them need support from this package — if it is a pydantic-ai capability, capabilities=[...] takes it.

docs.title: Name collisions
docs.text:
Both bridges take exclude_names, and precedence is fixed: the @tool registry wins, then the MCP server's, then spec tools. A duplicate that slipped through would make pydantic-ai raise UserError at run time, so the excluded set is threaded through composition instead.

Full signatures in the integrations reference.

docs.title: Moving from the old packages
docs.text:
django-spec-agents is two packages merged under one import path. The agent host was published as django-pydantic-agent, and django_spec_agents.spec_tools as djangorestframework-pydantic-ai. Both have had their final release, and both keep working exactly as that release did: nothing in them warns, breaks or re-exports. This page is for the day you move.

A project that used both moves both halves at once. Read the two sections below, then the seams 0.2.0 changes, which apply to anyone serving specs as tools.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install django-spec-agents

anthropic, openai, google and harness keep their names. drf-mcp is gone: [mcp] replaced it, bridging a django-spec-mcp server with MCPToolset where DRFMCPToolset bridged a drf-mcp one, and 0.7.0 removed the old extra. The [spec-tools] extra, which pulled djangorestframework-pydantic-ai, becomes django-spec-agents[specs].

docs.title: Imports
docs.text:
The package's layout carries over under the new root:

Was Now django_pydantic_agent django_spec_agents, with the same root names django_pydantic_agent.<module> django_spec_agents.<module>, such as django_spec_agents.contrib.store django_pydantic_agent.constants one module per name under django_spec_agents.types

ToolCategory, X_DESTRUCTIVE_KEY, X_CATEGORY_KEY, X_CONFIRM_KEY, X_SUMMARY_KEY and DESTRUCTIVE_METADATA_KEY keep their spelling and are imported from the root:

from django_spec_agents import DESTRUCTIVE_METADATA_KEY, ToolCategory, X_CONFIRM_KEY

ATTACHMENT_STORAGE_ALIAS is not a root name; import it from django_spec_agents.types.attachment_storage_alias.

docs.title: INSTALLED_APPS and the store's tables
docs.text:
1. Run migrate on django-pydantic-agent's final release first. The new store renames the old store's tables in place, and needs every one of the old store's migrations applied before it runs; short of them it stops with OldInstallBehindError and renames nothing.
  2. Replace the dependency, and change every django_pydantic_agent import to django_spec_agents.

  3. Change the INSTALLED_APPS entry:

    INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...,
    "django_spec_agents.contrib.store",  # was "django_pydantic_agent.contrib.store"
]

  4. Run migrate once. The app's label is django_spec_agents_store, and its first migration, 0001_initial, renames the tables, their named constraints and indexes, the content types and the migration records. Nothing is copied. The second, 0002_text_columns, then lifts the descriptive columns to TextField.

What the rename touches, what it leaves under the old names on PostgreSQL and how to roll it back are on the storage page.

A project migration that names the old label stops loading once the old app leaves INSTALLED_APPS: a dependency such as ("django_pydantic_agent_store", "0005_storedmemory_storedmemoryoperation") raises NodeNotFoundError, and a foreign key to "django_pydantic_agent_store.StoredConversation" fails the system check. Point the foreign key, in the model and in the migration, at django_spec_agents_store.<Model>, and the dependency at ("django_spec_agents_store", "0001_initial"). Your migration is recorded as applied and now depends on one that is not, which Django refuses as InconsistentMigrationHistory, so run that first migrate with the apps holding such migrations left out of INSTALLED_APPS, then put them back. The rows your foreign keys point at are kept.

docs.title: Names that keep their spelling
docs.text:
Each is stored or configured outside Python, so a rename would break a project silently. They keep django-pydantic-agent's spelling:

  • the attachment storage alias django_pydantic_agent_attachments;
  • the session key django_pydantic_agent_conversations;
  • the attachment upload prefix django_pydantic_agent/attachments/;
  • the django_pydantic_agent.audit and django_pydantic_agent.failure loggers;
  • the agent_store_* management commands.

docs.title: Names that change
docs.text:
• DESTRUCTIVE_METADATA_KEY is "django_spec_agents.destructive".
  • The attachments toolset id is django-spec-agents-attachments.
  • The audit ContextVar is named django_spec_agents.audit.execution.
  • Model-build and failure-policy messages start django-spec-agents:.
  • A registry tool registered under its own name, with @tool(registry, name="...") or as a ToolSpec registered directly, is offered to the model under that name, where django-pydantic-agent offered the function's. A require_approval or exempt entry, an approval prompt, or a query on the audit or step store's tool_name that named such a tool by its function name uses the registered name after moving. A require_approval entry left on the function name no longer matches, so that tool runs without approval.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install "django-spec-agents[specs]"

[specs] installs the spec kernel, django-service-specs, and nothing else. There is no [filter] extra: a project declaring a filter_set has django-filter installed already, and django-service-specs[filter] declares it. A project reaching the toolset through django-ag-ui installs django-ag-ui[specs] where it installed [spec-tools].

docs.title: Where each name went
docs.text:
Was Now rest_framework_pydantic_ai.SpecToolset django_spec_agents.spec_tools.SpecToolset rest_framework_pydantic_ai.SpecCapability django_spec_agents.spec_tools.SpecCapability rest_framework_pydantic_ai.AgentConventions django_spec_agents.spec_tools.AgentConventions rest_framework_pydantic_ai.AgentDeps django_spec_agents.AgentDeps, the host's own deps type rest_framework_pydantic_ai.QueryParam, UrlKwarg a kernel Parameter in the spec's reads= or shapes=; see Specs rest_framework_pydantic_ai.testing django_spec_agents.testing, with the same three doubles rest_framework_pydantic_ai.__version__ django_spec_agents.__version__ rest_framework_pydantic_ai.spec_toolset, .spec_capability, .types.agent_conventions the same module under django_spec_agents.spec_tools, such as django_spec_agents.spec_tools.spec_toolset for the SpecSource alias a subclass annotates with 
from django_spec_agents import AgentDeps
from django_spec_agents.spec_tools import AgentConventions, SpecCapability, SpecToolset

The logger is django_spec_agents.spec_tools. A LOGGING entry under rest_framework_pydantic_ai stops receiving the toolset's records, and nothing fails to tell you.

The host's AgentDeps has more fields. It is user, ip_address, state, progress, call_context, so a positional AgentDeps(user, reporter) binds the reporter to ip_address without complaint. Pass progress= by keyword.

docs.title: Specs
docs.text:
The toolset serves the kernel's specs, ServiceSpec and SelectorSpec from django_service_specs, in a mapping or a SpecRegistry. A djangorestframework-services spec is not a supported source: declare each spec the agent serves on the kernel. What that changes for a tool:

  • A read is a Parameter. What the model sends for the callable goes in reads=, and what shapes the output and reaches the presenter in shapes=. A selector or provider takes a read by its name, as an argument, and the call's shape values by declaring shapes.
  • Audiences are markings on the output. What agent_contract declared moves onto the spec: its reads to reads= and shapes=, its field audiences to a FieldMarking on each field of the presenter's output, as hiding plumbing from the model shows.
  • Permissions are the kernel's PermissionCheck instances, in permissions=. A spec declaring none is refused when the toolset is built; require_permissions=False downgrades that to a warning while migrating, and permissions=[Unrestricted()] says anyone may call it.
  • A filter's ordering is an array of sort names. A string is handed back to the model as ordering: Expected an array., so an agent prompt or a tool description that describes it as one comma-separated value says the wrong thing.
from django_service_specs import (
    DataclassPresenter,
    Parameter,
    Parameters,
    SelectorKind,
    SelectorSpec,
    Unrestricted,
)

list_orders_spec = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=list_orders,  # def list_orders(*, user, status=None)
    reads=Parameters.of(Parameter("status", "string")),
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(OrderOut),
    permissions=[Unrestricted()],
)

docs.title: Mount keywords
docs.text:
query_params=, tool_query_params=, url_kwargs= and tool_url_kwargs= are gone, and passing one raises TypeError. A read the model sends is declared on the spec, in reads=. A value the server supplies, such as a capture bound to the acting user's project, goes in tool_server_arguments=, one kernel ServerArguments per tool, built per run where the value depends on the user:

from django_service_specs import ServerArguments

toolset = SpecToolset(
    registry,
    tool_server_arguments={
        "list_document_vendors": ServerArguments(
            values={"project_pk": str(document.project_id)},
            withheld=frozenset({"draw_request_pk"}),
        ),
    },
)

A bound name is filled whatever the model sends, a withheld one is left to its default, and neither is advertised. See arguments the server supplies.

docs.title: The seams 0.2.0 changes
docs.text: These changed between django-spec-agents 0.1.0 and 0.2.0, so they apply to a project moving from either old package and to one already on 0.1.0.

docs.title: What a call carries besides its arguments
docs.text:
The toolset builds no request and no view for a call. What each part of a spec sees:

  • A permission check sees the call's arguments. A kernel PermissionCheck method declaring the keyword arguments is handed them, one declaring call_context the call's context, with the tool's name under action, and one named after a registered seed that seed's value. See what a permission check sees.
  • A provider or selector declaring request or view receives None unless the run puts one in call_context or a call_seeds override returns one. A value it used to read off view.kwargs or request.query_params it now takes by name, as a read.
  • A callable that told the transport by isinstance(view, OfflineServiceView) declares call_context and reads call_context["transport"], which is "agent" on every call the toolset makes (the string AGENT_TRANSPORT exports, so nothing needs importing to compare it). The request the run arrived on may be in call_context too, so its presence says nothing about how the call came.

The request a run arrived on goes in the run's context, where the toolset's http_request= and get_http_request= used to name it. A presenter can read it there to make a URL absolute, for example with request.build_absolute_uri, where host= named one; the kernel's presenters do not do this:

from django_spec_agents import AgentDeps

deps = AgentDeps(user=request.user)
deps.call_context["request"] = request
result = await agent.run(prompt, deps=deps)

docs.title: build_context becomes call_seeds
docs.text:
An override of build_context that varied the context per run becomes an override of call_seeds(*, ctx, tool_name), returning the call's own seeds, name to resolver. A view or request it returns replaces the call's own, a name the mount's pool_seeds registers too is refused with ValueError, and a seed for a read the spec declares, or for a read or parameter tool_server_arguments binds or withholds, is refused with ImproperlyConfigured:

from django_spec_agents.spec_tools import SpecToolset


class TenantToolset(SpecToolset):
    def call_seeds(self, *, ctx, tool_name):
        tenant = ctx.deps.tenant
        return {"tenant": lambda: tenant}

A view call_seeds returns is asked as it is. django-spec-rest's DRFPermissionCheck fills view.kwargs only on the view it builds when the call carries none, and only with the call's arguments its route_reads names. So a permission class reading a route capture finds none on a returned view whose kwargs the override left empty: one reading view.kwargs.get("project_pk") refuses, and one subscripting it raises KeyError. Return no view for such a spec, and name the capture in the check, DRFPermissionCheck([IsProjectMember], route_reads=["project_pk"]): the view it builds then carries the capture, and its action is the tool's name rather than a role the returned view set.

See per-call seeds and the run's context.

docs.title: Rendering and paging
docs.text:
• render_output(spec, result, *, ctx, projection, max_bytes) takes the kernel's DispatchResult and defaults to the kernel's present_for_audience. max_bytes, the tool's max_result_bytes, came in 0.26.0: an override with a closed signature adds it, or takes **kwargs and passes them to super(). The many, request, view and extras arguments are gone; an override that wants the unprojected payload calls the kernel's present(spec, result).
  • output_extras is gone, and with it the page, result and instance keys an output-context provider was handed. A presenter that batches lookups over the rendered page overrides the kernel's Presenter.presented_rows(values, context) instead, which the toolset calls once per page served, with that page's rows (a presenter that needs the whole page).
  • shape_page(rows, *, ctx, page, limit, max_page_size) returns the kernel's OutputPage, from django_service_specs. A subclass of another library's page type subclasses that one.
  • is_tool_listed(name, ctx) is unchanged: the seam for a per-run catalog, such as hiding a staff-only tool from a non-staff run. Hiding a tool grants nothing: the spec's permissions are asked on every call, whatever it returns.

docs.title: Other changes
docs.text:
• json_schema_registry= is gone. A field's schema is whatever the spec compiles for it; describe it on the spec.
  • The default id of SpecToolset and SpecCapability is spec-tools, where it was drf-specs. Pass id="drf-specs" to keep anything keyed on it.
  • A call is answered by the kernel's refusals only. Django REST Framework's PermissionDenied and ValidationError raised inside a callable escape the call unchanged; raise the kernel's NotPermitted and ServiceValidationError instead.

The full list is the changelog.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text: Two orthogonal concerns ride the Pydantic-AI capability seam: an audit trail over every tool call, and an approval gate for destructive ones. Both are off by default.

docs.title: Audit
docs.text:
Set an audit_logger on the config and build_agent composes an AuditCapability:

from django_spec_agents import AgentConfig, LoggingAuditLogger, build_agent

agent = build_agent(registry, AgentConfig(model=..., audit_logger=LoggingAuditLogger()))

It hooks pydantic-ai's tool execution itself, which is the point: it times and records every tool the agent runs, not just the ones in the registry — MCP and spec-toolset bridges, attachment tools, everything. A per-tool wrapper would miss the composed toolsets.

NullAuditLogger is the no-op default; build_agent skips composition entirely when the logger is null, so "auditing off" costs nothing.

docs.title: What lands in a record
docs.text:
AuditEvent carries tool_name, arguments_repr, duration_ms, success, and optional error / result_size.

There is one record per tool execution, and it describes the tool's own execution, whatever other capabilities sort ahead of audit, which is everything composed through AgentConfig.capabilities unless its own ordering places it inside audit, and on every supported pydantic-ai release:

  • arguments_repr holds the arguments the tool received, after every other capability's before_tool_execute has rewritten them.
  • success and error describe what the tool did. error reads Type: message for the exception the tool raised, before anything converts it or recovers from it.
  • result_size is the length of the tool's own result, before any after_tool_execute rewrites it.
  • duration_ms spans the tool alone: from after every other capability's before_tool_execute to before any on_tool_execute_error or after_tool_execute. Time spent in other capabilities' hooks is not in it.

A capability that sorts after audit, such as an innermost one passed to a single run, is outside that promise. It runs between audit and the tool, so what it does can reach the record, on every pydantic-ai release and through any of its hooks, and the record is then not the tool's own. A capability that sorts after audit says when a capability sorts there and gives measured examples of what it changes.

A failure is recorded as the failure, whatever a capability ahead of audit does with it next. The failure policy turns a tool's exception into a ToolFailed for the model, redacted unless include_detail is set; the record still names the exception the tool raised, because this is the operator's copy. A capability whose on_tool_execute_error returns a value in the exception's place has decided what the run does next, not what the tool did, so that failure is recorded as a failure too. One that sorts after audit is the exception: a recovery in its error hook is recorded as a success, and so is one in its wrapper when the tool raised ModelRetry or ToolFailed.

On an ordinary call two exceptions never reach any capability's error hook, and are recorded as they propagate. A ToolFailed that a tool raises itself is converted by pydantic-ai into a ToolFailedError carrying the same message, so raise ToolFailed("model copy") from e is recorded as ToolFailedError: model copy, and the policy is never handed it. The MCP bridge's refusals arrive the same way. A ModelRetry is recorded as ToolRetryError: <message>, and the retried call gets a record of its own. From a code-mode sandbox, whose nested tool manager converts neither, both are recorded as raised: ToolFailed: model copy and ModelRetry: <message>.

Once a tool's retry budget is spent, its ModelRetry is recorded differently. On an ordinary call pydantic-ai raises UnexpectedModelBehavior in its place, from inside the call, so it does reach the error hooks: the record reads UnexpectedModelBehavior: Tool '<name>' exceeded max retries count of <n>..., and the failure policy converts it into a failed result like any other exception.

A ToolFailed keeps its own message, cause or not, because whoever raised it chose that message as the outcome: a tool, or a toolset such as the spec bridge. Its cause can say less than the message does: a spec tool's timeout names the limit in the message, while the asyncio timeout it is raised from has no text at all. Neither an exception's cause nor its context is read into the record. A tool's own ToolFailed is recorded as "ToolFailedError: <message>", or as "ToolFailed: <message>" when it is called from a code-mode sandbox.

A call that never runs the tool produces no record. Two things mark one:

  • It stopped before audit's before_tool_execute, with any exception: a veto, a ModelRetry asking for different arguments, or an error.
  • Its outcome is one pydantic-ai treats as not executed: a SkipToolExecution veto, or a CallDeferred or ApprovalRequired deferral, wherever it was raised. A tool can raise either deferral itself, and a toolset can raise one for it, as pydantic-ai's FunctionToolset.approval_required() does.

So neither a call pydantic-ai-harness's guardrails or tool-call judge veto, nor a destructive call the gate holds for approval, nor any other call deferred for approval has a record. The approved call is recorded when it is resumed and runs, like any other. A call deferred to external execution never runs in this process, so it has no record here: the record belongs to whatever executes it, as a record of what was refused belongs to whatever refused it.

Audit never changes what the run sees. Its error hook re-raises what it is handed, and a sink that raises is caught and logged to the django_pydantic_agent.audit logger, costing the record rather than the run.

Arguments are stored as a string (typically JSON-encoded), deliberately: it keeps records cheap to serialize and discourages retaining raw sensitive values.

organization_id and target_type exist on the shape but are None at this layer — tool arguments are domain-opaque here. A custom AuditLogger fills them from its own tenancy and domain model.

docs.title: The run-level record
docs.text:
One record isn't a tool call: when a client disconnects mid-run, the transport records tool_name="agent.run" with success=False and an error starting "cancelled:". That keeps cancelled runs distinguishable in an audit sink without widening the AuditLogger protocol to carry a second event shape.

Write your own sink by implementing AuditLogger — a database table, a log-shipping pipeline, whatever your compliance story needs.

docs.title: The destructive-tool gate
docs.text:
Pydantic-AI supplies the mechanism: a tool whose definition is kind="unapproved" defers to an interrupt the client approves or denies. ToolGuard supplies the policy — at prepare_tools time it flips a plain function tool to unapproved when the tool is destructive, so server-side tools get the same confirmation gate a web component already applies to client-registered ones.

from django_spec_agents import AgentConfig, ToolGuardConfig

config = AgentConfig(
    model=...,
    tool_guard=ToolGuardConfig(
        enabled=True,
        exempt=frozenset({"send_receipt"}),
        require_approval=frozenset({"export_report"}),
    ),
)

Off by default. ToolGuardConfig.enabled is False, so the gate never surprises a project that hasn't opted in.

docs.title: How a tool is judged destructive
docs.text:
When enabled, a tool is gated unless its name is in exempt, and it is gated when either it is destructive or its name is in require_approval. exempt wins over require_approval.

A tool marked with SELF_GATED_METADATA_KEY asks for approval from its own body, with a card built from the call, as the routine writes do. The guard never flips it, so naming it in require_approval cannot replace its card with a generic one, and exempt cannot waive it; requires_approval answers True for it.

Destructiveness is unified from every vocabulary a toolset declares it in, so one hook covers every tool regardless of origin:

  • Registry tools — @tool(destructive=True). The flag lives on the spec and never reaches pydantic-ai as a bare callable, so the guard reads it from the registry directly at construction.
  • MCP bridged tools — the bridge maps each tool's annotations onto DESTRUCTIVE_METADATA_KEY, which the guard reads from pydantic-ai's tool metadata. A tool is marked unless its readOnlyHint is true or its destructiveHint is false, as MCP reads the pair; a tool listed with no annotations is not marked.
  • MCP tool annotations — metadata["annotations"], read by the bridge's own rule: annotations that say anything mark the tool destructive unless readOnlyHint is true or destructiveHint is false. A field that is None is unsaid, so the full dump a remote MCP client stores (every field present, the ones the server never sent None) reads as the plain dict does, and annotations that say nothing at all, {} or all None, mark nothing. It is how a toolset speaking MCP's own vocabulary says it mutates: a ServiceSpec exposed through SpecToolset writes readOnlyHint: False, and a remote server's tools arrive with its annotations. Without this the same spec would be gated over an MCP bridge and ungated attached in process, so a transport swap would remove the gate silently.
  • The x-destructive schema stamp at the root of parameters_json_schema, which is what build_input_schema writes. A project deriving a schema with that helper and attaching the tool through toolsets= gets the gate from it.
  • require_approval — an explicit opt-in for anything the rest miss.

A hint has to say something. Annotations that say nothing, an absent stamp, or metadata of some other shape entirely leave the tool alone — silence is not a claim, and require_approval is the answer for a tool whose source declares nothing. Annotations that say anything are read by MCP's defaults, as the bridge reads them.

DESTRUCTIVE_METADATA_KEY still rides tool metadata rather than only the schema, because metadata is the channel a bridge controls and the schema is the tool author's; the guard reads both, and a client reads the schema alone.

docs.title: What is gated, and what is not
docs.text:
Worth stating plainly, because a system prompt that promises a confirmation the server does not perform is worse than no promise at all:

  • With no tool_guard — the stock configuration — every server-side tool runs the moment the model calls it. There is no interrupt and no card.
  • With tool_guard enabled, a tool is gated when the registry, its metadata, its schema or require_approval says so, and not otherwise.
  • The browser's own confirmation card is a separate path: it reads a client-registered tool's parameters, so it never sees a tool that executes server-side. Neither path substitutes for the other.

A spec's confirmation is not an approval gate

The only human gate on a server-side tool is ToolGuard. Three ways a deployment ends up without the gate it assumes:
