  • It is off by default. A deployment that never sets ToolGuardConfig(enabled=True) has no approval gate on any tool.
  • exempt wins over require_approval. A name in both is never gated, and exempting a tool removes the human from its calls altogether.
  • A confirmation written into a spec is not a substitute. A spec that asks for confirmation by raising AdditionalInputRequired reaches the agent as an input_required result, because neither bridge can ask the caller mid-call; both turn it into a ModelRetry that tells the model to call the tool again with the missing argument (a confirmed flag, say). The model can supply that itself on the next turn. On a page that confirmation is a prompt for a person; on the agent route it is a retry, not a security boundary. An operation that needs a human decision belongs in require_approval. A bridged mutation is gated by default while the guard is enabled, but only until its name is in exempt or a registration overrides the annotation with readOnlyHint: True or destructiveHint: False.

docs.title: Answering a gated call in the run
docs.text:
A gated call ends the run and waits for a person, unless an in-run answerer approves it first. Two answerers ship, both on pydantic-ai's handle_deferred_tool_calls; the guard still gates the call, and the answerer only answers it:

  • GrantedApprovals(names, answered_by) approves a fixed grant. A routine's firing spec can pass GrantedApprovals(preapproved_exempt(routine), f"routine:{routine.pk}"): only the tools that were gated when granted, so a tool declared destructive since parks.
  • ReviewedApprovals, composed from AgentConfig.approval_reviewer, asks a second model, through pydantic-ai-harness's ApprovalReviewer (the [harness] extra), a yes/no risk question about each call. no approves the call, marked reviewer:<model>; yes, unsure and a failed review leave it for the person.
from django_spec_agents import AgentConfig, ApprovalReviewerConfig, ToolGuardConfig

config = AgentConfig(
    model=...,
    tool_guard=ToolGuardConfig(enabled=True),
    approval_reviewer=ApprovalReviewerConfig(
        model="anthropic:claude-haiku-5-5",
        question="Could this destroy data, spend money, or leak secrets?",
        tools=["archive_order", "send_receipt"],
    ),
)

tools names the tools the reviewer answers for, or is "all": every approval request, including those a ToolGuardrail or ToolCallJudge raises and tools added later, all under the one question. Name the tools the question was written for. The mark is the model string as given, or system:model_name for a Model instance.

A grant answers before the reviewer, whatever order the capabilities are listed in, so a granted call costs no review; a project's own HandleDeferredToolCalls answers after both.

Never answered in the run. The tools in NEVER_AUTO_APPROVED, create_routine, update_routine, pause_routine and the skill-authoring tools (create_skill, update_skill, disable_skill, enable_skill), park for the person under a name list, under "all" and in a grant: their approval card is the grant itself.

Who answered is recorded. Each answerer sets DeferredToolResults.answered_by and metadata[id]["answered_by"]. build_agent always composes AnsweredByMetadata, which copies the mark onto the call's ToolReturnPart.metadata, merged into a tool's own dict metadata such as an MCP Apps record. AuditEvent.answered_by carries it for the call that ran, and LoggingAuditLogger writes it as answered_by=. A project's own answerer gets both by setting the same metadata key, ANSWERED_BY_KEY.

A reviewer approves destructive calls in the person's place

The family's rule is that a destructive call runs only once a person approves it on its card. Listing a tool for the reviewer, or choosing "all", departs from that rule: a model's no runs the call, and no person sees it. The reviewer never denies, so every call it does not clear still reaches the person, and the audit record names the reviewer for every call it cleared. It is a filter on what a person is asked, not a security boundary: a tool that destroys data, spends money or exposes secrets still needs its own authorization.

docs.title: What a raising tool costs
docs.text:
Without a policy, a tool that raises ends the run. The transport emits RUN_ERROR, the turn stops, and everything the model had already produced goes with it — along with the results of every other tool in the same round. One broken integration costs the whole answer.

ToolFailurePolicy changes what the failure stops, and nothing else. The call comes back to the model marked failed, naming the tool, and the run carries on:

config = AgentConfig(model="openai:gpt-4o")  # on by default

Turn it off so a raising tool ends the run again, or opt into detail:

from django_spec_agents import ToolFailureConfig

AgentConfig(model=..., tool_failure=ToolFailureConfig(enabled=False))
AgentConfig(model=..., tool_failure=ToolFailureConfig(include_detail=True))

include_detail is off by default, and the split is deliberate. Whether the run survives is a reliability question; whether the exception's text reaches the model is a disclosure one. A traceback message can carry a query, a path or a credential, and anything handed to the model is also handed to whatever renders the transcript. The policy never redacts the operator's copy. Audit records the exception it is handed in full (what lands in a record), unless a capability sorts after audit and changes it, and whenever the policy converts a failure it first logs the exception, with its traceback, to the django_pydantic_agent.failure logger. That logger hears only about the failures the policy converts: nothing when another capability recovered the call or answered for the model with its own ModelRetry or ToolFailed, when an authorization refusal passes through, or when the exception never reached the error hooks at all, as a tool's own ToolFailed does not, nor its ModelRetry while it has retries left. A tool's ModelRetry with no retries left does reach them, as UnexpectedModelBehavior, so the policy converts it and logs it.

Three things worth knowing:

  • It hangs off on_tool_execute_error, not a try around the handler. Pydantic-AI does not route control-flow exceptions to that hook — SkipToolExecution, CallDeferred, ApprovalRequired, the ModelRetry retry signal, or an explicit ToolFailed. So the approval gate above passes through untouched, and so does a ModelRetry while the tool has retries left. A hand-written except Exception would have caught ApprovalRequired and silently disabled the gate. The policy neither spends nor grants retries, but it does change what happens when a tool's own budget runs out: pydantic-ai raises UnexpectedModelBehavior in the last ModelRetry's place from inside the call, which is routed to that hook, so the policy converts it like any other failure. The run continues with a failed result where without the policy it would end. A capability's ModelRetry is different: pydantic-ai checks its budget after every error hook has run, outside the policy's reach, so it still ends the run when the budget is spent.
  • It converts last. It is pinned outermost and build_agent places it first, so its on_tool_execute_error runs after every other capability's (see ordering). Every other error hook is handed the exception the tool raised, never the policy's redacted copy: a step recorder such as pydantic-ai-harness's StepPersistence logs the real failure, and a capability that recovers by returning a value answers before anything is converted. An earlier error hook that raises ModelRetry or ToolFailed in the exception's place has answered for the model, so that passes through unconverted. A ModelRetry passed through spends the tool's retry budget, and once that is spent the run ends with UnexpectedModelBehavior, which pydantic-ai raises after every error hook has run, so the policy never sees it. That is the opposite of a tool's own ModelRetry, above.
  • It spends no retry budget, because ToolFailed deliberately doesn't. A model can call a persistently broken tool again; bound that with run-level UsageLimits rather than expecting this to stop it.

docs.title: A tool that has spent its retries
docs.text:
A tool that keeps raising ModelRetry is told to try again until its retry budget (AgentConfig.retries) is spent. Without the policy the next ModelRetry ends the run with UnexpectedModelBehavior. With it, that exception is converted: the model gets a failed result, the run continues, audit and the django_pydantic_agent.failure logger record UnexpectedModelBehavior, and the model is free to call the tool again.

That default has a cost. The tool keeps executing on later calls, so any side effect it has repeats after its budget is spent. Two things bound it: the model taking the failed result's "do not retry" at its word (with include_detail off; with it on, the model gets the exception text and no such instruction), and pydantic-ai's default request limit, which ends a run that keeps calling. Set run-level UsageLimits when a tool's side effects matter.

To have a spent budget end the run, name the exception in reraise:

from django.core.exceptions import PermissionDenied as DjangoPermissionDenied
from django_service_specs import NotPermitted, PrincipalUnavailable
from pydantic_ai.exceptions import UnexpectedModelBehavior

AgentConfig(
    model=...,
    tool_failure=ToolFailureConfig(
        reraise=(
            UnexpectedModelBehavior,
            DjangoPermissionDenied,
            NotPermitted,
            PrincipalUnavailable,
        ),
    ),
)

The example re-lists every denial the default set holds, so it assumes the kernel is installed. Leave out the ones your project cannot raise, and add the refusal class of any other stack your own tools call.

Two caveats:

  • reraise replaces the default set, it does not extend it. The default is django.core.exceptions.PermissionDenied, and NotPermitted and PrincipalUnavailable from django_service_specs when the kernel is installed (the [specs] or [mcp] extra) (a denial is not a tool failure). A tuple that leaves them out converts denials again, so re-list each one your project can raise.
  • It ends the run for every UnexpectedModelBehavior a tool raises, not only for its own spent budget: a tool that lets a sub-agent's exhausted budget propagate ends the run too. The two cannot be told apart by type or __cause__: both are UnexpectedModelBehavior with a ModelRetry cause.

docs.title: A denial is not a tool failure
docs.text:
An authorization refusal passes through untouched and ends the run, exactly as it would with the policy off. Three classes are in the default set, because Django's and the kernel's are unrelated:

  • django.core.exceptions.PermissionDenied, always. The MCP bridge raises it for a permission refusing the user (JSON-RPC -32006).
  • django_service_specs.NotPermitted, when the kernel is installed (the [specs] or [mcp] extra); the kernel's dispatch raises it when a permission check refuses the principal.
  • django_service_specs.PrincipalUnavailable, with it; the kernel raises it for a principal that cannot act at all, such as a deactivated account.

Converting one would leave the run alive with the model free to try the next row, and a converted denial stays distinguishable from a missing row. A sweep over ids therefore turns the permission boundary into an existence oracle over rows the acting user cannot read — inside a single turn, spending no retry budget, bounded by nothing build_agent sets.

A tool of your own that calls into another stack may raise that stack's refusal class, which is in none of the above. Name it in reraise=, with the three above, to keep it exempt.

A missing row and a converted denial share an outcome — both are failed — so the two are not told apart by the result's shape. They are still told apart by its words: one says the row is not there and the other says the tool failed. An oracle needs one bit, and a message is a place to find one.

The set is a project decision:

ToolFailureConfig(reraise=())  # convert everything, denials included
ToolFailureConfig(reraise=(PermissionDenied, LookupError))

docs.title: A run that loops
docs.text:
AgentConfig.loop_detection composes pydantic-ai-harness's DetectLoops (the [harness] extra), which watches the run for the same tool call made again and again, the same call returning the same result, two calls in turn, and the same text answered over and over, and checks each streamed response for a passage that keeps repeating.

from django_spec_agents import AgentConfig, LoopDetectionConfig

config = AgentConfig(model=..., loop_detection=LoopDetectionConfig(action="error"))

action decides what a loop costs:

  • "nudge", the default, tells the model which loop it is in and asks it to change its approach. The run carries on, so a model that ignores the nudge still needs a usage limit or a spend limit to stop it.
  • "error" ends the run with LoopDetectedError, an AgentRunError, so it ends the way any run that raises does. A child session reports it to its parent as failed, its text naming the loop: The run was stopped in a loop (<pattern>): and the loop's description, with the tools involved.

Each threshold is how many repeats make a loop: repeated_call_threshold (5) the same call within the last window (10) calls, repeated_result_threshold (3) the same call returning the same result, alternating_calls_threshold (3) A-B cycles, and repeated_text_threshold (3) responses with the same text and no tool call. None turns that check off. A tool polled on purpose with unchanging arguments is a loop to these checks, so raise or turn off the thresholds it trips. stream_checks=False drops the checks within a response.

docs.title: Spend limits
docs.text:
AgentConfig.spend_limits composes pydantic-ai-harness's SpendLimits (the [harness] extra). Each response's price is added to every budget's counter, and once a counter is spent the next model request is refused with SpendLimitExceeded.

from decimal import Decimal

from django_spec_agents import AgentConfig, SpendBudget, SpendLimitsConfig
from django_spec_agents.contrib.store.default_spend_store import DefaultSpendStore

spend_store = DefaultSpendStore()  # built once, shared by every run

config = AgentConfig(
    model=...,
    spend_limits=SpendLimitsConfig(
        store=spend_store,
        budgets=[
            SpendBudget("run", usd=Decimal("1"), window="run"),
            SpendBudget("user_day", usd=Decimal("5"), window="day", per_user=True),
            SpendBudget("mount_month", usd=Decimal("500"), window="month", warn_at=0.8),
        ],
    ),
)

A budget's window is one run, one conversation, a UTC day or month, or the total. per_user counts each acting user (AgentDeps.user) apart; every run with no authenticated user shares one anonymous counter. Without it, the whole mount shares one counter, as long as the same store holds it. A budget with neither usd nor tokens only counts.

SpendLimitExceeded subclasses UsageLimitExceeded, so a tripped spend limit ends a run the way a usage limit does: a child session reports it as budget. The request that crosses the line completes, and concurrent runs can each find a budget unspent and pass it together, so a ceiling bounds spend rather than capping it exactly.

A response is priced from the genai-prices registry. price prices it first, for a self-hosted model or a negotiated rate; return None to fall through to the registry. A model the registry does not know costs nothing in dollars unless price covers it.

The store is a harness BatchSpendStore. DefaultSpendStore keeps the counters in the store app's tables, so every worker on the database enforces one budget (see Storage). The harness's InMemorySpendStore counts each process on its own.

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
Each capability here declares its own place through get_ordering(), and pydantic-ai's CombinedCapability sorts them topologically, with list order breaking ties within a tier. Add your own to AgentConfig.capabilities in any order; build_agent positions its own around them.

  • Audit is innermost, the capability closest to the tool: its before_tool_execute runs last, and its on_tool_execute_error and after_tool_execute run first. build_agent appends it after config.capabilities, which keeps it inside other innermost capabilities too, such as pydantic-ai-harness's guardrail and tool-call judge, so the record carries the arguments after their rewrites and a call they veto never reaches audit's before_tool_execute.
  • The failure policy is outermost, and build_agent places it first, which keeps it outside other outermost capabilities. pydantic-ai runs error hooks innermost first, so the policy's runs last.
  • The guard is orthogonal. It touches only prepare_tools, before any call is made.

Composing these by hand rather than through build_agent, keep the same places: AuditCapability after any other innermost capability, and ToolFailurePolicy before any other outermost one.

docs.title: A capability that sorts after audit
docs.text:
A capability that sorts after audit runs between audit and the tool. Three compositions put one there, whatever build_agent did:

  • an innermost capability passed to a single run, as in agent.run(..., capabilities=[...]), which pydantic-ai sorts after the agent's own capabilities;
  • an innermost capability composed by hand after audit;
  • a capability whose own ordering places it inside audit, wherever it is composed, AgentConfig.capabilities included, as CapabilityOrdering(position="innermost", wrapped_by=[AuditCapability]) does.

The rule: what such a capability does can reach the record, through any of its hooks, and the record is then not the tool's own. The examples below were measured with real agent runs; they are examples, not a list of the only ways.

  • Through its before_tool_execute, on_tool_execute_error and after_tool_execute. A record misses its argument rewrite; records a ModelRetry its before_tool_execute raises as a failure, though the tool never ran; records its recovery as a success, measuring the recovered value, and an exception it raises in place of the tool's; records a ModelRetry its after_tool_execute raises as a failure, though the tool succeeded; measures its result rewrite; and times its hooks with the tool.
  • Through its wrap_tool_execute, when the tool raised ModelRetry or ToolFailed. pydantic-ai routes both past every error and result hook, audit's included, so the record is whatever this wrapper hands back. A record carries its rewrite of the failure's message, as pydantic-ai-harness's result_guard does; records its recovery as a success; and records an exception it raises in their place. If it runs the tool again, the record describes the later run alone, and the run that failed has none; if a capability ahead of audit refuses that rerun, the record pairs the first run's arguments with the refusal, timed across both.
  • A rerun by its wrap_tool_execute after a failure audit's error hook saw, or after a success. Audit's own hook settled the first run, so the tool gets one record, of that run. Reruns it makes concurrently, as through asyncio.gather, share one record, which can pair one run's arguments with another's result.

A veto it raises is still not recorded, because a SkipToolExecution is a call that did not execute.

Everything composed through AgentConfig.capabilities is unaffected, unless its own ordering places it inside audit. build_agent appends audit after all of it, so audit sorts last among the innermost capabilities there, and the record is the tool's own. pydantic-ai-harness's tool guardrail and tool-call judge are innermost: in config.capabilities they sort before audit, and passed to a single run they sort after it. There, a guardrail's retry verdict is recorded as a failure, a retry from its result_guard turns the tool's success into a failure, and its result_guard's replace is what the record measures. Its result_guard also screens the message of a tool that raised ModelRetry or ToolFailed, from its wrapper, so a replace there is the message the record names.

docs.title: Why audit needs all four hooks
docs.text:
pydantic-ai runs every capability's before_tool_execute, on_tool_execute_error and after_tool_execute inside the wrap_tool_execute chain. A wrapper that recorded only what it saw would therefore record a failure another capability recovers from as a success, a vetoed call as a failure, the arguments before a rewrite and the result after one, and other capabilities' hooks in the duration.

For everything that sorts ahead of it, audit records the tool's own outcome, because it observes the tool from all four hooks. Its before_tool_execute captures the arguments and the start, its on_tool_execute_error the tool's exception, and its after_tool_execute the tool's result. Its wrapper is the only one that writes the record, once per execution, as it exits, preferring what the hooks captured over what it saw itself. The wrapper encloses every hook, and the captures are what keep the record the tool's. The arguments and the start come from before_tool_execute alone: the wrapper takes neither, because a call that never reached that hook never ran the tool and is not recorded. Each call's captures belong to that call, so parallel calls in one run and concurrent runs of one agent never read each other's, nor does a tool that runs another agent composed with the same capability, nor does a code-mode script that calls tools inline. Reruns that a capability sorted after audit makes concurrently, inside one call, are one call to audit, and share its captures.

Full signatures in the policy reference.

docs.title: Routines
docs.text:
A routine is a stored prompt for one agent, a schedule, and the user it runs as: "every weekday at 8, run /what-is-on and tell me what is overdue". The package gives you the model's fields, a policy protocol, the schedule vocabulary, the next-firing computation, and the functions that write a routine. You bring the concrete model, its tenant relation, its migration and the policy. No concrete routine model ships in the package, and no default policy.

This page covers the storage, the rules, the sweep that fires a routine on schedule and the spec each firing runs. Showing a firing's thread is the transport's.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
Subclass AbstractRoutine and add whatever scopes a routine in your project:

from django.db import models

from django_spec_agents.routines import AbstractRoutine, RoutinePolicy


class Routine(AbstractRoutine):
    team = models.ForeignKey("teams.Team", on_delete=models.CASCADE)

    @classmethod
    def routine_policy(cls) -> RoutinePolicy["Routine"]:
        return OwnRoutinesPolicy()


class OwnRoutinesPolicy:
    def visible(self, request):
        return Routine.objects.filter(principal=request.user)

    def can_write(self, request, routine):
        return routine.principal_id == request.user.pk

    def can_run(self, principal, routine):
        return principal.is_active and routine.team.members.filter(pk=principal.pk).exists()

    def new_routine(self, request):
        return Routine(team=request.user.team)
Field Meaning name What the person calls it, at most 120 characters agent_id The agent the routine runs prompt The message each firing sends, at most 20,000 characters schedule The schedule, as the JSON schedule_to_json writes; read it with get_schedule() timezone The IANA zone the schedule's wall times are read in; get_timezone() loads it principal The user each firing runs as: always the user who created the routine enabled, paused_reason Off means it does not fire; a pause by the system says why preapproved_tools The tools a firing may call without parking, each with its pinned flag next_fire_at The next firing, in UTC, indexed; None while the routine is disabled last_run_id The queue's run id for the last firing last_thread_id The thread the last firing ran into created_by, created_at, updated_at Who wrote it, and when

docs.title: The policy
docs.text:
RoutinePolicy is four methods:

  • visible(request) returns every routine the caller may see, disabled ones too.
  • can_write(request, routine) decides whether the caller may save routine, a new unsaved one or an existing row.
  • can_run(principal, routine) decides whether routine may fire now as its principal. A firing has no request, so it is asked with the user alone.
  • new_routine(request) returns the unsaved routine a create writes to, with its scope already set.

docs.title: The schedule
docs.text:
The vocabulary is closed, and there are no cron strings:

  • WeeklySchedule(weekdays, at) fires on each weekday (0 is Monday, 6 is Sunday) at the wall time at, to the minute, in the routine's timezone.
  • IntervalSchedule(every_hours) fires every N hours of elapsed time, whatever the timezone's clock changes do. An interval shorter than MIN_ROUTINE_INTERVAL, an hour, or longer than MAX_ROUTINE_INTERVAL, 366 days, is refused.

parse_schedule(data) reads a schedule from its JSON, {"kind": "weekly", "weekdays": [0, 1, 2, 3, 4], "at": "08:00"} or {"kind": "interval", "every_hours": 6}, and raises InvalidRoutineError for anything else. schedule_to_json writes it back.

next_fire_at(schedule, timezone, after) returns the first firing strictly after after, in UTC. A weekly wall time a DST change skips fires shifted by the gap, so 02:30 on a spring-forward night fires at 03:30. A wall time it repeats fires once, at its first occurrence. An interval adds its hours to after, so pass the firing just claimed rather than the clock, or every late sweep pushes the cadence later.

docs.title: Writing
docs.text:
from datetime import time

from django_spec_agents.routines import RoutineDraft, WeeklySchedule, create_routine

policy = Routine.routine_policy()
create_routine(
    policy,
    request,
    RoutineDraft(
        name="Overdue digest",
        agent_id="assistant",
        prompt="/what-is-on: tell me what is overdue",
        schedule=WeeklySchedule(weekdays=frozenset(range(5)), at=time(8, 0)),
        timezone="Europe/London",
        preapproved_tools=("archive_invoice",),
    ),
    guard=agent_guard,
    tool_defs=agent_tool_defs,
)
  • create_routine makes the caller the principal and created_by, and refuses an anonymous caller with RoutineWriteRefusedError. It raises InvalidRoutineError once the caller holds MAX_ROUTINES_PER_USER (25) routines, counted on the model by principal, disabled ones included. The count is read before the insert, so two creates racing at the cap can both pass it; a host that needs a hard cap holds a lock around the call.
  • update_routine replaces the fields but never the principal, whoever edits. next_fire_at moves only when the schedule, the timezone or enabled changes, so an edit to the prompt keeps an interval's cadence. An enabled routine carries no paused_reason, so turning one back on clears it.
  • Both ask can_write, and raise RoutineWriteRefusedError when the policy refuses. An update asks twice, once about the row as stored and once about the result, and a refusal leaves the instance it was given as it was. A blank name, agent or prompt, an oversized one, and a timezone zoneinfo cannot load raise InvalidRoutineError.

docs.title: Letting the agent write routines
docs.text:
authoring_toolset(policy, request, *, agent_id, guard) gives a conversation's agent four tools over the caller's own routines. Build it per request, with the mount's agent id and the ToolGuard the agent runs with, and pass it in the run's toolsets:

from django_spec_agents.routines import authoring_toolset

toolset = authoring_toolset(
    Routine.routine_policy(), request, agent_id="assistant", guard=agent_guard
)
  • list_routines lists the routines the policy shows the caller whose principal is the caller, disabled ones too: a teammate's routine the policy happens to show is left out. It asks nobody.
  • create_routine, update_routine and pause_routine always ask the user first. The tool raises ApprovalRequired itself and is marked with SELF_GATED_METADATA_KEY, so the guard never flips it: its exempt cannot waive the card, nor can require_approval swap it for a generic one. All three are in NEVER_AUTO_APPROVED, so GrantedApprovals and ReviewedApprovals leave them to the person; a project's own HandleDeferredToolCalls answers whatever it is given, so it must skip these names too. An approval that edits the arguments writes nothing and tells the model to call again, so the edited routine gets a card of its own. The call's deferred metadata carries an x-confirm card naming the principal, the agent, the prompt, the schedule and timezone, whether the routine is enabled, and every pre-approved tool, a destructive one marked (destructive, runs unasked). A change to the grant is an update, so it gets the card.
  • The model never names a principal or an agent. A created routine runs as the caller on agent_id; an update or a pause reaches a routine by id only among the caller's own ones, and an update only one on agent_id, since its grant is pinned against this agent's tools. Every write still goes through can_write, and a refusal comes back to the model as text, before any card when it can be known then.
  • Each granted name is pinned through guard against the tools this run offers, leaving out client tools and these four, since a firing has neither. A broken draft, an unknown name or a schedule outside the vocabulary is sent back to the model as a retry, before the user sees a card.

Compose it into browser runs only. A routine's firing hides all four (ROUTINE_AUTHORING_TOOLS), whatever its mount offers, and a headless run has nobody to answer the card.

docs.title: Pre-approved tools
docs.text:
A routine's firings run with no one watching, so a gated tool call parks the thread unless the routine pre-approved the tool. The grant is made when the routine is created or edited, and that edit is where a person approves it.

The grant pins each tool's flag. pin_preapproved_tools(guard, tool_defs, names) asks the agent's ToolGuard.requires_approval about each named definition and records the answer as destructive. A name none of tool_defs carries raises InvalidRoutineError, so a typo is never recorded as a grant. create_routine and update_routine pin through it, checking every granted name against the agent's tools on each write. While the agent stays the same, an update keeps the flag already pinned for a tool the routine held, so an unrelated edit never re-approves a tool declared destructive since. Moving the routine to another agent pins every tool afresh against that agent's guard. A tool dropped from the list is revoked, and pins afresh if named again.

preapproved_exempt(routine) returns the names a firing's guard exempts: only the tools that were gated when granted. A tool granted while ungated and declared destructive later is not among them, so its call parks. Passed to GrantedApprovals with f"routine:{routine.pk}", the same names are approved in the run and each call's result and audit record carry the routine as answered_by.

docs.title: Firing due routines
docs.text:
The package ships no schedule of its own. Your project runs the run_due_routines management command every minute or so, from cron, a systemd timer or its task scheduler, and each run fires the routines that have come due since the last. It needs django_spec_agents in INSTALLED_APPS.

The command sweeps every installed routine model whose routine_sweep() returns a RoutineSweep; a model that keeps the default None is left alone:

from django_spec_agents.routines import AbstractRoutine, RoutineSweep


class Routine(AbstractRoutine):
    ...

    @classmethod
    def routine_sweep(cls) -> RoutineSweep:
        return RoutineSweep(queue=firing_queue, spec_name="run_routine")
  • queue is your FiringQueue, the same seam a queued headless run goes through, filled from django-spec-tasks or another task queue.
  • spec_name is the name your queue's registry holds the firing spec under. The sweep enqueues it as the routine's principal with {"routine_id": <pk>, "thread_id": <id>}, a fresh thread id per firing, which the spec runs into.
  • grace is how late a missed firing may still run. Leave it None for one schedule period, measured from the firing that was missed: a day for a daily routine, three days for a weekday routine's Friday firing.

due_routines(model, sweep, now=None, limit=100) is what the command calls, for a project that would rather call it from its own task. It claims the due rows in one query on the indexed next_fire_at, with select_for_update(skip_locked=True), and moves each to its next firing in the transaction that enqueues it. Two sweeps that overlap therefore fire a routine once: the second passes over the rows the first holds. Run it on a database that honours skip_locked, such as PostgreSQL; SQLite ignores the lock.

For each claimed routine, in this order:

The routine The sweep Its last firing lapsed: the worker died, or the principal or the spec went away Pauses it: enabled off, next_fire_at and last_run_id cleared, paused_reason naming the run It is later than its grace, say after downtime Skips it, logs it, and counts it as missed Its last firing is still pending, or its thread still waits (below) Skips it The policy's can_run refuses its principal Pauses it with that reason Otherwise Enqueues the firing with a fresh thread id, and stores the run id as last_run_id and the thread as last_thread_id

However late the sweep, next_fire_at moves to the first firing after now, stepped from the one claimed, so an outage fires a missed routine at most once and an interval keeps its cadence. A routine whose handling raises is rolled back, logged and left for the next sweep, and the others go on. The command prints one line per model, and due_routines returns the same counts as a SweepResult of primary keys.

docs.title: A firing parked on a person
docs.text:
A firing that reaches a gated tool it was not granted parks its thread until someone answers the approval card. Starting the next firing beside it would leave two threads waiting on the same question, so the sweep asks the model first:

from asgiref.sync import async_to_sync
from django.http import HttpRequest

from django_spec_agents import ThreadRunStatus
from django_spec_agents.contrib.store.default_run_store import DefaultRunStore


class Routine(AbstractRoutine):
    ...

    @classmethod
    def thread_waits(cls, thread_id, principal) -> bool:
        request = HttpRequest()
        request.user = principal
        state = async_to_sync(DefaultRunStore().get)(thread_id, request=request)
        return state is not None and state.status == ThreadRunStatus.WAITING

thread_waits(thread_id, principal) is asked about last_thread_id, as the routine's principal, and a True skips this firing. The hook is synchronous and the run store is async and scoped by the owner a request carries, so it builds a request for the principal and bridges the call. The default returns False, so a project that does not fill it fires on schedule whatever its last thread is doing.

docs.title: The firing spec
docs.text:
The sweep enqueues the firing; run_agent_spec is the kernel spec your queue's worker runs it with. It needs the [specs] extra, so import it from its module:

from django_spec_agents.routines.run_agent_spec import run_agent_spec

registry.register("run_routine", run_agent_spec(Routine, headless_runner, timeout=600.0))

Register it under the spec_name your RoutineSweep names. headless_runner is the transport's HeadlessRunner, and timeout is required: every firing's run has a deadline, in seconds.

The worker runs it as the routine's principal with the sweep's {"routine_id", "thread_id"}. Its permission check refuses a routine that does not exist, a caller who is not the routine's principal, and a routine your policy's can_run refuses. The queue asks it at enqueue and the worker again before the run, so a routine your policy stops allowing in between lapses the firing, and the next sweep pauses the routine.

It runs the routine's prompt on its agent, into the sweep's thread, one thread per firing, passing the runner routine_id=str(routine.pk), which the runner saves on the thread's conversation (Conversation.routine_id), so every firing's thread names its routine and not only the newest. It returns at the run's first stop, presenting {thread_id, run_id, outcome, waiting}:

outcome What happened completed The run ended with an answer waiting A gated call the routine did not pre-approve parked the thread; waiting lists each call it parked on timed_out The run passed timeout; what it produced is kept error The run failed, a refused tool call included

Each is a firing that ran, so the task ends SUCCEEDED whatever the outcome. A parked thread is resumed by a person on its approval card, never by the queue.

The run is composed with three things beside the mount's own:

  • GrantedApprovals over preapproved_exempt(routine), marked routine:<pk>. A pre-approved tool that was gated when granted runs in the same run without parking, and its result carries answered_by: "routine:<pk>". A tool granted ungated and declared destructive since is not among them, so its call parks. The approval is the only step it skips: the kernel's own authorization still runs, so a pre-approved spec tool the principal may not call is refused, and the run ends error.
  • The grant, recorded on the thread: the firing's first request carries, under ROUTINE_GRANT_KEY in its metadata, the routine's id, its last edit (updated_at), the answered_by mark and the pre-approved tools as granted, each with its pinned flag.
  • No routine-authoring tools: none of ROUTINE_AUTHORING_TOOLS (create_routine, update_routine, pause_routine, list_routines) is offered to a firing, whatever the agent's mount offers.

The spec declares atomic=False, so no transaction spans the run, and idempotent=False: a worker that dies mid-run is not run again, its firing reads lapsed, and the sweep pauses the routine.

docs.title: Finding the model, and refusing one with no policy at startup
docs.text:
There is no setting naming the routine model: the core reads no Django settings. Your code holds the model and its policy, and passes the policy to every function above and to whatever transport serves routines, as a constructor argument.

Add the package's opt-in app to INSTALLED_APPS, as for user skills. Its system check walks Django's app registry: every installed concrete model that subclasses AbstractRoutine must bring a policy, so manage.py check, runserver and migrate fail otherwise:

Id When django_spec_agents.E002 An installed AbstractRoutine subclass's routine_policy() returns None, which is AbstractRoutine's default

An abstract layer between AbstractRoutine and your model is not checked, because it has no table. Import django_spec_agents.routines once the app registry is ready, because it defines an abstract model.

docs.title: Timeouts and prompt caching
docs.text: Both are pydantic-ai features that an agent from build_agent takes as it is. A run's deadline goes on the run. The cache setting goes on the config.

docs.title: A run's deadline
docs.text:
pydantic-ai takes timeout= on each run (run, run_stream, run_stream_events, iter, and the UI adapters' run_stream / run_stream_native), not on the Agent, so build_agent has nothing to set. Whatever starts the run passes it:

from pydantic_ai.exceptions import RunTimedOut

try:
    result = await agent.run(prompt, deps=deps, timeout=120.0)
except RunTimedOut as error:
    partial = error.all_messages()

The timeout= covers the whole run: every model request, every tool call, and any agent run a tool starts, which inherits the deadline and can only shorten it. When the deadline passes, the run stops the way a cancel does. RunTimedOut subclasses RunCancelled, so catch it first if the two mean different things to you. It is also a TimeoutError. all_messages() holds what the run completed. A streamed run that times out mid-answer also keeps the text streamed so far, and you can resume from there.

The capabilities build_agent composes leave the timeout alone. Suppose the deadline passes while a tool is running. ToolFailurePolicy does not turn that into a failed tool call, and the run carrying on would be wrong. The run ends with RunTimedOut, and the policy logs nothing.

A tool can read the time it has left with ctx.deadline (a UTC datetime, or None when the run has none) or ctx.remaining_time() (seconds). For example, it can pass that time on to a slow call of its own.

Two limits apply to each model request rather than to the run, through model_settings:

AgentConfig(model=..., model_settings={"request_timeout": 30.0, "max_retries": 2})

request_timeout bounds one model request and max_retries sets how often the provider client retries it; pydantic-ai's ModelSettings reference has the exact semantics per provider.

docs.title: Testing a deadline
docs.text:
django_spec_agents.testing.slow_model(delay, chunks) is a model whose requests take delay seconds. The wait sits in the request, where a provider's wait is, and the double never raises TimeoutError itself. When streamed, every chunk but the last arrives before the wait. So a run that times out keeps those chunks as its partial answer, exactly as when a real provider's stream stalls:

import pytest
from pydantic_ai.exceptions import RunTimedOut
from django_spec_agents.testing import slow_model

agent = build_agent(registry, AgentConfig(model=slow_model(3600.0, ("partial ", "late"))))
with pytest.raises(RunTimedOut):
    await agent.run("go", deps=deps, timeout=0.1)

docs.title: Prompt caching
docs.text:
pydantic-ai's unified cache setting places the provider's cache breakpoints: on the tool definitions and static instructions, and on the growing conversation. You can turn it on through model_settings, or with the Caching capability:

from pydantic_ai.capabilities import Caching

AgentConfig(model=..., model_settings={"cache": True})
AgentConfig(model=..., capabilities=[Caching(retention="1h")])

It is off by default, because a cache write costs more than uncached input: 1.25x for a 5-minute cache, and 2x or more for longer ones. A cache read costs about 0.1x, so caching pays on a long session that re-sends the same prefix, which is what an admin chat does. A cached run's usage reports what it wrote and read, as cache_write_tokens and cache_read_tokens, for a provider that reports them.

The capabilities build_agent composes, AuditCapability, ToolGuard and ToolFailurePolicy, leave the tool definitions and instructions unchanged from one request to the next. So the cached prefix stays valid for the whole run.

With the [harness] extra, CodeMode (pydantic-ai-harness 0.63 and later; the extra's floor is 0.69) defaults to dynamic_catalog=True. Its catalog of sandboxed tools then goes into the instructions, and a newly discovered tool is appended to the history rather than rewriting run_code's description, so a discovery keeps the cache warm.

docs.title: User skills
docs.text:
A user skill is a named set of model instructions that a person writes and keeps in the database, rather than a SKILL.md file shipped with the code. The package gives you the model's fields, a policy protocol, and functions that read and write skills through that policy. You bring the concrete model, its tenant relation, its migration and the policy. No concrete skill model ships in the package, and no default policy.

This page covers the storage and the rules. Offering stored skills to the agent and to the browser's palette is a transport's job.

docs.title: The model
docs.text:
Subclass AbstractSkill and add whatever scopes a skill in your project. That can be an organisation, a workspace, or the user alone:

from django.conf import settings
from django.db import models
from django.db.models import F, Q

from django_spec_agents.skills import AbstractSkill, SkillPolicy


class Skill(AbstractSkill):
    owner = models.ForeignKey(
        settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, null=True, blank=True, on_delete=models.CASCADE
    )

    @classmethod
    def skill_policy(cls) -> SkillPolicy["Skill"]:
        return PersonalFirstPolicy()


class PersonalFirstPolicy:
    def visible(self, request):
        return Skill.objects.filter(Q(owner=request.user) | Q(owner=None)).order_by(
            F("owner").asc(nulls_last=True), "pk"
        )

    def can_write(self, request, skill):
        if skill.owner_id is None:
            return request.user.is_staff
        return skill.owner_id == request.user.pk

    def new_skill(self, request):
        return Skill(owner=None if request.user.is_staff else request.user)

AbstractSkill holds the fields every consumer needs:

Field Meaning name The kebab-case /token the palette and the agent share, at most 64 characters description What the skill is for, at most 1024 characters body The instructions, at most 20,000 characters user_invocable Whether a person may pick it; SKILL.md's user-invocable model_invocable Whether the model may load it; the negation of SKILL.md's disable-model-invocation enabled Off means it neither shows nor shadows created_by, created_at, updated_at Who wrote it, and when

The package puts no uniqueness constraint on name, because two scopes may each hold a skill of the same name. Add the constraint that fits your scopes, such as one name per owner.

docs.title: The policy
docs.text:
SkillPolicy is three methods, and every function below goes through them:

  • visible(request) returns every skill the caller may see, disabled ones too, in precedence order. The first skill of a name wins, so ordering personal skills before company ones lets a personal skill shadow a company one.
  • can_write(request, skill) decides whether the caller may save skill, which is either a new unsaved one or an existing row.
  • new_skill(request) returns the unsaved skill a create writes to, with its scope already set.

docs.title: Reserving the names of code-registered skills
docs.text:
A stored skill shares its /token with skills registered in code, such as a transport's own. To keep a stored skill from taking one of those names, give the policy a fourth method, reserved_names(request), which returns the names no stored skill may take. A policy that has it satisfies ReservedSkillNames:

class TenantSkillPolicy:
    ...

    def reserved_names(self, request):
        return {"summarize", "translate"}

create_skill, import_skill_md and a rename through update_skill then raise InvalidSkillError for a reserved name, so the skill tools and an editor endpoint refuse it the same way. A skill that already holds a name reserved since it was stored can still be edited. A policy without the method reserves nothing, and the bundled create-skill is never reserved, so a stored skill may shadow it.

docs.title: Scanning what users write
docs.text:
A skill's description and body are text a user wrote that reaches the model. To check them for prompt injection, credential exfiltration, hidden HTML comments and invisible characters, give the policy a scanner attribute holding pydantic-ai-harness's ArtifactScanner. A policy that has it satisfies SkillScanning:

from pydantic_ai_harness import ArtifactScanner


class TenantSkillPolicy:
    scanner = ArtifactScanner()
    ...

The scanner comes with the [harness] extra (pip install "django-spec-agents[harness]"). The package never imports it itself: your policy does, so an install without the extra loads nothing of the harness. Any object with the same scan(content, *, source) method, SkillScanner, works in its place, such as an ArtifactScanner with extra_patterns.

With a scanner set:

  • create_skill, update_skill and import_skill_md scan the cleaned description and body, and raise InvalidSkillError with field set to the first one flagged. The message names the threats and patterns found, never the flagged text, so the skill tools can send it back to the model to retry. A refused update leaves the row and the instance as they were. An update scans the new draft, not the row as stored, so it can repair a flagged row.
  • A stored row the scanner flags is left out of what StoredSkills offers a run and of what the list_skills tool lists. That covers rows written before the scanner was set, or under older patterns. It still holds its name, so the company skill of the same name is not offered in its place, and the bundled create-skill stays hidden behind a flagged stored create-skill. list_visible_skills and resolve_skill still return it, so an editor shows it and update_skill or disable_skill can fix it.

A policy without the attribute, or with scanner = None, scans nothing.

docs.title: Labelling a skill personal or shared
docs.text:
A transport that lists skills for an editor can show whose each one is. To tell it, give the policy a scope(request, skill) method returning "personal" for a skill in the caller's own scope and "shared" for one another scope holds, such as a company skill. A policy that has it satisfies SkillScoping, and the values are the SkillScope literal:

class TenantSkillPolicy:
    ...

    def scope(self, request, skill):
        return "personal" if skill.owner_id == request.user.pk else "shared"

django-ag-ui's skill editor, from 0.91.0, carries it as each entry's scope key. The method is optional, and a policy without it labels nothing: the editor then leaves the key out. scope is a protocol of its own rather than a fourth SkillPolicy method because a protocol has no optional members, so a policy written before it still satisfies SkillPolicy under a type checker. Nothing in this package calls it, and the list_skills tool lists the same fields either way.

docs.title: Reading and writing
docs.text:
Every function takes the policy and the request:

from django_spec_agents.skills import SkillDraft, create_skill, list_visible_skills

policy = Skill.skill_policy()
create_skill(policy, request, SkillDraft("triage", "Sort the inbox.", "Read, then sort."))
list_visible_skills(policy, request)
  • list_visible_skills returns the caller's enabled skills, one per name. resolve_skill returns the one a name reaches, or None. A disabled skill shadows nothing, so disabling a personal skill brings back the company one of the same name.
  • create_skill, update_skill, disable_skill and enable_skill write. Each one asks can_write and raises SkillWriteRefusedError when the policy refuses. That error is a Django PermissionDenied. A create asks about the new skill. An update, a disable and an enable ask twice, once about the row as stored and once about the result. A refused update, disable or enable leaves both the row and the instance you passed as they were.
  • A name that is not kebab-case raises InvalidSkillError. So do a blank or oversized description or body. A create or an enable by a caller who already sees MAX_VISIBLE_SKILLS (100) enabled skills raises SkillLimitError, a subclass of it. An enable asks can_write before it counts the cap, so a refused caller sees the refusal.
  • InvalidSkillError.field names the draft field that broke the rule: name, description or body, and from a SKILL.md also user_invocable or model_invocable. It is None when no one field is at fault, as for the visible-skill cap, an unsupported frontmatter key or a malformed frontmatter. Build the error without field and it is None, so existing callers are unaffected.
  • list_visible_skills stops at MAX_VISIBLE_SKILLS, in the policy's order, because its list is the catalog that reaches the model. A create can be admitted while other callers already see the cap, for example when staff add a company skill that a member with many personal skills also sees. The list still holds, and since personal skills come first in the policy's order, the member's own skills and their shadows survive the cut.

Descriptions are stripped, and bodies lose their leading and trailing blank lines and take LF line endings. The harness's Skills loads a SKILL.md the same way.

docs.title: SKILL.md
docs.text:
export_skill_md(skill) writes a skill as a SKILL.md. import_skill_md(policy, request, text) creates one from a SKILL.md, through create_skill and so through can_write. parse_skill_md(text) only reads it, into a SkillDraft. The trip is lossless: an exported skill imports to the same name, description, body and flags. The harness's Skills loads the exported file to the same fields too, from a directory named after the skill. enabled and the scope are not part of the file.

The import reads a strict subset of YAML: one-line entries for name, description, user-invocable and disable-model-invocation. A value may be plain, single-quoted or double-quoted. Any other field, such as allowed-tools, raises InvalidSkillError, and so does a multi-line value. Dropping either one silently would lose part of the file.

docs.title: Offering stored skills to the agent
docs.text:
Pass StoredSkills in the per-run capabilities=, built for the request the run serves:

from django_spec_agents.skills import StoredSkills

capabilities = [StoredSkills(Skill.skill_policy(), request, authoring=True)]

On every run it reads the caller's visible skills through the policy, and offers each enabled skill with model_invocable set as a deferred capability. The capability's id is the skill's name. Until the model calls load_capability with that id, it sees only the name and the description. After that, the body joins its instructions. A skill created or changed between two runs is offered on the next run, with no agent rebuild.

A skill grants nothing. It has no tools, and it cannot lift an approval. With the tool guard enabled, a destructive tool waits for approval, and the policy's can_write refuses a write, whatever a body says.

authoring=True adds build_skill_tools' five tools:

Tool Gated Does list_skills no the visible skills: name, description, the two flags, and writable. No body create_skill yes create_skill with the name, description, body and flags given update_skill yes replaces the draft of the enabled skill the caller reaches by name disable_skill yes disable_skill on that skill enable_skill yes enable_skill on the first disabled skill of that name the policy yields

The four writes carry the destructive marker, so when the tool guard is enabled ToolGuard defers them for approval and the approval card shows the body. ToolGuardConfig.enabled is off by default, and with it off the writes run at once, so pair authoring=True with ToolGuardConfig(enabled=True). A draft that breaks a rule is sent back to the model to retry. A write the policy refuses is reported to the model as text, and nothing changes, and so is a create or an enable by a caller at MAX_VISIBLE_SKILLS: a retry cannot clear it.

It also adds the bundled create-skill skill, which interviews the user, drafts a name, description and body, and calls create_skill. A visible stored skill named create-skill replaces the bundled one, by the same rule that lets a personal skill replace a company one.

docs.title: Refusing a model with no policy at startup
docs.text:
No setting names your model. Your code holds it and passes Skill.skill_policy() to every function, and to a transport as a constructor argument. To have startup refuse a model with no policy, add the package's opt-in app to INSTALLED_APPS:

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...,
    "django_spec_agents",
    "myproject.skills",
]

The app registers a Django system check that walks the app registry for every installed model subclassing AbstractSkill, so manage.py check, runserver and migrate fail when one of them is unguarded. An abstract layer has no table and is not checked.

Id When django_spec_agents.E001 An installed AbstractSkill subclass's skill_policy() returns None, which is AbstractSkill's default

The app has no models and no migrations. Its label, django_spec_agents, does not clash with the store app's label, django_spec_agents_store. A project that has no skills leaves the app out, and nothing changes for it.

Import django_spec_agents.skills once the app registry is ready, for example from a models.py, a view or a policy, because it defines an abstract model.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text: Storage here is contracts plus reference implementations. The protocols are core because every transport needs the same persistence semantics; the HTTP views over them are not — a browser thread drawer and an agent-to-agent peer model the same history completely differently.

docs.title: The contracts
docs.text:
Three Protocols, all runtime_checkable, all fully async so an implementation can use the async ORM or a network backend:

  • ConversationStore — load / save / delete a conversation, plus listing metadata for a history drawer.
  • AttachmentStore — save / open / delete files a user attached.
  • RunStore — a thread's run status and each run's event log, for runs that outlive their request (below).

You pass an instance to your transport; nothing is resolved from a dotted path.

docs.title: Owner scoping is the security boundary
docs.text:
Both contracts are owner-scoped, and this is the part to get right in a custom implementation: a store filters by the acting user so one user can never read or delete another's data.

AttachmentStore.open returns None for a missing or cross-owner id rather than raising, so a caller maps both to a 404 — a cross-owner id must not be distinguishable from a missing one.

AttachmentStore.save deliberately validates nothing about size or type. That is the calling view's job, from its own config; the store just persists bytes and returns a durable AttachmentRef.

docs.title: The read_attachment tool
docs.text:
The bytes never travel on the wire. A transport that has an attachment store composes build_attachment_toolset(store, request) into the agent, and the model reaches a file server-side, by id, only when it asks — through the same owner-scoped open a download view would use.

Reading one has three outcomes:

The attachment What the model gets Textual (text/*, JSON, XML, JavaScript, YAML, SVG) and valid UTF-8 Its text, inline. A type providers can read — PDF, PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP — within the size cap The bytes, as attached file content it can look at directly. Anything else: an unreadable type, an oversized file, undecodable "text" A one-line note with the name, type and size.

Tune the middle row with AttachmentInlineConfig:

from django_spec_agents import AttachmentInlineConfig
from django_spec_agents.agent.attachment_toolset import build_attachment_toolset

toolset = build_attachment_toolset(
    store,
    request,
    inline=AttachmentInlineConfig(max_bytes=1024 * 1024),
)

The type list is an allowlist rather than "everything that is not text", and that is on purpose. Bytes a provider cannot interpret are worse than useless: a .zip or a .exe handed over as file content makes the provider reject the whole request, so a broad rule would trade a model that cannot read your PDF for a run that does not start.

The size cap is much smaller than any upload cap you would set, and for a different reason: it bounds what one request carries. An inlined file rides in a synthetic user message that the tool return serialises into, and that message stays in the run's history, so every further model request in the same run ships the file again. Base64 adds about a third — a 4 MiB PDF is roughly 5.5 MiB of provider payload each time, in tokens, in latency, and in the memory the run holds it in.

It does not cost the conversation. The bytes never travel on the event stream, so the client never receives them and the history it posts on the next turn carries none; whether they outlive the run is the transport's decision, and the AG-UI transport strips them on the way to storage. A follow-up question about the same file is answered by reading the attachment again, server-side. That is why the default sits at 4 MiB rather than at whatever your upload endpoint accepts.

To never attach bytes:

toolset = build_attachment_toolset(
    store,
    request,
    inline=AttachmentInlineConfig(media_types=frozenset()),
)

AttachmentRef.mime is client-declared, so the decision is made on a hint. The failure mode of a mislabelled file is a provider rejecting the request, not a disclosure — the store is owner-scoped either way.

Pass the same AttachmentInlineConfig to the spec tools (attachment_inline= on SpecToolset, SpecCapability and build_spec_capability), so one config governs a file a spec returns as well as an attachment the model asks for. The declared AttachmentRef.size is trusted for the over-limit refusal: a file declaring more than max_bytes is refused without being read, and one declaring less is still read no further than max_bytes + 1 bytes. The read runs thread-sensitive, on the thread the rest of the request's synchronous work uses, and a cancelled call still finishes it and closes the handle.

docs.title: Threads key by (owner_id, thread_id)
docs.text:
Which has a consequence worth knowing before you mount two endpoints: two transports sharing one store share one user's thread list. A conversation started at /internal/agent shows up in /public/agent's history and can be resumed there — under the public agent's model, tools and guard policy.

ScopedConversationStore partitions them without a migration:

from django_spec_agents import ScopedConversationStore

internal = ScopedConversationStore(store, scope="internal")
public = ScopedConversationStore(store, scope="public")

: is reserved in a scope name and one containing it is refused. The partition is the key prefix scope:, so a scope name that extends another — admin and admin:readonly — makes the shorter scope's prefix match the longer one's threads: it lists them, and load, rename and delete resolve there too, silently and in both directions. Names that merely share a prefix (admin / administrators) are fine; the separator ends the scope.

docs.title: What ships
docs.text: Implementation Use it when NullConversationStore The default. load returns None, save/delete no-op — the server stays stateless and the conversation lives in the client's posted history. A transport treats this as "persistence off". NullAttachmentStore The default. Uploads off. DjangoSessionConversationStore Per-user persistence with no migration — conversations live in the Django session. Good for a demo or a small deployment. ModelConversationStore / ModelAttachmentStore Abstract model-backed bases to subclass against your own models. ScopedConversationStore Wraps any of the above to partition by scope.

docs.title: The reference models
docs.text:
The base package ships no model of its own, so projects that don't opt in get no migration. To use the ready-made ones:

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...,
    "django_spec_agents.contrib.store",
]

Then migrate, and pass the matching store to your transport (conversation_store= / attachment_store= / step_store=). The app provides DefaultConversationStore, DefaultAttachmentStore, DefaultStepStore, DefaultMemoryStore and DefaultRunStore, and each is imported from its own module:

from django_spec_agents.contrib.store.default_attachment_store import (
    DefaultAttachmentStore,
)
from django_spec_agents.contrib.store.default_conversation_store import (
    DefaultConversationStore,
)
from django_spec_agents.contrib.store.default_memory_store import (
    DefaultMemoryStore,
)
from django_spec_agents.contrib.store.default_run_store import DefaultRunStore
from django_spec_agents.contrib.store.default_step_store import DefaultStepStore

The shorter from django_spec_agents.contrib.store import DefaultConversationStore is the natural guess and it does not exist. It cannot: this is a Django app, so INSTALLED_APPS imports the package itself, and a re-export there would import models before the app registry is ready — AppRegistryNotReady at startup, for every project, whether or not it uses the stores. The leaf path is the price of the package being importable at all.

docs.title: How long an id may be
docs.text:
Each id the stores key on is a CharField(max_length=255): owner_id, thread_id, conversation_id, run_id, parent_run_id, tool_call_id and operation_id, on every model that holds them. They sit in unique constraints and indexes, so they stay bounded. The default stores check each one against its column before they write, and raise IdentifierTooLongError, a ValueError exported from django_spec_agents, naming the field and its limit. Nothing is written. A read with an over-long id finds nothing, so load returns None and the step and memory reads come back empty, on every database.

Without the check, SQLite would store the value and PostgreSQL would refuse the row with a DataError midway through a run, after the model call. A transport that takes threadId or runId from the client can answer the error as a bad request. In memory's namespace mode the owner is the path's first segment, so that segment is held to the same limit.

docs.title: Refusing an id before the run starts
docs.text:
The write-time check fires when the store writes, which a streaming transport reaches after the model and its tools have run. To refuse earlier, call preflight_identifiers(store, **ids), exported from django_spec_agents, before the run starts:

from django_spec_agents import IdentifierTooLongError, preflight_identifiers

try:
    preflight_identifiers(conversation_store, thread_id=thread_id)
    preflight_identifiers(step_store, run_id=run_id, conversation_id=thread_id)
except IdentifierTooLongError as error:
    return HttpResponseBadRequest(str(error))

It calls the store's check_identifiers method when the store has one, and does nothing otherwise. The method reads the column widths only: it resolves no owner, runs no query and writes nothing, so it is safe on the event loop. It is on no protocol, so a custom store without it still satisfies ConversationStore and MemoryStore, and its ids are checked, if at all, when it writes. The keywords each default store takes:

Store check_identifiers keywords DefaultConversationStore thread_id DefaultStepStore run_id, conversation_id, parent_run_id, tool_call_id DefaultMemoryStore operation_id

A keyword the store does not take is a TypeError, so a misspelt id fails loudly rather than passing the preflight. DefaultAttachmentStore has no method: the only id it keys on that a caller supplies is the owner, which the preflight leaves to the write. ModelConversationStore, ModelAttachmentStore, DjangoSessionConversationStore and the null stores have none either, having no columns of their own.

ScopedConversationStore offers check_identifiers only when the store it wraps has it, and applies its scope: prefix to thread_id before forwarding, so the prefix counts against the column. A thread_id it refuses, there or in save, is reported as the client sent it, against the room the prefix leaves: thread_id is 247 characters, over its 246-character limit in this scope under scope="internal".

The default stores' errors carry field, length and limit beside the message, so a transport can build its own answer; each is None on an error raised without them.

The descriptive columns no index reads are TextFields and take any length: an attachment's name and mime, agent_name, tool_name, a tool effect's idempotency_key and a memory operation's fingerprint. Migration 0002_text_columns widens them.

docs.title: The app label, and upgrading from django-pydantic-agent
docs.text:
The app's label is django_spec_agents_store, so its nine tables are django_spec_agents_store_<model> and its content types, and the permissions hanging off them, sit under that label.

The same app shipped in django-pydantic-agent as django_pydantic_agent_store. A database that installed it upgrades with the migrate a deploy runs anyway: swap the INSTALLED_APPS entry,

INSTALLED_APPS = [
    ...,
    "django_spec_agents.contrib.store",  # was "django_pydantic_agent.contrib.store"
]

and run migrate. The app's first migration, 0001_initial, sees the old tables and renames them in place: the tables, their constraints and named indexes, and the content types, so permissions, group grants and admin log entries come along by key. The old app's rows in django_migrations are deleted, and nothing is copied, so the rows are the ones you had.

  • The old install has to be at its last migration, 0005, which shipped in django-pydantic-agent 0.20. Short of it, migrate stops with OldInstallBehindError and renames nothing: run migrate under django-pydantic-agent first.
  • Rolling back is one command before the old pin goes back: migrate django_spec_agents_store zero renames everything back and records the old app's migrations again.
  • Some objects Django named itself keep the old names on PostgreSQL: the index on an attachment's file, the check on its size, the link table's foreign keys and each table's primary key and sequence. When a later migration drops or replaces one of them, Django asks the database for the column's constraints rather than computing the name, so the old names show only to a person reading the schema. The exception is the _like index PostgreSQL keeps beside the file column, which Django drops by a name it computes, so the upgrade renames it too. On SQLite a constraint changes only by remaking its table, so there every name comes out new.

Unapplying does the same on a database that never ran django-pydantic-agent. The migration cannot tell how it was applied, so on a fresh install migrate django_spec_agents_store zero does not drop the store's tables: it leaves them under django-pydantic-agent's names, records that package's five migrations in django_migrations and moves the content types to its label. To remove the store from such a database, drop those tables and delete those rows yourself.

What the upgrade leaves alone is everything stored or configured outside the schema: the attachment storage alias and the stored files' django_pydantic_agent/attachments/ prefix, the session key DjangoSessionConversationStore keeps conversations under, and the django_pydantic_agent.audit and django_pydantic_agent.failure loggers. Each keeps django-pydantic-agent's spelling, so a project's STORAGES, LOGGING, live sessions and stored files need nothing.

DefaultAttachmentStore keeps bytes in Django Storage and metadata in a row, so S3 and friends come free through STORAGES — you don't configure anything here beyond your normal Django storage backend.

docs.title: Putting attachments somewhere other than the default
docs.text:
Agent uploads are user-supplied files, and a project often wants them in a private bucket rather than wherever its other media goes. Name a backend under the django_pydantic_agent_attachments alias and attachments use it; leave the alias out and they use default:

STORAGES = {
    "default": {"BACKEND": "django.core.files.storage.FileSystemStorage"},
    "staticfiles": {"BACKEND": "django.contrib.staticfiles.storage.StaticFilesStorage"},
    "django_pydantic_agent_attachments": {
        "BACKEND": "myproject.storages.PrivateMediaStorage",
    },
}

The alias is resolved once, when the model's field is constructed, so it has to be in STORAGES before the app's models are imported — settings, in other words, which is where it already is.

Point it somewhere new and the old attachments do not come with it. Rows keep the path they were written with, and that path is asked of the new backend — so every attachment written before the switch reads as unavailable until you move the blobs across yourself. Re-uploading is not a shortcut: it writes fresh copies rather than finding the originals. Move the files, or accept the loss knowingly.

The bucket policy needs s3:ListBucket if you point the alias at S3. Saving an attachment asks the backend whether a matching blob is already there, and with that permission S3 answers 404 for a key that is absent. Without it S3 answers 403 instead, which django-storages re-raises — turning an upload that would have been deduplicated into a 500.

A misspelled BACKEND raises rather than falling back to default. Silently writing user-supplied files to the public default over a one-character typo is the outcome this alias exists to prevent.

Everything from here down is the reference implementation's behaviour, not the contract. ConversationStore and AttachmentStore stay id-based, the wire is unchanged, and a session-backed or S3-only store you plug in yourself owes none of this.

docs.title: The same file, uploaded twice
docs.text:
StoredAttachment carries a sha256 of the file's bytes, hashed in chunks at upload so a large file is never held in memory whole just to fingerprint it. When an upload matches one the same owner already has, the new row points at the blob already in storage instead of writing a second copy.

A row per upload, even on a hit. The row holds the name the composer shows on the chip, so the same bytes sent again as contract-final.pdf keep that name rather than inheriting the first upload's. What is shared is the file underneath; the bytes are removed only when the last row pointing at them goes.

Deduplication never crosses owners, and that is not an oversight. Sharing one copy of a document held by a hundred tenants would be the better trade on storage alone. It is not available: a cross-owner hit tells you another tenant holds a file whose bytes you already have, which is how you confirm that a named party is a customer, or where a leaked document came from. The lookup is scoped to one owner, and the index on the column leads with owner_id so the cross-tenant question is not even the cheap one to ask.

Rows written before the column existed have no hash, so they cannot be matched until agent_store_backfill_hashes fills them in.

docs.title: Attachment lifecycle
docs.text:
An attachment is reachable as long as a conversation refers to it, and the reference is derived, not declared. Saving a conversation reconciles the StoredConversation.attachments relation from the attachment ids its own messages carry — the web component already puts them there, on the user message, as an attachments array of the refs it uploaded. No wire change and no client change: the ids are in the payload either way.

The parse is total. A malformed entry degrades to "no reference" rather than raising inside a save, and an id is resolved only against its own owner's attachments, so a guessed or copied id links nothing.

Two consequences:

  • Deleting a conversation deletes the attachments nothing else refers to, and their bytes. One quoted by a second thread survives untouched.
  • An upload that was never sent belongs to no conversation, so no cascade will ever reach it. agent_store_prune_attachments is what collects those.

StoredAttachment.thread_id is untouched by all of this and stays. It is a loose label a project may set; the relation, not the column, is what lifecycle runs on.

Nothing is ever deleted on a timer the library set up. Deletion happens on a cascade you can point at, or on a command you schedule. There is no TTL sweep.

Deleting StoredConversation rows by another route — a queryset delete(), the admin — skips the cascade and leaves the attachments unreferenced. They are not stranded permanently; the prune command is exactly what collects them.

docs.title: Maintenance commands
docs.text:
The contrib.store app ships five, all of them opt-in and none of them scheduled for you:

Command What it does agent_store_backfill_hashes Hash attachments stored before the sha256 column existed, so they can take part in deduplication. A missing blob is a reported skip, not a failure. agent_store_prune_attachments Delete unreferenced attachments older than --older-than (default 24h). agent_store_strip_inline_bytes Rewrite stored conversations to drop inlined base64 file content. agent_store_purge_memory Erase every stored memory file for one owner. agent_store_prune_run_logs Delete the event logs of runs that ended over --older-than ago (default 24h), never a live run's; see Run status and event logs.

All five take --dry-run.

--older-than is why the prune command is safe to run. References alone cannot tell an upload abandoned last month from one sitting in a composer right now — both have zero. The threshold is the floor on how long an upload must survive before it counts as abandoned, so set it to comfortably more than the longest a message may sit unsent in your product:

python manage.py agent_store_prune_attachments --older-than 7d --dry-run

docs.title: Reclaiming space from threads that inlined files
docs.text:
A transport that hands the model an attachment inline serialises the file into the message list as base64, and the message list is persisted: a 2.6 MB PDF costs roughly 3.5 MB in one row, loaded whole every time the thread is opened. Transports have stopped writing them and strip them on the way in, but a row already written keeps its payload until something rewrites it:

python manage.py agent_store_strip_inline_bytes --dry-run
python manage.py agent_store_strip_inline_bytes

It edits the JSON structurally rather than round-tripping it through a message type, because that round trip is exactly what would drop each message's id and the non-standard attachments array — the array that renders the chips and that the attachment relation is reconciled from. The bytes themselves are not lost: the attachment is untouched in the attachment store, and the model reaches it the way it always does, by id.

docs.title: Step persistence
docs.text:
DefaultStepStore is the durable, owner-scoped equivalent of pydantic-ai-harness's own SqliteStepStore / FileStepStore. Note the direction of the contract: it structurally satisfies harness's StepStore protocol — that protocol is upstream's, not this package's, and this package does not redeclare it. Owner scoping is entirely ours; no harness record carries one, which is what makes the store multi-tenant rather than a single-user ledger.

It needs the [harness] extra, since the protocol it satisfies lives there.

Resuming a run reads its latest snapshot with latest_snapshot(run_id=...). That is the newest snapshot by insertion order, not the highest step_index, and only complete ones unless you pass include_interrupted=True. A complete snapshot is a safe point to resume from. An interrupted one is a rescue point saved mid tool cycle, for example after a crash, so its pending tool calls may need to be re-run or closed out. Check list_unresolved_tool_effects for the run before resuming from one. Its messages are already a list[ModelMessage], ready for Agent.run(message_history=...).

docs.title: list_runs answers oldest first
docs.text:
Ascending started_at is upstream's documented protocol order — StepStore invites callers to take the most recent run with [-1] — so the store keeps it rather than serving the order a list happens to want to display. A UI showing recent runs first sorts where it renders; a store that reversed the contract would hand that idiom the oldest run instead, silently, and only where more than one run exists.

Full signatures in the persistence reference.

docs.title: Spend counters
docs.text:
DefaultSpendStore is the database equivalent of pydantic-ai-harness's PostgresSpendStore, for PostgreSQL and for SQLite (see below), and the store a SpendLimitsConfig names. It satisfies harness's BatchSpendStore protocol and needs the [harness] extra.

from django_spec_agents.contrib.store.default_spend_store import DefaultSpendStore

spend_store = DefaultSpendStore()

Build it once and share it, unlike DefaultStepStore: it holds no request and scopes nothing, since a budget's key already names its partition (a user, a run, a day).
