Each window is a StoredSpendCounter row, keyed by the SHA-256 of its key so a long conversation id fits the index, with dollars held as whole billionths. Every window of one response is applied in one transaction, so all of them count or none does. A response presented twice, as recovery outside a durable journal can, is counted once while its StoredSpendMarker lives, dedup_retain (an hour) or the window's own horizon, whichever is shorter; dedup_retain=None keeps no markers.

A window past its horizon reads as zero and restarts at its next write. Horizons are measured on clock, the application's clock (timezone.now unless given), not the database's, so keep the workers' clocks in step. Every sweep_every (256) entries a store writes, it deletes the expired rows, skipping any another connection holds; a failed sweep is logged and the write still counts. A key cannot contain a NUL character, which PostgreSQL refuses in text, and dedup_retain must be positive or None.

SQLite refuses a second writer's lock upgrade at once, with database is locked and no wait, so concurrent workers on it need "transaction_mode": "IMMEDIATE" in the database OPTIONS, which Django 5.1 added; below 5.1 concurrent workers on SQLite can fail a write. One ASGI process is unaffected.

DATABASES = {
    "default": {
        "ENGINE": "django.db.backends.sqlite3",
        "NAME": BASE_DIR / "db.sqlite3",
        "OPTIONS": {"transaction_mode": "IMMEDIATE", "timeout": 20},
    }
}

docs.title: Run status and event logs
docs.text:
A run started on the server with no stream, or one whose browser leaves, has to be visible from anywhere: which thread is busy, which is waiting on an answer, what the run has said so far. A RunStore holds that, apart from the transcript, which stays in the ConversationStore with any partial output. It is a separate protocol, so a ConversationStore written before it still satisfies its own. A transport with no run store behaves as it always has: no claim, no conflict, no detach.

DefaultRunStore is the reference implementation, one instance for every request, keyed by the owner it resolves from each request:

from datetime import timedelta

from django_spec_agents.contrib.store.default_run_store import DefaultRunStore

run_store = DefaultRunStore(log_retention=timedelta(hours=6))

One run per thread. claim(thread_id, run_id, request=..., lease=...) takes the thread in one conditional update: it wins when no run holds the thread or the holder's lease has lapsed, and a second claim loses with the holder's id in the answer, for a transport's 409. The holder keeps its claim with renew and gives it up with finish. A run that is no longer the live holder cannot renew, append or finish, so an owner presumed dead never overwrites the run that replaced it.

Resuming a park, and giving a claim back. DefaultRunStore is also a ResumableRunStore, a sub-protocol of RunStore with two more pieces. A store written against RunStore alone stays one, so a transport checks isinstance(store, ResumableRunStore) before it uses either. That check sees method names only, so a store of your own that defines release must also take resumes= on claim:

  • claim(..., resumes=parked_run_id) wins only while the thread is waiting with that run as its last_run_id, and the condition is part of the claim's one conditional update. Of two resumes of the same park, a double click or two tabs, exactly one wins. Every refused resume raises RunNotParkedError and writes nothing, never a busy answer, so no client retries a resume that cannot succeed: the thread is running (the error's active_run_id names the holder, the winning resume or another run), idle, failed, parked on another run, or running under a lapsed lease.
  • release(thread_id, run_id, request=...) gives back a claim the run still holds: the thread's status, reason, waiting record and last_run_id return to what they were before the claim, its lease and cancel are cleared, and the released run's log is deleted, so its id may be claimed again. A claim that displaced a holder whose lease had lapsed restores the thread as failed with reason interrupted, as get read it before the claim. A transport that claims and then has its enqueue refused releases the claim, so a resumed park stays parked rather than reading failed. A thread that held no run before reads as unknown again. release answers False and changes nothing for a run that is not the live holder, and for a claim taken before the 0007_thread_run_prior migration, which has no prior state to restore.

How a run ended goes to finish as a RunOutcome:

Outcome Thread status Reason completed idle waiting waiting, with a RunWaiting for each call it parked on cancelled idle timed_out idle timed_out error failed error

A thread still running after its lease lapses, as after a restart, reads as failed with reason interrupted. The run's id stays on the thread as last_run_id after it ends: a parked run's id is what a resume answers to.

waiting is a tuple everywhere it is carried: on ThreadRunState, finish, RunStop and ChildSession. It holds one RunWaiting for each deferred call the run parked on, in the order the run deferred them, and is empty when the thread is not waiting. finish and RunStop take a non-empty waiting exactly when the outcome is waiting, and raise ValueError otherwise. The 0008_waiting_calls migration rewrites a stored single call, in waiting and prior_waiting, as a one-element list; unapplied, it keeps each list's first call.

A transport builds one RunWaiting per deferred call with build_run_waiting(requests, tool_call_id, summary=..., destructive=...), which reads kind from the run's DeferredToolRequests: approval, question for a tool that deferred with CallDeferred(kind="question"), or external. These are upstream's DeferredToolKind values, so a row stored before kind was typed loads unchanged.

Run ids are single-use per owner. The resumed run, like a retried one, claims the thread under a fresh id; claim refuses an id its owner has claimed before with RunIdReusedError, writing nothing, so a transport can answer it as a client error rather than a server one.

The log is append-only and numbered. append(run_id, events, request=...) numbers a batch of opaque JSON events on from the run's last, starting at 1, and read(run_id, after=n) pages from any number, so a reader that reconnects asks for what it has not seen. Nothing edits an entry. An append is one conditional update, which checks the run still holds a live lease and takes the next numbers in the same statement, then the insert of the batch (UPDATE ... RETURNING on PostgreSQL and SQLite 3.35 or later; elsewhere the update is followed by a read of the new number).

Pruning is the host's to schedule. prune() deletes whole logs once their run has been over for log_retention (a day by default), counting a run that never finished from its last write and never touching one under a live lease. Nothing calls it for you, and it reads no setting: schedule the agent_store_prune_run_logs command (cron, a Celery beat, a platform scheduler), passing your store's window as --older-than:

python manage.py agent_store_prune_run_logs --older-than 6h

Waiting on a log. A reader that follows a live run, as a reattached browser does, asks the store to tell it when there is more rather than re-reading the log on a timer. That is wait(run_id, after=n, timeout=..., request=...) on the optional WatchableRunStore, a sub-protocol of RunStore in the shape of ResumableRunStore: a store written against RunStore alone stays one, and a reader checks isinstance(store, WatchableRunStore) before it calls wait, polling read itself otherwise. wait answers True once the log has an entry numbered above n or the run has ended, and at once if either already holds or the run has no log; False when the timeout passes. A run whose owner died without finishing never ends this way, so a reader bounds each wait and checks get, which reads the lapsed lease as failed.

DefaultRunStore.wait polls: each tick is one indexed read of the log's next number and end, and between ticks it pauses half a second, doubling up to two seconds while nothing changes. Every call starts from the shortest pause, so a reader that comes back after an entry polls quickly again. poll_interval=(0.5, 2.0) on the constructor sets both, and a pair that could not back off (a first pause of zero or less, or one longer than the largest) raises ValueError.

On PostgreSQL a store can wake its readers instead of letting them poll. The package ships no such store, because it would hold a connection per waiting reader and tie the store to one database; this is a recipe to adapt, written against psycopg 3.2 or later (notifies(timeout=)):

from datetime import timedelta

import psycopg
from asgiref.sync import sync_to_async
from django.db import connection

from django_spec_agents.contrib.store.default_run_store import DefaultRunStore

CHANNEL = "agent_run_log"


def _notify(run_id):
    with connection.cursor() as cursor:
        cursor.execute("SELECT pg_notify(%s, %s)", [CHANNEL, run_id])


class NotifyingRunStore(DefaultRunStore):
    def __init__(self, *, conninfo, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        self._conninfo = conninfo

    async def append(self, run_id, events, *, request):
        last = await super().append(run_id, events, request=request)
        if last is not None:
            await sync_to_async(_notify)(run_id)
        return last

    async def finish(self, thread_id, run_id, outcome, *, request, waiting=()):
        finished = await super().finish(
            thread_id, run_id, outcome, request=request, waiting=waiting
        )
        if finished:
            await sync_to_async(_notify)(run_id)
        return finished

    async def wait(self, run_id, *, after, timeout, request):
        now = timedelta(0)
        async with await psycopg.AsyncConnection.connect(
            self._conninfo, autocommit=True
        ) as listener:
            # Listen first, then look: a write between the two is not missed.
            await listener.execute(f"LISTEN {CHANNEL}")
            if await super().wait(run_id, after=after, timeout=now, request=request):
                return True
            async for note in listener.notifies(timeout=timeout.total_seconds()):
                if note.payload == run_id and await super().wait(
                    run_id, after=after, timeout=now, request=request
                ):
                    return True
        return False

A notification is sent when the writer's transaction commits, so a reader woken by one reads the entries it announces. One reader's wait holds one listening connection for its timeout, which counts against PostgreSQL's max_connections; a deployment with many reattached readers shares one listener per process and fans the notifications out instead.

request_cancel records a cancel for the live run, for its owner to act on from wherever it runs, and mark_read stamps last_read_at for an unread marker. get_many reads a page of threads' states at once.

docs.title: Child sessions: the parent link and the inbound queue
docs.text:
A child session is a thread one agent starts on another, or on itself. Two things in the store make it durable.

The parent link. Conversation.parent and ConversationMeta.parent name the thread that started this one, as a ThreadRef: the parent's thread_id, as its client sees it, and the scope it lives in (the agent id or ScopedConversationStore scope; None for an unscoped store). The scope is spelled out because a child usually lives under another agent: ScopedConversationStore passes the link through untouched, so a child in scope b reads back a parent in scope a.

from django_spec_agents import Conversation, ScopedConversationStore, ThreadRef

children = ScopedConversationStore(store, scope="b")
await children.save(
    Conversation(thread_id="c1", parent=ThreadRef("t1", scope="a")), request=request
)

DefaultConversationStore writes the link when a save names one and leaves it alone when a save does not, so a later turn typed in the child, which saves with parent=None, keeps it. A store written before the field existed still satisfies ConversationStore; its threads read back with no parent.

Clearing the link is a method of its own, unlink_parent(thread_id, *, request), on the optional UnlinkableConversationStore protocol, so a store without it still satisfies ConversationStore; a caller checks isinstance(store, UnlinkableConversationStore) first. DefaultConversationStore has it: it writes NULL to the thread's two parent columns and its lineage, owner-scoped, and leaves the thread's place in the list alone. ScopedConversationStore offers it only over a store that has it, and ModelConversationStore only to a subclass that defines the _unlink_parent(thread_id, owner_id) hook.

The routine link. Conversation.routine_id and ConversationMeta.routine_id name the routine whose firing started the thread, as a string. DefaultConversationStore keeps it in a routine_id column (the 0009_conversation_routine migration) and, as with the parent, writes it when a save names one and leaves it alone otherwise, so every firing's thread keeps naming its routine.

The inbound queue. Reports, questions, answers and steering reach a thread through an InboundQueue, its own protocol so ConversationStore gains no method. Messages are addressed by ThreadRef and owner-scoped like every store. Delivery is at least once: pending(thread) reads without removing, and ack(thread, ids) removes exactly the ids the reader has handed on, so a message read by a process that then died is read again. Ids are allocated at insert and seen at commit, so one can become visible behind a higher id already read, and pending(after=n) used as a cursor can miss it. A reader that must see every message calls pending without after and acks what it read.

A run reads its thread's queue through a claim instead. take(thread, run_id, lease=...) claims the thread's inbox for that run, or renews its claim, and marks and returns the messages the run has not taken yet; while another run's claim is live it returns nothing. release(thread, run_id) drops the claim and untakes the run's unacked messages, so the next run takes them. A claim whose lease lapsed, its run having died, is taken over, with the messages that run took and never acked. pending still lists every unacked message, taken or not.

from django_spec_agents import InboundKind
from django_spec_agents.contrib.store.default_inbound_queue import DefaultInboundQueue

queue = DefaultInboundQueue()
await queue.enqueue(
    ThreadRef("t1", scope="a"),
    InboundKind.REPORT,
    {"text": "done"},
    request=request,
    sender=ThreadRef("c1", scope="b"),
)
messages = await queue.pending(ThreadRef("t1", scope="a"), request=request)
await queue.ack(ThreadRef("t1", scope="a"), [m.id for m in messages], request=request)

DefaultInboundQueue keeps the queue in StoredInboundMessage rows, added by the store app's 0004_child_sessions migration with the two parent columns on StoredConversation. A run's claim is a StoredInboxClaim row, one per owner, scope and thread, and a message's taken_by names the run that took it; both come with the 0006_inbox_claim migration. ModelInboundQueue is the base for a queue over a model of your own: it implements _take and _release beside _enqueue, _pending and _ack.

docs.title: Per-user memory
docs.text:
pydantic-ai-harness ships a complete memory capability — four tools (write_memory, read_memory, delete_memory, search_memory), a MemoryStore protocol, bounded injection, compare-and-set versioning and idempotency receipts. This package does not reimplement any of it. It ships one thing the harness cannot: a Django-backed store, and the scoping that makes it multi-tenant.

DefaultMemoryStore is that store, and the direction of the contract is the same as DefaultStepStore's: it structurally satisfies harness's MemoryStore protocol, which is upstream's and is not redeclared here. It needs the [harness] extra.

from pydantic_ai_harness.memory import Memory

from django_spec_agents import memory_namespace_for_user
from django_spec_agents.contrib.store.default_memory_store import (
    DefaultMemoryStore,
)

capability = Memory(
    DefaultMemoryStore(),
    namespace=lambda ctx: memory_namespace_for_user(ctx.deps.user),
)

Hand it to your transport the way you would any other capability — AGUIServer(capabilities=[capability]) for django-ag-ui. There is no settings key and no new configuration surface: AgentConfig.capabilities already reaches Agent(capabilities=...).

The resolver reads ctx.deps, not a request, and that is not incidental. A capability list is resolved once, at mount time, where no request exists — so nothing request-shaped can be closed over in it. Per-user scoping rides the run instead: pydantic-ai clones every capability per run, and Memory re-resolves its namespace in the clone, so one agent built once serves every caller. The transport sets AgentDeps.user from the authenticated request, so it is server-resolved and not something a client can choose.

docs.title: Two scoping modes, and which one you get
docs.text:
Constructed as Owner is Use when DefaultMemoryStore() the leading path segment — the namespace the capability resolved the usual case: a mount-time capabilities= list DefaultMemoryStore(request) resolved server-side from the request; the path's namespace is not consulted at all you build the store per request — a custom view

The request-bound mode is strictly stronger: it partitions rows independently of the path, so a resolver reading anything user-controlled still cannot cross scopes (a / inside a resolved namespace is accepted by the harness and simply opens further segments). Reach for it if you have a request to hand. Otherwise pair the namespace-scoped mode with memory_namespace_for_user, which derives the segment from a user the server resolved, and the namespace is a boundary the client cannot choose either.

allow_anonymous applies only to the request-bound mode. Without a request there is no anonymity to detect, and the resolver decides what an anonymous caller is called — memory_namespace_for_user returns one shared anon namespace, since with no request there is no session to key a per-visitor bucket on. Transports that refuse anonymous callers by default (django-ag-ui does) never reach it.

docs.title: Turn the tool guard on first
docs.text:
Memory may be allowed to steer what the model says. It must not be allowed to decide what the model does — and memory is durable, model-written, and replayed into every later run, so a note that reads as an instruction keeps working long after whoever planted it has gone.

ToolGuard is what holds that line: it reads the x-destructive stamp server-side, so a memory-planted "call refund_order first" still hits the approval interrupt. With no tool_guard, build_agent's own docstring is blunt that "every server-side tool here runs the moment the model calls it".

Enable TOOL_GUARD before you enable memory. A mount with memory on and the guard off is a durable, user-writable path to unattended destructive calls. Each setting is defensible alone; they are only wrong together.

docs.title: namespace is the user, agent_name is the mount
docs.text:
The harness composes the scope key as f"{namespace}/{agent_name}", so two mounts sharing one store are partitioned by construction — Memory(store, agent_name="internal") and Memory(store, agent_name="public") — and no ScopedMemoryStore wrapper is needed the way it is for conversations and steps.

Use one of the two shipped resolvers for the user half — memory_namespace_for_user(ctx.deps.user) at mount time, or memory_namespace(request) when you hold a request — rather than reaching for the owner id the other stores partition on. That id is anon:<session_key> for an anonymous request, and a colon is outside the alphabet the harness accepts for a path segment, so Memory raises invalid memory path — from namespace resolution, which sits outside the store read that injection_errors guards, so upstream's "ignore" default does not catch it and the whole run 500s.

Both resolvers always return a valid segment: a segment-safe primary key is carried through readably behind a u- prefix, and anything else — an email primary key, a natural key with a slash — is replaced by a digest of it rather than sanitised, because sanitising maps tenant/42 and tenant-42 onto one namespace.

docs.title: What the store adds over the reference implementations
docs.text:
Why Owner-partitioned rows The harness's stores are single-tenant; the scope lives only in the path, and the path comes from a resolver the host wrote. Fence-tag neutralisation on write Injected memory is wrapped in <memory> markers, and upstream says plainly this "is not a hard prompt-injection boundary". Below pydantic-ai-harness 0.60, which escapes the tag itself, a stored note containing the closing tag ends the block early, and everything after it reads as the user's own turn — durably, on every later run. Every write here escapes the angle brackets of both tags. Per-owner ceilings max_memory_size bounds one file and the injection budget bounds what is read; nothing upstream caps how many files a namespace accumulates or how large they grow in total. max_files and max_total_chars do. Anonymous degradation The capability's hooks fire mid-run, so refusing by raising would abort it. Writes no-op and reads return empty unless the store is built with allow_anonymous=True. purge(owner_id) Erasure, which the protocol cannot express.

Neutralisation happens on write rather than read on purpose: it makes the stored bytes safe for every consumer — the injection, read_memory, search_memory, an app-side read — and it keeps write_memory's old_text replacement working, because the model edits against the same escaped text it was shown. It rewrites only the literal tag forms, never the word memory, which belongs in ordinary notes.

docs.title: App-authored facts do not belong in the store
docs.text: The store has no provenance column, so a trusted fact written there becomes indistinguishable from a model-written one at read time — and it is quoted back inside the same <memory> framing that tells the model this is unverified background. A fact the operator vouches for belongs in the operator channel: your transport's instructions hook, or AgentDeps for something a tool should read. The missing provenance column is not a gap to fill; it is a boundary telling you which facts belong in it.

docs.title: Erasure
docs.text:
Memory is durable personal data written about a user, so an erasure request has to be able to reach it. The MemoryStore protocol has no bulk or prefix delete — composing list_paths with delete needs each path's current version, giving an unbounded read-then-delete loop a concurrent write_memory can lose to — so the store carries a non-protocol purge(owner_id) that is one statement, plus a command:

python manage.py agent_store_purge_memory u-42 --dry-run
python manage.py agent_store_purge_memory u-42

The argument is the owner id the memory was filed under, not the bare user key. With the usual mount-time namespace from memory_namespace_for_user, that is u- followed by the user's primary key, so u-42 for user 42 (a digest of the key replaces it when the key is not a safe path segment). A store built per request files rows under the bare primary key, 42. Anonymous memory is filed under anon in the mount-time mode and, where the store allows anonymous callers, under anon:<session key> in the per-request mode. Run the command with --dry-run first to see how many files the id matches.

It is deliberately not wired to a post_delete signal on your user model. Whether deleting an account erases its memory is a product policy; a library's job here is to make the operation possible.

docs.title: Memory must be inspectable before it is switched on
docs.text: A model quietly accumulating durable notes about someone, replayed into every future session with no surface listing them, is what makes this feature feel spooky rather than tailored. The minimum honest surface is list, read and delete, and the protocol provides all three (list_paths, read, delete), so a host can build one. Do that before turning memory on for real users.

docs.title: Registering one
docs.text:
A tool is a plain typed callable registered on a ToolRegistry:

from django_spec_agents import ToolCategory, ToolRegistry, tool

registry = ToolRegistry()


@tool(registry, category=ToolCategory.UI_READ)
def find_order(order_id: int) -> dict:
    """Look up an order by id."""
    ...

The name defaults to the function's name, and the description to the first paragraph of its docstring; both can be overridden. Registering a name twice raises ValueError rather than shadowing.

The name you register is the name the model is offered, and the one the tool guard, the audit record and the tool catalog use. An explicit description= is what the model reads in place of the docstring, an empty one excepted: some supported Pydantic-AI versions treat it as none. A tool with no description= is offered exactly what Pydantic-AI derives from the docstring, which keeps more than the first paragraph the registry's own description holds. A description= identical to that first paragraph is indistinguishable from none, so the model gets the fuller text.

ToolRegistry state lives on the instance — a transport holds one, and tests build a fresh one per scenario. There is no global registry.

docs.title: Tools must be typed
docs.text:
The registry derives each tool's JSON Schema from the signature at registration time, so every parameter and the return need a concrete annotation. There is no **kwargs: Any escape hatch: an untyped parameter has no schema, and the model would be guessing.

Sync and async callables both work. ToolRegistry.acall dispatches either; ToolRegistry.call is the sync entry point and raises TypeError for an async tool.

docs.title: Metadata, and where it surfaces
docs.text:
@tool takes four pieces of metadata beyond name and description. All of them end up as JSON-Schema extension keys, because a schema is the one channel that reaches a client without inventing a side channel:

Argument Schema key What it is for destructive=True x-destructive This tool mutates. AG-UI has no native destructive-tool concept, so it is stamped at the schema root and read client-side to gate execution behind a confirmation — and server-side by the tool guard, for a tool whose schema is the only place its author said so. category= x-category Coarse grouping (ToolCategory) so a frontend can group or filter, or a system prompt can reason about capability classes. confirm="Activate this project?" x-confirm The confirmation prompt shown instead of a generic "Run tool?". summary="Query orders" x-summary A short display label shown on a tool-call card instead of the raw tool name.

category does not gate anything. It is advisory metadata for grouping and policy; destructive is the flag that drives the approval gate.

There is a fifth key that is not a schema stamp: DESTRUCTIVE_METADATA_KEY ("django_spec_agents.destructive") rides pydantic-ai's ToolDefinition metadata rather than the schema, because metadata is the channel a bridge controls where the schema belongs to the tool's author. It is read server-side at prepare_tools time by the tool guard, which needs destructiveness for tools whose flag doesn't come from the @tool registry at all — a bridged MCP tool, whose readOnlyHint and destructiveHint annotations the bridge maps onto this key.

A registry tool's own destructive=True never travels either channel: it stays on the spec, and the guard reads it from the registry directly. What reaches the guard through the schema is the case where build_input_schema was used on its own and the tool attached through toolsets=.

docs.title: The tool catalog
docs.text:
Server-side tools execute server-side, so their JSON Schema never reaches the browser — which means a web component can't read an x-summary off it. That is what build_tool_catalog is for: a list of {"name", "summary", "description"?} entries a frontend fetches to label tool-call cards.

summary is always present, resolved through a fallback chain — for registry tools, @tool(summary=…) then a prettified name; for the tools of the server passed as mcp_server=, display_name then title then a prettified name.

from django_spec_agents import build_tool_catalog

catalog = build_tool_catalog(registry, mcp_server=server, service_specs=specs)

docs.title: What the catalog does not cover
docs.text:
Only the sources above. A tool reaching the agent through a transport's capabilities= / toolsets= — an arbitrary AbstractToolset attached directly — is not listed, and its card falls back to a prettified tool name.

This is a stated boundary, not a gap waiting to be filled. Pydantic-AI's enumeration is AbstractToolset.get_tools, which is async and takes a RunContext; the catalog is built at configuration time, from a view, with no run in sight. Enumerating "the toolsets we recognise" and skipping the rest would produce a catalog that looks complete and is not — the failure this stack spends its time removing, traded for cosmetics.

Route spec tools through a covered source instead. A SpecToolset or SpecCapability passed to django-ag-ui's service_specs= (0.30+) is attached as itself and enumerated here, so it keeps its labels.

An unlabelled card is a degraded label, not a broken call: the tool executes normally and the frontend shows a prettified name.

docs.title: Deriving a schema on its own
docs.text:
build_input_schema is the same derivation the registry runs, exposed for projects that want a tool's schema outside the registration flow:

from django_spec_agents import build_input_schema

schema = build_input_schema(find_order, destructive=False, category=ToolCategory.UI_READ)

A leading ctx: RunContext[...] parameter is not a tool argument and is left out of the schema: pydantic-ai fills it from the run, so advertising it would ask the model to invent a value for something it cannot supply. Dispatch follows the same rule — registry.call(name, arguments, ctx=ctx) binds it from the caller, and a tool that declares one and is dispatched without a ctx raises rather than being handed None.

docs.title: What the hand-built schema carries
docs.text:
The default derivation maps str, int, float, bool, list[T] (and tuple, set, frozenset), dict, X | None and other unions. Anything else, a model or an enum say, is an empty fragment: it constrains nothing and stays wire-valid.

Annotated[T, ...] is read as T plus what its metadata maps to:

Metadata Schema keys Field(description=...), Field(title=...), Field(examples=...) description, title, examples ge, gt, le, lt, multiple_of (a Field's, or annotated_types' Ge, Interval and so on) minimum, exclusiveMinimum, maximum, exclusiveMaximum, multipleOf min_length, max_length (or annotated_types.Len) minLength / maxLength on a string, minItems / maxItems on a list, minProperties / maxProperties on a dict, nothing on a union pattern, a string or a compiled str pattern pattern

A title appears only when the Field passes one. Other Field arguments (alias, json_schema_extra, deprecated) are not carried, nor is any other metadata, such as a plain string.

A Field given as the parameter's default, n: int = Field(ge=1), reads as one inside Annotated does, after the annotation's own metadata, so its keys win. A Field with no default makes the parameter required, as pydantic does, and ToolRegistry.call refuses a call that omits it with TypeError. A Field with a default shows it as default, in JSON mode (left out when it does not serialise), and a default_factory makes the parameter optional with no default shown. An omitted one reaches the tool as that default, or as a fresh value from the factory, never as the FieldInfo itself. A plain default, n: int = 1, makes the parameter optional and is not shown. A string or forward reference nested in an annotation, Annotated["int", Field(ge=1)] or list["int"], is resolved in the globals the top level is evaluated in: the module of the function inspect.signature reads, through a decorator's __wrapped__, a functools.partial's func or a callable instance's __call__. One that does not resolve is an empty fragment, as an unknown type is. Every value carried serialises to JSON: a bound that is not an int or float (a Decimal, a date), or is infinite or NaN, is left out, and examples are rendered as pydantic renders them (a Decimal as its string), or left out when they do not serialise or hold an infinite or NaN float.

docs.title: Choosing a strategy
docs.text:
schema_strategy= picks the derivation in three places: on build_input_schema for one call, on ToolRegistry(schema_strategy=...) for every binding the registry derives, and on one tool, as @tool(schema_strategy=...) or ToolSpec(schema_strategy=...). A tool's own strategy wins over its registry's; a tool that sets none (None, the default) takes the registry's. So one registry can hold tools of both strategies:

registry = ToolRegistry()  # hand-built, the default


@tool(registry, schema_strategy=SchemaStrategy.PYDANTIC)
def place_order(order: OrderDraft) -> Order: ...  # pydantic's schema, $defs and all


@tool(registry)
def find_order(n: int) -> list[Order]: ...  # the registry's hand-built schema

It takes a SchemaStrategy:

  • SchemaStrategy.HAND_BUILT, the default: the mapping above.
  • SchemaStrategy.PYDANTIC: a pydantic model over the same parameters (the RunContext and *args / **kwargs left out), with extra keys forbidden, and its model_json_schema(). It carries whatever pydantic does, models and enums included.

Under either, a property is keyed by its parameter's name, never by a Field alias (alias= or validation_alias=), because ToolRegistry.call binds the arguments by name: s: Annotated[str, Field(alias="other")] is advertised as s, and a payload keyed other is refused. The pydantic strategy passes by_alias=False, so a nested model's fields are keyed by name too.

The x-* keys are stamped at the root under either. The strategy shapes the schema build_input_schema returns and ToolBinding.input_schema; the schema the agent offers the model for an @tool tool is pydantic-ai's own under both.

For this tool:

def find_order(
    n: Annotated[int, Field(description="How many.", ge=1)],
    note: str | None = None,
) -> list[Order]: ...

the hand-built strategy gives a flat schema with no titles, nullable for X | None, and no defaults but a Field's:

{
  "type": "object",
  "properties": {
    "n": {"type": "integer", "description": "How many.", "minimum": 1},
    "note": {"type": "string", "nullable": true}
  },
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "x-category": "other",
  "required": ["n"]
}

and schema_strategy=SchemaStrategy.PYDANTIC gives pydantic's, with a title on the root (the function's name) and on each property, anyOf with a null branch for X | None, the default, and a nested model or enum under $defs, reached by $ref:

{
  "additionalProperties": false,
  "properties": {
    "n": {"description": "How many.", "minimum": 1, "title": "N", "type": "integer"},
    "note": {
      "anyOf": [{"type": "string"}, {"type": "null"}],
      "default": null,
      "title": "Note"
    }
  },
  "required": ["n"],
  "title": "find_order",
  "type": "object",
  "x-category": "other"
}

Where they differ in failing. Under both, an annotation that does not evaluate at the top level, x: Missing (in a module with from __future__ import annotations, any unresolvable name), raises NameError from inspect.signature, so at registration for a ToolRegistry. Past that, the hand-built strategy does not raise on a type: what it cannot map, or a nested reference that does not resolve, is an empty fragment. The pydantic strategy raises at derivation, so at registration for a ToolRegistry, where pydantic does: a type it cannot build a schema for (PydanticSchemaGenerationError), a reference that does not resolve (NameError), and a parameter pydantic would not keep as a field, a leading underscore or model_config (TypeError, rather than a schema silently missing an argument). A default that is not JSON-serialisable is left out of its schema, with pydantic's warning.

Pick the hand-built strategy for a schema that stays as it is across pydantic releases and does not fail a registration on a type it cannot map; pick pydantic's when a client should see what the agent's own validation sees, nested models and enums included, bar one difference: a field is keyed by its parameter's name, not by a Field alias, where the agent's validation reads the alias.

See the registry reference for the full signatures.

docs.title: Agent
docs.text: Construction: a ToolRegistry plus an AgentConfig in, a pydantic_ai.Agent out. See Concepts for what gets composed.

docs.title: AgentConfig dataclass
docs.text:
Resolved construction parameters for a Pydantic-AI Agent.

Bundles everything build_agent needs so the call site passes one record instead of a long keyword list. A transport resolves these from its own configuration and hands the record down; toolsets and capabilities arrive already resolved to instances (never dotted paths — this substrate resolves nothing from settings).

docs.title: model instance-attribute
docs.text:
model: Any

The Pydantic-AI model (a model string or Model instance).

docs.title: instructions class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
instructions: str | None = None

System/instructions prompt for the agent.

docs.title: audit_logger class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
audit_logger: AuditLogger | None = None

Wraps every server-side tool call for timing and success/failure records. None means no auditing.

docs.title: audit_ip_address class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
audit_ip_address: str | None = None

Client IP stamped onto every audit event this agent records (the view fills it from the driving request). None leaves the field unset.

docs.title: model_settings class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
model_settings: dict[str, Any] | None = None

Pydantic-AI ModelSettings (temperature, max_tokens, …).

docs.title: retries class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
retries: int | None = None

Default tool/output retry budget.

docs.title: toolsets class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
toolsets: Sequence[Any] | None = None

Extra Pydantic-AI toolsets composed alongside the registry tools.

docs.title: capabilities class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
capabilities: Sequence[Any] | None = None

Pydantic-AI capabilities passed to the Agent.

docs.title: tool_guard class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
tool_guard: ToolGuardConfig | None = None

Server-side destructive-tool approval policy. When set and enabled, build_agent composes a ToolGuard built from the registry's destructive tools; None or disabled leaves the agent ungated.

docs.title: tool_failure class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
tool_failure: ToolFailureConfig = field(default_factory=ToolFailureConfig)

What an unhandled tool exception costs. On by default, so a raising tool fails its own call and the run carries on, with the exception still reaching the audit logger and the Python logger. A plain record rather than ... | None because there is no third state, and None would have to mean "on" to keep that default — backwards next to tool_guard.

docs.title: approval_reviewer class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
approval_reviewer: ApprovalReviewerConfig | None = None

A second model that may approve a gated call in the person's place, through a ReviewedApprovals (the [harness] extra). None, the default, leaves every gated call to the person.

docs.title: loop_detection class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
loop_detection: LoopDetectionConfig | None = None

Watches the run for repeated calls, results and text, through pydantic-ai-harness's DetectLoops (the [harness] extra). None, the default, watches nothing.

docs.title: spend_limits class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
spend_limits: SpendLimitsConfig | None = None

Prices each response and refuses the next request once a budget is spent, through pydantic-ai-harness's SpendLimits (the [harness] extra). None, the default, counts nothing.

docs.title: AttachmentInlineConfig dataclass
docs.text:
Which attachment types read_attachment hands back as file content.

Tunes build_attachment_toolset, and, passed as attachment_inline=, the file results of SpecToolset, SpecCapability and build_spec_capability. media_types governs the binary attachments, where the choice is between attaching the bytes for the model to look at and returning a one-line note about a file it will never see; AttachmentInlineConfig(media_types=frozenset()) switches inlining off entirely. A textual attachment is decoded and returned as text without consulting that allowlist.

max_bytes governs both. A decoded text file reaches the provider and stays in the run's history exactly as inlined bytes do -- decoding changes the encoding, not the cost -- so a file over the limit is described rather than returned whichever branch it takes.

media_types is an allowlist rather than "everything that is not text" because bytes a provider cannot interpret make it reject the whole request: a broad rule would trade a model that cannot read your PDF for a run that does not start. max_bytes sits far below any sane upload cap because what it bounds is one request, not a stored thread — the bytes ride in a synthetic user message that stays in the run's history, so every further model request ships the file again, base64 and all.

None of it reaches the client: the bytes never travel on the event stream, and a follow-up question about the same file is answered by reading the attachment again, server-side. The decision is made on AttachmentRef.mime, which is client-declared, so a mislabelled file costs a rejected request rather than a disclosure — the store is owner-scoped either way, and the model only reaches files the acting user uploaded.

docs.title: media_types class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
media_types: frozenset[str] = frozenset(
    {"application/pdf", "image/png", "image/jpeg", "image/gif", "image/webp"}
)

Content types whose bytes are attached to the tool result; anything outside the set falls back to the one-line note.

docs.title: max_bytes class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
max_bytes: int = 4 * 1024 * 1024

Largest file, in bytes, returned rather than described -- text and binary alike. A declared AttachmentRef.size over it is trusted and refused unread; a file is otherwise measured by the bytes the store returns.

docs.title: AgentDeps dataclass
docs.text:
Per-run dependencies handed to the agent as ctx.deps.

Pydantic-AI's seam for threading request-scoped values into a run: tools, toolsets and capabilities read them off RunContext.deps instead of closing over a request, which is what lets one agent serve many requests. spec_tools' SpecToolset already reads ctx.deps.user as its default user extractor, so a run given these deps binds the acting user with nothing passed at the call site.

For more per-run context, subclass this and build it in your transport's deps_factory (AGUIServer(deps_factory=...) for django-ag-ui); the fields below are the ones the framework itself reads. The factory belongs to the transport rather than to AgentConfig because the deps are per-request and the config is not — an agent built once serves every run.

docs.title: user instance-attribute
docs.text:
user: Any

The acting Django user (request.user), or None for an unauthenticated run. Any because it is a Django boundary: a User, an AnonymousUser, or a project's own model.

Required, with no default. Pydantic-AI types deps as AgentDepsT = None and never validates it, so nothing downstream would catch a run built without one. A registry tool does not fail closed the way a spec tool does: it runs with no user context, audit records it with the fields it has, and the answer reads like any other. Saying user=None is one word, and it is a decision rather than an omission.

docs.title: ip_address class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
ip_address: str | None = None

The client IP this run was driven from, stamped onto every audit event AuditCapability records. Per-run, so it belongs here rather than on the capability's constructor — a transport that closes over an IP has an agent good for one request. The constructor argument remains the right home for a value that is genuinely fixed for the endpoint, and an unset run falls back to it.

docs.title: state class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
state: Any = None

AG-UI shared state for this run, inbound only.

Present so the deps satisfy StateHandler: the UI adapter validates the client's RunAgentInput.state into this field, and drops the state with a UserWarning when the deps type does not match. Nothing emits STATE_SNAPSHOT / STATE_DELTA back — a tool has to return those itself as ToolReturn metadata.

None keeps the default transport-agnostic: the adapter passes a raw mapping through unvalidated. Seed it with a Pydantic model instance to get validation, which the adapter runs against type(deps.state).

docs.title: progress class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
progress: Callable[..., None] | None = None

Where a spec's progress(...) calls go for this run, or None.

A django-service-specs ProgressReporter: a callable (progress, *, total, message, meta) -> None. SpecToolset reads this field by name and forwards it into the dispatch pool, so a service that declares a progress parameter reports to whatever the caller passed. Typed structurally rather than as the Protocol, which lives in an optional dependency.

Nothing here constructs one. Where a report should go is a transport's decision — an SSE frame, a task record, a log line — and a substrate that picked one would have chosen a transport it does not own. None is the honest default and costs nothing: the kernel substitutes its no-op, so a service declaring progress runs unchanged whether or not anyone is listening. A transport that wants the reports on the wire supplies the sink from its deps_factory and emits the events itself.

docs.title: call_context class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
call_context: dict[str, Any] = field(default_factory=dict)

The run's context: one plain dict of values every tool call may read.

SpecToolset reads this field by name and hands each dispatch a copy of it as the kernel's call_context, with the tool's name under action, "agent" under transport, both replacing an entry the run put there, and request, view and format set to None where the run put none. So:

  • the run's entries reach every call of the run as the same objects -- the request a run arrived on, under request, is the one a serializer, a permission check or a spec callable declaring request reads;
  • what a stage writes to the context during one call does not reach the next call, nor this dict: two calls of one run may run at once, and each carries its own action.

A new dict per deps, never a shared default. Whoever starts the run fills it, typically a transport's deps_factory. A project's own deps type without this field gets an empty context per call.

docs.title: build_agent
docs.text:
build_agent(registry: ToolRegistry, config: AgentConfig) -> Agent[AgentDeps, Any]

Build a Pydantic-AI Agent from a registry and an AgentConfig.

Each registry tool is registered as a plain Pydantic-AI tool, and config supplies the model, the toolsets and capabilities composed alongside them, and the policies below. Frontend tools declared in the AG-UI RunAgentInput are merged by the adapter, not registered here.

Three capabilities are added from config on request: an AuditCapability that times and records every tool the agent runs — registry tools and composed toolsets alike — a ToolGuard that flips destructive tools to require approval, and a ToolFailurePolicy, on unless turned off, so a raising tool fails its own call rather than the whole run. Each declares its position through get_ordering and pydantic-ai sorts them: audit innermost, so it records the tool's own execution, and the policy outermost, so it converts a failure only after every other capability has seen it. Within a tier list order breaks ties, so audit is appended after config.capabilities and the policy placed before them. What sorts after audit regardless, such as an innermost capability passed to a single run, can still reach the record; AuditCapability states that exception.

Two more are composed: config.approval_reviewer's ReviewedApprovals, when set, and always an AnsweredByMetadata, which copies an in-run answerer's answered_by mark onto the call's result. config.loop_detection adds a DetectLoops and config.spend_limits a SpendLimits (both [harness]); DetectLoops sorts outermost.

A destructive tool is not confirmed unless a config asks for it. The approval interrupt exists only when config.tool_guard is enabled, and even then it reaches a tool only if that tool's source declares the mutation — a registry @tool(destructive=True), an MCP tool, bridged or carrying its annotations in a toolset's own metadata, whose readOnlyHint is not true and destructiveHint is not false, an x-destructive schema stamp, or an explicit require_approval name. With no tool_guard, every server-side tool here runs the moment the model calls it. The browser's own confirmation card is no substitute: it is driven by a client-registered tool's schema and never sees a tool that executes server-side. A transport describing this agent to the model should say which of the two it configured.

The agent is typed Agent[AgentDeps, ...], so every run must be given AgentDeps through deps=.

docs.title: build_model_fallback
docs.text:
build_model_fallback(
    *models: str | Model, fallback_on: Any = None, sticky: bool = False
) -> ModelFallback[Any]

A ModelFallback capability whose models are built now, not mid-outage.

Pass it in AgentConfig.capabilities. When the agent's model fails, refuses (finish_reason='content_filter') or is cut off at max_tokens (finish_reason='length'), the next model here serves the same request step, and the answer's ModelResponse.model_id names the model that gave it.

Each "provider:name" string goes through the same builder as the agent's own model, so the gemini: alias applies and a name no provider resolves, or a provider with no key in its environment variable, raises ImproperlyConfigured here, at configuration time. A bare ModelFallback("provider:name") would resolve the string only on its first attempt, the moment the primary is already down. The agent's api_key is never reused: a fallback usually sits at another provider, so a string reads that provider's own environment variable, and a model needing an explicit key or provider is passed as a built Model.

fallback_on and sticky pass through to ModelFallback; left out, fallback_on keeps its default (ModelAPIError, ContentFilterError, OutputTokenLimitExceeded). With sticky=True, a conversation that fell back stays on the model that answered, across later runs continuing the stored history.

An agent spec needs none of this: ModelFallback.from_spec builds it from a spec's capabilities list, resolving its names on attempt.

docs.title: build_tool_catalog
docs.text:
build_tool_catalog(
    registry: ToolRegistry,
    *,
    mcp_server: Any = None,
    service_specs: dict[str, Any] | None = None,
) -> list[dict[str, Any]]

The agent's server-tool catalog for the frontend to label tool-call cards.

Server-side tools execute server-side, so their JSON Schema never reaches the browser and a web component cannot read an x-summary off it. This catalog is that channel: the component fetches it and maps tool name to label.

Each entry is {"name", "summary", "description"?}. summary is always present, resolved from @tool(summary=...) for registry tools and from display_name then title for an MCP server's, falling back to a prettified name. description is carried through when the source has one.

The catalog covers these sources and no others. A tool attached through a transport's capabilities= / toolsets= is not listed and its card falls back to a prettified name — a degraded label, not a broken call. Enumerating those is not possible here: pydantic-ai exposes tool names only through AbstractToolset.get_tools, which is async and needs a RunContext, while this runs at configuration time with no run in sight. Route spec tools through a transport's service_specs= to keep labels.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default registry ToolRegistry

The @tool registry, listed first; it wins name collisions.

required mcp_server Any

A django-spec-mcp MCPServer whose registered tools are appended.

None service_specs dict[str, Any] | None

A name -> spec mapping whose tools are appended, each described by its service or selector callable's docstring.

None

Returns:

Type Description list[dict[str, Any]]

One entry per tool, in that source order.

docs.title: AgentFactoryFn
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

The escape-hatch signature for a transport's agent_factory= argument.

A callable of this shape fully replaces build_agent, giving a project complete control over Agent construction. It receives the server-side tool registry and the calling transport's own resolved config record, which is untyped here because this substrate owns no settings namespace; each transport documents the concrete type its users receive.

The returned agent must be built with deps_type=AgentDeps. Transports hand every run an AgentDeps, and that is how the acting user reaches spec tools and how AG-UI state reaches deps.state. A factory that omits it produces an agent whose tools see no user.

docs.title: Child sessions
docs.text: The toolset, the lineage a child carries, the report frame, the delivery of a thread's inbound messages and the types around them. See Child sessions for the narrative. Each imports from its own module under django_spec_agents.child_sessions, except ChildLineageRecord, which a Conversation holds and so lives under django_spec_agents.persistence.types.

docs.title: ChildSessionsToolset
docs.text:
Bases: FunctionToolset[Any]

Tools to start, list, check, message, answer and cancel child sessions; a child asks.

start_session starts a child on one of agents (an id to a description the model reads) through runner, as the run's own user, and returns a ChildSessionReceipt naming its thread. list_tasks, check_task, message_task, answer_task and cancel_task keep upstream TaskControl's names, so a mount carrying both is refused by pydantic-ai's duplicate-name check; ask_parent is offered in a child only, and parks it as waiting on a question.

Needs the [harness] extra. Starts run one at a time, so each reads the index after the last; an anonymous run is refused. A start passes the runner lineage= alone, from which it composes child_lineage_for; with spend, an exhausted budget refuses it first. Each limit in limits refuses a start with a ChildSessionRefusal.

The run's thread is ctx.conversation_id and its request is ctx.deps.call_context["request"], as a transport's default deps put it there.

docs.title: ChildLineage dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: AbstractCapability[Any]

Where a child run sits in its tree, and the tools its parent had: composed into the child.

depth counts from the root thread at 0. The child sees only the tools named in tools beside the child-session tools, so it is never wider than its parent, and a tool named in gated asks for approval in the child as it did in the parent, on top of the child mount's own guards.

docs.title: ChildReport dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: AbstractCapability[Any]

Enqueues a child run's report on its parent's inbound queue when the run settles.

Needs [harness], checked when built. A run that parks, or is cancelled before its deadline, sends nothing; a failed enqueue is logged and never replaces the run's own. A spend limit reports budget, as a usage limit does, and a DetectLoops stop failed, its text naming the loop. With user_joined, the report's framed body ends with a line telling the parent that the user joined the child's session, so its result may reflect the user's direction.

docs.title: child_lineage_for
docs.text:
child_lineage_for(
    conversation: Conversation,
    *,
    agent_id: str,
    owner: str,
    queue: InboundQueue,
    spend: ChildSessionSpend | None = None,
    user_joined: bool = False,
) -> list[AbstractCapability[Any]]

The capabilities a run of a child's thread composes, rebuilt from its stored lineage.

The same ones start_session gave its first run: the parent's tool bounds, the report on settle, and, with spend, the tree and day budgets. agent_id is the child's mount and owner its user's id; a thread with no stored lineage gets none. user_joined is passed to the report, for a run the user joined in the child's thread.

docs.title: ChildLineageRecord dataclass
docs.text:
What a child thread keeps of its lineage, so a later run of it rebuilds the same bounds.

root and depth place it in its tree; tools and gated are its parent's tools and the ones the parent gated, as sorted lists so the record crosses a queue.

The record as the JSON a store keeps.

from_json(data: dict[str, Any]) -> ChildLineageRecord

docs.title: DrainInbound dataclass
docs.text:
Bases: AbstractCapability[Any]

Hands a thread's inbound messages to its model: at each model request, and before it ends.

Compose it into every run of a mount whose threads receive reports, questions, answers or steering, with the mount's agent_id as the thread's scope. A report arrives as the <task_output> text its child framed, a question as <task_question> data naming the asking thread, an answer or steering as the parent's plain words. A report's and a question's TextContent.metadata holds origin and task; an answer and steering carry none. A message that arrives after the last request is delivered by a further request, unless the run parks: then it waits for the resume.

The run takes the thread's inbox with queue.take under its run_id, renewing its claim for lease at each take, so one run holds a thread's inbox at a time and sees each message once. It acks each message once the model request carrying it is answered, and releases the inbox when it ends, parks or fails, handing on what it took and never acked; the messages of a run that dies wait until its lease lapses. A run with no signed-in user in call_context["request"] reads nothing.

    prompt: str = _WAKE_PROMPT,
) -> HeadlessStart | None

Start a headless run on thread if it is idle and its inbound queue holds messages.

Call it after enqueueing for thread, and the runner after each run ends. By the thread's state in runs: running, it does nothing, since the run reads the queue at its next model request, or, for one that lands after its last read, the runner's wake once it ends; waiting on questions only, with an ANSWER pending for each, it resumes the parked calls, starting the run with answers= mapping each waiting call's id, in order, to the oldest answers' texts. It pairs them under a claim on the inbox (take, then release) held across the start, so of two wakes racing on one park only one pairs them, and the resumed run's drain takes nothing until the wake acks them once the start returns; a wake that finds the inbox claimed starts nothing, and a start that fails, is cancelled or dies before the run claims the thread leaves the answers pending for the next wake. An ack lost once the run started lets its drain deliver them again, as the queue's at-least-once, and the claim holds the thread's other messages from the resumed run until the wake releases it. Waiting on anything else, or on more questions than there are answers, it does nothing, since a second run must not start before the resume, which reads the queue; idle, failed or never run, with messages pending, it starts one run on the thread's scope as request.user, with prompt as its new message (by default a line saying messages arrived), and returns it. For a runner opted in as a PromptMetadataRunner, that start also passes prompt_metadata={"origin": "wake"}, for the runner to keep on the stored message, whatever prompt says; a resume sends no prompt and passes none. The run's mount composes DrainInbound to read them.

It never passes the runner capabilities. With conversations, the store the thread's mount reads (scoped as that mount scopes it), a child's thread is started with the parent and lineage its conversation stores, from which the runner composes its bounds; a thread with neither stored, or no conversations, is started with neither. It passes the stored routine_id the same way, and as parent_run_id the parked run a resume answers, None for any other start. A message another run took and has not released starts nothing: that run hands it on when it releases the inbox, and a run that died holding it leaves it for the next run the thread starts once its lease lapses.

When two wakes race, the runner's claim lets one run start; the other's refusal is absorbed once the thread reads as running.

docs.title: WakingInboundQueue dataclass
docs.text:
An InboundQueue that wakes the thread it enqueues for, through wake_thread.

Pass it where the toolset and child_lineage_for take a queue: a child's report and question then wake an idle parent, and message_task or answer_task wakes a settled child. conversations maps an agent id to the store its mount reads, so a child's thread wakes with its stored parent and lineage. A wake that fails is logged and the message stays queued for the thread's next run.

docs.title: report_frame
docs.text:
report_frame(
    child: ThreadRef, *, agent_id: str, output: str, outcome: ReportOutcome = "ok"
) -> UserPromptPart

A settled child's report to its parent, framed as <task_output> data.

The frame is upstream's DelegationTask.report() tag and attributes, rendered with pydantic_ai.framing.wrap so the text keeps its escaping once it crosses a queue: the child's output never enters system voice, cannot close its own frame and cannot forge a <task_question>. The task id is the child's thread id, and outcome is on the tag only when it is not ok. The text's TextContent.metadata, which the model never sees, holds origin (task_output) and task: taskId, threadId, agentName, outcome (ok included) and body, output unframed.

A child session as its parent sees it: the child's thread and where its runs stand.

A child is live while it runs or waits, since a parked child still holds its slot; waiting holds the calls it parked on; reason says why its last run ended early.

docs.title: ChildSessionIndex
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Finds child sessions, for the limits and for cancel: the two questions no store answers.

Keyed like a ConversationStore, by the owner each method resolves from its request. A child's link to its parent is the parent its conversation stores, in any scope, so an index reads those links and the children's run status beside them. A child must be listed from the moment HeadlessRunner.start returns, or two starts in a row both pass the per-thread limit.

docs.title: ChildSessionLimits dataclass
docs.text:
How far child sessions may go: their depth, how many run at once, and each run's deadline.

timeout is each child run's deadline in seconds, required as a routine's is. A root thread is depth 0, so the default max_depth of 2 allows a child and a grandchild. The running limits count children that run or wait: per parent thread, and per user across every thread.

docs.text:

tree_usd caps the whole tree under one root thread, for all time; day_usd caps one user's children per day. store is the harness BatchSpendStore the counters live in, Any because the harness is optional: it must be one every worker shares, never an in-memory store. None for a budget counts and never stops.

docs.title: Integrations
docs.text: Optional bridges exposing declared specs as agent tools. Each is lazily imported and lives under django_spec_agents.integrations rather than being re-exported at the package root, so the base install pulls none of their dependencies. See Integrations for which to choose.

docs.title: build_spec_capability
docs.text:
build_spec_capability(
    specs: Mapping[str, Any] | SpecSource,
    *,
    exclude_names: frozenset[str] = frozenset(),
    attachment_inline: AttachmentInlineConfig | None = None,
) -> Any

A SpecCapability over specs, acting as the run's deps.user.

Each spec is called in process through the kernel's dispatch, which enforces its permissions. Nothing here closes over a request: SpecToolset's default extractor already reads ctx.deps.user, so a run given AgentDeps binds the acting user natively and the capability stays request-independent, which is what makes an agent built once reusable across runs.

Every spec here needs its own permissions. A spec with permissions=None makes SpecCapability raise ImproperlyConfigured rather than expose an ungated tool: over HTTP None may mean inherit, from the view and then the project's defaults, and off HTTP there is nothing to inherit from, so a spec properly guarded behind a view would become callable by whatever the model decides to call.

The require_permissions=False migration flag is not exposed here; a project migrating a large registry constructs SpecCapability itself and passes it to AgentConfig(capabilities=...). That path skips the tool-catalog registration this function participates in, so tool-call cards render unlabelled — a migration step, not a destination.

A registry is passed through as a registry, narrowed with its own subset when exclude_names bites. Flattening it to a mapping first would drop everything the entry carries beyond the spec -- including the OfflineContract that says what a caller with no HTTP request has to be told -- and drop it silently, since the resulting toolset is well-formed and merely missing declarations nobody asked it for.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default specs Mapping[str, Any] | SpecSource

A name -> ServiceSpec/SelectorSpec mapping, or a spec registry to read one from. Prefer the registry: it is the same specs plus the per-entry declarations an agent transport reads.

required exclude_names frozenset[str]

Names a higher-precedence source (the @tool registry, the MCP bridge) already claimed. They are dropped so that source wins the collision, since pydantic-ai raises UserError for a duplicate name at run time.

frozenset() attachment_inline AttachmentInlineConfig | None

The AttachmentInlineConfig a spec tool's file result is read with, as SpecToolset's keyword of that name. Pass the one read_attachment is given, so one config governs both.

None

docs.title: resolve_spec_mapping
docs.text:
resolve_spec_mapping(specs: Mapping[str, Any] | SpecSource) -> Mapping[str, Any]

Return the name -> spec mapping, whether given one or a registry.

A SpecSource is recognised structurally, by having a specs() method.

Public because a transport needs the same normalisation before build_spec_capability runs, when it reserves each tool name for collision detection: iterating a registry yields RegisteredSpec records rather than names, so a transport that iterated the raw argument would fill its set with dataclasses and silently stop detecting collisions.

docs.title: SpecSource
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Anything that can hand back a name -> spec mapping.

django-service-specs' SpecRegistry is the intended implementation: a project exposing the same specs over more than one transport declares them there once, and each transport reads that source.

It is matched structurally rather than imported, because this substrate depends on pydantic-ai-slim alone and the kernel arrives only with the optional [specs] extra. Naming SpecRegistry in a signature would force that dependency on every install or bury the type behind a lazy import where a signature cannot reach it.

A plain dict is not a SpecSource — it has no specs() — which is what lets a caller accept either and tell them apart.

docs.title: specs
docs.text:
specs() -> dict[str, Any]

The name -> spec mapping this source declares.

docs.title: MCPToolset
docs.text:
Bases: AbstractToolset[Any]

Exposes a django-spec-mcp MCPServer's tools as a Pydantic-AI toolset.

Built per request, so the agent acts as the request's logged-in user. Both schemas and execution route through django-spec-mcp's public in-process surface (MCPServer.list_tools / acall_tool), so the advertised parameters, the kernel's argument validation and the spec's permissions match the HTTP transport exactly, without the network hop. Tool definitions carry the default kind="function", the in-process kind the run loop calls itself; an external tool would instead be deferred to the client and never run.

Definitions once, availability every step. django-spec-mcp leaves a tool out of tools/list while an operation-scope affordance refuses it, and whether one does can change mid-run — an admin closes the books. So the definitions are listed once, with every tool the user may see, and each step asks django-spec-mcp which of them a fresh listing would leave out (aunavailable_tools): those are not offered that step, and the instructions name each with its reason, so a model asked for one can say why rather than guess or deny the operation exists. A server declaring no such condition answers that without leaving the event loop.

Failures split four ways, along MCP's protocol-vs-tool boundary:

  • JSON-RPC -32602 and tool-level validation_error and input_required results raise pydantic_ai.ModelRetry, so the model calls again with the field errors fixed or the missing input supplied, instead of the run dying;
  • every other tool-level failure (service_error, not_found, a timeout, an oversized result) raises pydantic_ai.ToolFailed, so the model reads the sentence and the call is recorded outcome="failed";
  • a permission refusing the user (-32006) raises Django's PermissionDenied, which ToolFailurePolicy passes through by default, so the run ends;
  • every other protocol fault raises RuntimeError: auth, rate limits, and an internal error (-32603), which is also the answer to a service asking for an input its spec does not declare in reads=, since no answer to it could reach the service. ToolFailurePolicy converts it to a failed call, so the run goes on.

Running in process, the server has no client to ask, so a service's AdditionalInputRequired for inputs its spec declares arrives degraded, as input_required.

The mapping is the one spec_tools applies to the same exceptions raised in process, except for a selector's AdditionalInputRequired: django-spec-mcp builds no input round for a selector, so it arrives as a service error and raises ToolFailed, where spec_tools raises ModelRetry. A refusal reads identically through both: The books are closed. (code: books_closed).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default server Any

The django-spec-mcp MCPServer whose registry is bridged.

required request HttpRequest

The request carried into every call; its user is the acting user.

required exclude_names frozenset[str]

Names the @tool registry has already claimed. A colliding server tool is skipped, so the registry wins — the rule build_tool_catalog applies — because pydantic-ai raises UserError for a duplicate name at run time.

frozenset() max_retries int

Per-tool retry budget: how many times a ModelRetry is fed back to the model before the run aborts. The default matches pydantic-ai's own function-tool default.

1

docs.title: get_tools async
docs.text:
get_tools(ctx: Any) -> dict[str, ToolsetTool[Any]]

The tools this step may call: every definition, less the unavailable.

Definitions come from django-spec-mcp's tools/list once per toolset, which is once per request. Availability is asked again here every step, because pydantic-ai calls this once per step and a condition may flip between two: offering a tool django-spec-mcp would leave out only invites a refusal, and withholding one that became available hides an operation the model could now perform. The call enforces every condition whatever was offered.

docs.title: get_instructions async
docs.text:
get_instructions(ctx: Any) -> str | None

Name each tool left out this step, with the reason its condition gives.

get_tools withholds such a tool, so without this the model sees neither it nor any sign it exists, and a user asking for it gets a guess where a sentence was available. None when nothing is left out, which is every step for a server declaring no operation condition.

Asked separately from get_tools, as the spec-tools route asks: the run context carries no key that could safely scope one answer to one step, and asking twice costs a second evaluation of conditions that read only seeds. A condition flipping between the two reads can leave one step's tools and instructions disagreeing about a tool; the call's own enforcement is authoritative either way.
