docs.title: Persistence
docs.text: Store contracts, their value types, and the shipped implementations. See Storage for owner scoping, thread keying, and the reference models.

docs.title: ConversationStore
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Pluggable server-side persistence for AG-UI conversations.

Handed to a transport. The package ships NullConversationStore (the server stays stateless) and a session-backed implementation; projects supply their own. All methods are async so an implementation can use the async ORM or a network backend.

Threads key by (owner_id, thread_id), so two endpoints sharing a store share one user's thread list. Wrap with ScopedConversationStore to partition them.

list returns owner-scoped metadata only, no message bodies, capped at limit rows (None for the store's own default); a store that cannot enumerate returns an empty list. exists is a presence check that loads no message body, so a rename or probe does not deserialize a whole thread just to 404. rename sets a display title, and is a no-op in a store that cannot persist one.

docs.title: Conversation dataclass
docs.text:
A persisted conversation, keyed by thread_id.

messages are JSON-serialisable records whose shape the calling transport owns: this substrate persists and returns them verbatim and never interprets them, which is what keeps the storage contract neutral. The AG-UI transport stores its own wire Message shape, so client message ids survive a round trip untouched; another transport stores its own.

owner_id scopes the conversation to a user for authorization. parent is the thread that started this one as a child session, and lineage the bounds it runs under; a store that keeps either writes it when given and leaves it alone when it is None. routine_id is the routine whose firing started the thread, kept the same way.

docs.title: ConversationMeta dataclass
docs.text:
Lightweight metadata for one conversation: the thread-drawer row shape.

Returned by ConversationStore.list, and carrying no message bodies, which is what keeps a thread list cheap. title defaults to a truncation of the first user message unless a store records a rename, preview is a one-line excerpt of the latest message, and updated_at is None in a store that does not track it. owner_id scopes the conversation to a user and is not surfaced on the wire. parent is the thread that started this one as a child session, in any scope; None for a thread of its own. routine_id is the routine whose firing started it, None for any other thread.

docs.title: NullConversationStore
docs.text:
The default store: no-op, keeping the server stateless.

load returns None and save / delete do nothing, so the conversation lives entirely in the client's posted history. A transport treats this store as "persistence off".

docs.title: DjangoSessionConversationStore
docs.text:
Conversation persistence in the Django session, needing no migration.

Conversations are namespaced by thread_id inside the user's own session, so owner scoping is implicit and durability lasts as long as that browser session. For cross-device or audited persistence, use a model-backed store.

docs.title: ModelConversationStore
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

Abstract base for a model-backed (or any sync) ConversationStore.

Provides the async wrapping and per-request owner scoping; a subclass implements the three abstract synchronous row operations (_fetch / _store / _remove) against its own Django model, and may override _list / _exists / _rename. Model-agnostic on purpose — the package ships no concrete model, so it forces no migration and consumers define the fields and the owner relation.

Each hook receives the resolved owner_id (the user's id, or anon:<session key> for an anonymous visitor when allow_anonymous is on; otherwise the request is refused before the hook runs) and must filter by it, so threads never cross users.

allow_anonymous governs whether anonymous requests are served. False refuses them rather than collapsing every anonymous visitor into one shared owner bucket where they could read and delete each other's data. It is a store policy, so two endpoints sharing a store necessarily agree on it. Pass it explicitly: this substrate reads no Django settings.

unlink_parent (see UnlinkableConversationStore) is offered only by a subclass that defines a synchronous _unlink_parent(thread_id, owner_id) hook, which clears that owner's thread's parent link and lineage. A subclass without one is not unlinkable, so a transport never believes a link it cannot clear was cleared.

Example:

class MyStore(ModelConversationStore):
    def _fetch(self, thread_id, owner_id):
        row = MyConversation.objects.filter(
            thread_id=thread_id, owner_id=owner_id,
        ).first()
        return None if row is None else Conversation(...)
    def _store(self, conversation, owner_id): ...
    def _remove(self, thread_id, owner_id): ...

docs.title: ScopedConversationStore
docs.text:
Partition another ConversationStore by a scope name.

Stores key threads by (owner_id, thread_id). Two AG-UI endpoints sharing one store therefore share one user's thread list: a conversation started at /internal/agent appears in /public/agent's history drawer and can be resumed there — under the public agent's model, tools and guard policy.

Wrapping fixes that without a migration:

internal = AGUIServer(
    registry,
    conversation_store=ScopedConversationStore(store, scope="internal"),
)
public = AGUIServer(
    registry,
    conversation_store=ScopedConversationStore(store, scope="public"),
)

The partition is a thread-id prefix, so this composes with any implementation, third-party ones included, where a scope column would mean a migration and a breaking change to the ConversationStore protocol every custom store implements.

Opt in explicitly. A transport does not wrap by itself: doing so from its namespace would silently orphan the whole thread history of an existing single-endpoint project the moment it set one.

check_identifiers is forwarded, with the prefix applied to thread_id, only when the inner store has it; preflight_identifiers skips one without. unlink_parent is offered the same way, only over an UnlinkableConversationStore. A thread_id refused there or by save is reported at the length the client sent, against the room the prefix leaves.

The scope is invisible on the wire. Thread ids are echoed back to the client unchanged; only the storage key carries the prefix.

: is reserved and a scope containing one is refused. The prefix is the whole partition, so an ambiguous prefix is an ambiguous partition: with scopes admin and admin:readonly, the readonly mount's thread keys to admin:readonly:t1, which the admin mount's own prefix filter matches. It would list that thread as readonly:t1, and load, rename and delete would all resolve there — silently, in both directions, since thread ids come from the client. Refused at construction rather than escaped at the key, because escaping would rewrite the storage key of every thread already saved. Scopes that merely share a prefix (admin / administrators) are unaffected: the separator ends the scope.

docs.title: list async
docs.text:
list(*, request: HttpRequest, limit: int | None = None) -> ConversationMetaList

This scope's threads only, with storage keys translated back.

limit is applied by the inner store before this filter, so a busy sibling scope can crowd out rows. A store needing exact per-scope paging should partition at the query rather than by wrapping.

docs.title: UnlinkableConversationStore
docs.text:
Bases: ConversationStore, Protocol

A conversation store that can clear a thread's parent link.

A ConversationStore with one more method. Optional: a store written against ConversationStore alone stays one, and a transport checks isinstance(store, UnlinkableConversationStore) before it calls unlink_parent. DefaultConversationStore is one, and so is a ScopedConversationStore over one.

docs.title: unlink_parent async
docs.text:
unlink_parent(thread_id: str, *, request: HttpRequest) -> None

Clear the owner's thread's parent and lineage, leaving an ordinary thread.

Owner-scoped like every other method: a missing thread, or another owner's, is left alone. Saving the thread again with a parent links it again, so a caller unlinks a child once its run has ended.

docs.title: AttachmentStore
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Pluggable server-side storage for files a user attaches to a conversation.

Handed to a transport. The package ships NullAttachmentStore (uploads off) and the abstract ModelAttachmentStore; the opt-in django_spec_agents.contrib.store app adds a ready DefaultAttachmentStore keeping bytes in Django Storage and metadata in a row.

Every method is async and owner-scoped: a store filters by the acting user so one user can never read or delete another's files, the security boundary for the whole feature. save validates nothing about size or type — the view does that from its own config — and just persists the bytes, returning a durable AttachmentRef. open returns None for a missing or cross-owner id rather than raising, so a caller maps both to a 404 and the two stay indistinguishable. open must not block the event loop; read_attachment reads the handle in a thread.

Attachments need no scoped wrapper of the kind conversations have: they are id-referenced with no enumeration and already owner-scoped, so two endpoints sharing a store expose nothing across the user boundary. Thread lists are the case that leaks.

docs.title: AttachmentRef dataclass
docs.text:
A durable, lightweight reference to one uploaded file.

What an upload returns and what travels on the wire — never the bytes. The file is uploaded out of band, the client holds this ref on the message, and the agent reads the bytes server-side through the read_attachment tool.

id is the opaque, owner-scoped handle the store resolves back to bytes. mime is client-declared, so treat it as a hint. url is an optional direct fetch URL, such as an owner-checked download endpoint, and stays None unless a store fills it in.

docs.title: OpenedAttachment dataclass
docs.text:
An attachment's metadata paired with a readable byte stream.

Returned by AttachmentStore.open, so a download view and the read_attachment tool both get the content and the AttachmentRef in one owner-scoped call.

content is an open binary stream rather than the bytes, so a large attachment streams out instead of being buffered. The consumer owns it and must read it exactly once — hand it to FileResponse, which closes it, or read it under a with block.

docs.title: NullAttachmentStore
docs.text:
The default attachment store: uploads disabled, server stays stateless.

A transport's attachments view detects this store and answers 410 Gone, so a misconfigured client gets a clear "uploads are off" signal rather than a silent success, and save is never reached. Called directly it raises, rather than fabricating a ref. open returns None so every fetch is a 404, and delete is a no-op: the endpoint is inert until a real store is configured.

docs.title: ModelAttachmentStore
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

Abstract base for a model-backed (or any sync) AttachmentStore.

The attachment twin of ModelConversationStore — same async wrapping, same per-request owner scoping, same allow_anonymous policy — over a subclass's own storage: a Django Storage for the bytes, a model row for the metadata. The opt-in django_spec_agents.contrib.store app supplies a concrete pair.

Each _save / _open / _remove receives the resolved owner_id (the user's id, or anon:<session key> for an anonymous visitor when allow_anonymous is on; otherwise the request is refused before the hook runs) and must filter by it, so files never cross users.

Example:

class MyStore(ModelAttachmentStore):
    def _save(self, upload, owner_id):
        row = MyAttachment.objects.create(owner_id=owner_id or "", ...)
        row.file.save(row.attachment_id, upload, save=True)
        return AttachmentRef(id=row.attachment_id, name=..., mime=..., size=...)
    def _open(self, attachment_id, owner_id): ...
    def _remove(self, attachment_id, owner_id): ...

docs.title: memory_namespace
docs.text:
memory_namespace(request: HttpRequest) -> str

The per-user namespace for pydantic_ai_harness.memory.Memory, from a request.

For a host that builds the capability per request and therefore holds one::

Memory(store, namespace=lambda ctx: memory_namespace(request))

Most transports do not: AGUIServer(capabilities=...) resolves its list once at mount time, where no request exists. Reach for memory_namespace_for_user there. The one thing this resolver can do that the other cannot is key an anonymous caller to their browser session, so anonymous visitors get separate namespaces instead of sharing one.

Not resolve_owner_id, and the difference is load-bearing. That helper returns anon:<session_key> for an anonymous request, and a colon is not in the alphabet the harness accepts for a path segment -- so Memory raises ValueError: invalid memory path for every anonymous visitor. That raise happens in the capability's for_run, which is outside the store read that injection_errors guards, so the harness's own "ignore" default does not catch it and the whole run aborts. Hence a separate resolver whose only contract is that its result is always a valid segment.

An identifier that is already segment-safe is used as-is behind a prefix; one that is not is replaced by a digest of it rather than sanitised, because stripping the offending characters maps tenant/42 and tenant-42 onto one namespace.

docs.title: memory_namespace_for_user
docs.text:
memory_namespace_for_user(user: Any) -> str

The namespace for pydantic_ai_harness.memory.Memory, from the acting user.

The resolver to use when the capability is constructed at mount time, which is where every transport takes it — AGUIServer(capabilities=...) resolves its list once, and no request exists yet::

Memory(store, namespace=lambda ctx: memory_namespace_for_user(ctx.deps.user))

Reading the user off ctx.deps rather than closing over a request is what lets one agent, built once, serve every caller: pydantic-ai clones each capability per run and Memory re-resolves its scope in the clone. AgentDeps.user is set by the transport from the authenticated request, so it is server-resolved and not something a client can choose.

Use memory_namespace instead when the store really is built per request and you hold one: it can key an anonymous caller to their browser session, which this cannot. With no request there is no session, so every unauthenticated caller shares one namespace — a real limitation rather than an oversight, and rarely reached, since a transport that serves anonymous callers at all has opted into it deliberately.

The result is always a valid harness path segment: a segment-safe primary key is carried through readably behind a u- prefix, and anything else — an email-address primary key, a natural key with a slash, a pathological 200-character pk that no longer fits once prefixed — is replaced by a digest.

docs.title: AnonymousOperationError
docs.text:
Bases: Exception

Raised when a model-backed store is asked to act for an anonymous request.

The reference stores refuse anonymous operations unless constructed with allow_anonymous=True, since otherwise every anonymous visitor would share one owner bucket and could read or delete the others' data. A transport's persistence views catch this and return 403.

docs.title: IdentifierTooLongError
docs.text:
Bases: ValueError

Raised before a store write when an id is longer than the column that holds it.

Its message names the field and the limit; nothing was written. The default stores also set field, length and limit; each is None when the raiser did not say.

docs.title: RunIdReusedError
docs.text:
Bases: ValueError

Raised by a run store's claim for a run id its owner has claimed before.

Run ids are single-use per owner: a resumed or retried run claims under a fresh id. Nothing was written; run_id names the refused id. A transport maps it to a client error rather than a server one.

docs.title: preflight_identifiers
docs.text:
preflight_identifiers(store: object, **ids: str | None) -> None

Refuse ids too long for store before a run writes them, writing nothing.

Calls store.check_identifiers(**ids) when the store has that method, which raises IdentifierTooLongError for an id longer than its column. A store without it, a custom one included, is accepted and nothing happens: the method is on no protocol, so an id it cannot hold is still refused when it writes. Each default store of django_spec_agents.contrib.store documents the keywords it takes.

docs.title: Runs
docs.text: A run's status and event log, and the protocol a transport implements to start runs on the server. See Storage.

docs.title: RunStore
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Where a thread's run status and each run's event log live, apart from its transcript.

A run that outlives its request (detached from a browser, or started with no stream at all) needs both: a status any process can read, and a log a reader can catch up on. The transcript, partial output included, stays in the ConversationStore; this protocol adds no method to it.

Keyed like a ConversationStore: every method but prune takes the request, and the store scopes rows by the owner it resolves from it.

One run per thread. claim takes active_run_id in one conditional update, won when the thread holds no run or its holder's lease has lapsed; a second claim loses and learns the holder. The holder keeps its claim alive with renew and gives it up with finish. renew, append and finish refuse, returning False or None, a run that is not the thread's live holder, so an owner presumed dead cannot overwrite its successor.

A lapsed lease reads as a failure. get reports a running thread whose lease has lapsed as failed with reason interrupted.

The log is append-only and numbered. append numbers a batch of opaque JSON events on from the run's last, starting at 1; nothing edits or removes an entry but prune, which drops whole logs a window after their run ended.

docs.title: claim async
docs.text:
claim(
    thread_id: str, run_id: str, *, request: HttpRequest, lease: timedelta
) -> RunClaim

Take the thread for run_id with a lease of lease, unless a live run holds it.

Run ids are single-use per owner: a resumed or retried run claims under a fresh id, and an id the owner has claimed before raises RunIdReusedError with nothing written.

docs.title: renew async
docs.text:
renew(thread_id: str, run_id: str, *, request: HttpRequest, lease: timedelta) -> bool

Extend the live holder's lease to lease from now; False if run_id lost it.

Release the claim and record how the run ended; waiting goes with WAITING.

docs.text:

Append events to the run's log, numbered; the last number, or None if refused.

The run's entries numbered above after, in order, at most limit of them.

The thread's run state, or None if no run ever claimed it.

The run state of each listed thread that has one, keyed by thread id.

docs.title: ResumableRunStore
docs.text:
Bases: RunStore, Protocol

A run store that resumes a parked run once and gives a claim back.

A RunStore with two more pieces.

Optional: a store written against RunStore alone stays one, and a transport checks isinstance(store, ResumableRunStore) before it passes resumes= or calls release. That check sees method names only, so a store that defines release must also take resumes=. DefaultRunStore is one.

docs.title: claim async
docs.text:
claim(
    thread_id: str,
    run_id: str,
    *,
    request: HttpRequest,
    lease: timedelta,
    resumes: str | None = None,
) -> RunClaim

RunStore.claim; with resumes, won only while the thread is parked on that run.

The condition and the claim are one conditional update, so of two claims resuming the same parked run exactly one wins. A refused resume raises RunNotParkedError, never answers busy, and writes nothing: the thread is running (its holder named), idle, failed, parked on another run, or running under a lapsed lease.

docs.title: release async
docs.text:
release(thread_id: str, run_id: str, *, request: HttpRequest) -> bool

Give back a claim run_id still holds, restoring what the claim replaced.

The thread's status, reason, waiting record and last_run_id return to what they were before the claim (a holder the claim displaced reads as failed, interrupted), its lease and cancel are cleared, a thread no run had claimed reads as unknown again, and the released run's log is deleted, so its id may be claimed again. False, with nothing changed, if run_id is not the thread's live holder.

docs.title: WatchableRunStore
docs.text:
Bases: RunStore, Protocol

A run store a reader can wait on, rather than reading the log again and again.

A RunStore with one more method.

Optional: a store written against RunStore alone stays one, and a reader checks isinstance(store, WatchableRunStore) before it calls wait, falling back to its own polling of read otherwise. DefaultRunStore is one.

docs.title: wait async
docs.text:
wait(run_id: str, *, after: int, timeout: timedelta, request: HttpRequest) -> bool

Return once the run's log has an entry numbered above after, or the run ended.

True then, and at once when either already holds; False when timeout passes with neither. A run with no log (never claimed by this owner, released or pruned) answers True at once, so the reader goes back to read and get rather than waiting on nothing. A run whose owner died without finishing is not ended: the reader's timeout and get, which reads its lapsed lease as failed, cover it.

docs.title: RunNotParkedError
docs.text:
Bases: ValueError

Raised by claim(..., resumes=...) when the thread is not waiting on the run it resumes.

The thread is running (another resume may have won it), idle, failed, parked on another run, or its run's lease lapsed. Nothing was written; run_id names the run the claim meant to resume, and active_run_id the thread's live holder, if any. A transport maps it to a conflict answer, not a server error.

docs.title: RunClaim dataclass
docs.text:
The answer to RunStore.claim: whether the run won the thread.

active_run_id is the run holding the thread afterwards: the claimant on a win, the run that kept it on a loss, so a transport's 409 can name it.

docs.title: RunOutcome
docs.text:
Bases: StrEnum

How a run ended, as its owner reports it to RunStore.finish.

Outcome Thread status Reason completed idle none waiting waiting none cancelled idle none timed_out idle timed_out error failed error

docs.title: RunWaiting dataclass
docs.text:
One deferred call a parked run waits on, which a person has to answer.

kind is upstream's DeferredToolKind: approval, question (a tool that deferred with CallDeferred(kind="question")) or external (a client tool for a detached browser run); build_run_waiting reads it from the run's DeferredToolRequests. summary is the approval prompt where one is configured and the tool's name otherwise. destructive is ToolGuard.requires_approval's answer for the call's tool.

docs.title: build_run_waiting
docs.text:
build_run_waiting(
    requests: DeferredToolRequests,
    tool_call_id: str,
    *,
    summary: str,
    destructive: bool,
) -> RunWaiting

The RunWaiting a run parked on tool_call_id records.

Its kind is requests.kind(tool_call_id), so a stored row carries upstream's word for the deferral; a tool_call_id the requests do not hold raises ValueError.

docs.title: ThreadRunState dataclass
docs.text:
One thread's run status, as a RunStore reads it.

active_run_id is the run holding the claim, None once it ends or its lease lapses. last_run_id outlives it: a parked run's id is what a resume answers to, while the resumed run claims a fresh id. A running thread whose lease has lapsed reads as failed with reason interrupted. waiting holds every call a parked run waits on, empty otherwise. cancel_requested is set by a cancel the run's owner has yet to act on. last_read_at is when a reader last marked the thread read, None if never.

docs.title: ThreadRunStatus
docs.text:
Bases: StrEnum

Where a thread's runs stand, as a RunStore reports it.

running while a run holds the thread's claim under a live lease; waiting when the last run parked on deferred calls; failed when it raised or its lease lapsed; idle otherwise, a cancel or a timeout included.

docs.title: RunEndReason
docs.text:
Bases: StrEnum

Why a thread's last run ended badly, kept beside its status.

error (the run raised) and interrupted (its lease lapsed, as after a restart) come with failed. timed_out comes with idle: a timeout is a cancel on the wire, and the reason is kept server-side.

docs.title: RunLogEntry dataclass
docs.text:
One numbered entry in a run's append-only log.

seq counts from 1 within the run, so a reader that has seen nothing asks for entries after=0. event is opaque JSON: the store never reads it, and a transport decides what it holds.

docs.title: HeadlessRunner
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Starts an agent run on the server, with no browser and no stream.

A transport implements it over its mounts; a routine's firing or a parent run's child calls it. agent_id names the mount. prompt is the run's only new user message: prior history comes from the server, and a headless run carries no client tools.

The principal is a user, never anonymous. The run's owner is str(principal.pk), the id every owner-scoped store already resolves from an authenticated request; an anonymous principal is refused, since its bucket needs a browser session. The caller authorizes the run, not the transport: a routine by its own permission check, a child by its parent's run.

Every headless run has a deadline. timeout is passed to the run as pydantic-ai's timeout=, in seconds; a run past it ends RunTimedOut, which the runner records as RunOutcome.TIMED_OUT with the partial kept.

capabilities are composed into the run beside the mount's own, such as a guard that pre-approves a routine's tools. parent names the thread a child run belongs to, with its scope, since a child often runs on another agent. lineage is the bounds the child runs under: the runner saves both on the child's conversation and composes child_lineage_for from them on every run of its thread, the first included, since capabilities cannot cross a queue; a child's start passes no capabilities. run_id on run_to_first_stop adopts the run already claimed under this id, as a queued start claims its thread before a worker runs it; without one the call claims.

answers resumes a thread parked on a question: it maps each waiting call's tool_call_id to its answer's text. A runner given it must resume the thread's stored history with DeferredToolResults(calls=answers) and send no new user message, so prompt is not sent; pydantic-ai refuses a new prompt while the history holds the unanswered call. Callers pass it only when set, so a runner without it serves every other run. A message can land after a run's last read of its queue, and an answer before the asking run parks; so after recording any run's end with RunStore.finish, a runner calls wake_thread for its thread once, which starts or resumes it when messages are still queued.

prompt_metadata marks a prompt no user wrote: a runner keeps it as the metadata of the user message it stores for the prompt, and never sends it to the model. Only a wake of an idle thread passes it, and only to a runner that opted in as a PromptMetadataRunner, so a runner without it serves every run. A queued start carries it in its HeadlessFiring.

parent_run_id is the run this one comes from: the parent run that started a child, or the parked run a resume answers; the runner reports it as the run's RUN_STARTED.parentRunId. routine_id is the routine a firing runs; the runner saves it on the thread's conversation, as it saves parent, so every firing's thread names its routine. Every caller in this package passes both on every call, so a runner must accept them.

docs.title: PromptMetadataRunner
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

A HeadlessRunner's opt-in to prompt_metadata.

A runner sets accepts_prompt_metadata = True once its start and run_to_first_stop take prompt_metadata. Only then does wake_thread pass the wake line's mark; a runner without the attribute, or with it False, is woken without the keyword. A runner that hands wake_thread a wrapper of itself sets it on the wrapper.

docs.title: HeadlessStart dataclass
docs.text: A headless run that has claimed its thread: where it runs, and as which run.

docs.title: RunStop dataclass
docs.text:
Where a headless run first stopped: it ended, or it parked on a deferred call.

waiting holds every call it parked on, non-empty exactly when outcome is RunOutcome.WAITING.

docs.title: FiringQueue
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

Runs a declared kernel spec on a worker, outside the process that asked.

The host fills it, from django-spec-tasks' enqueue and state_of over a binding whose registry holds the specs it may be asked for, so this package takes no dependency on a queue. A detached or headless start enqueues run_headless, and a routine's firing its own spec, through the same queue.

Both methods are synchronous, as the queue's are: a caller enqueues inside its own transaction, and the queue sends the run when that transaction commits.

docs.title: enqueue
docs.text:
enqueue(spec_name: str, params: Mapping[str, Any], *, actor: Any) -> str

Check the call now, record it, and send it on commit; the run's id.

actor is the principal the worker runs the spec as, loaded again by its primary key there, so it is required and never anonymous. What the spec refuses at the call (its permissions, its arguments) is raised here and nothing is recorded.

docs.title: state
docs.text:
state(run_id: str) -> FiringState | None

Where the run is; None for an id the queue does not hold, or no longer does.

docs.title: FiringState
docs.text:
Bases: StrEnum

Where a run is, as the queue that took it reports: a FiringQueue.

  • pending: it waits for a worker, or runs on one. In django-spec-tasks, PENDING and RUNNING.
  • lapsed: it ended without its body finishing, because its worker died, its principal lost the right to run it or its spec or binding is gone: ABANDONED, AUTHORIZATION_LAPSED, SPEC_UNAVAILABLE.
  • finished: it ended any other way, its answer or refusal kept: every other terminal state.

docs.title: run_headless
docs.text: Needs the [specs] extra, so it is imported from its module, never from the root.

docs.title: run_headless
docs.text:
run_headless(
    runner: HeadlessRunner, *, permissions: Sequence[PermissionCheck]
) -> ServiceSpec

The kernel spec a worker runs a queued headless start with, over runner.

Register it in the registry a FiringQueue's worker reads. Its body is runner.run_to_first_stop with the arguments of a HeadlessFiring and the worker's principal, so the run's owner lives in the worker, and the firing presents the RunStop. A firing's run_id, answers and prompt_metadata are each passed only when set, so a runner without them still serves the rest; parent_run_id and routine_id are always passed, so a runner must take both.

It declares atomic=False, since one transaction must not span a whole agent run, and idempotent=False, since a second call is a second paid run. A worker that dies mid-run is not run again: the run's lease lapses, so its thread reads failed with reason interrupted, and the queue reports the firing lapsed.

permissions are the spec's, checked at enqueue and again on the worker.

docs.title: HeadlessFiring dataclass
docs.text:
The arguments run_headless takes.

They are those of HeadlessRunner.run_to_first_stop that cross a queue as JSON. capabilities cannot, so a queued run carries none. run_id adopts the run already claimed under this id, as a queued start claims its thread before the worker takes the firing up. answers resumes a thread parked on a question, a tool_call_id to its answer's text; the run sends no new prompt. inbox_mark is the thread's inbox mark taken when the firing was enqueued, for the worker to wake on mail newer than it; None for a firing that carries none. parent_run_id and routine_id are the runner's own, the run and the routine the firing comes from. prompt_metadata is the mark of a prompt no user wrote.

docs.title: Child sessions
docs.text: A thread one agent starts on another keeps a link to the thread that started it, and every thread can have a durable queue of messages waiting for it.

docs.title: ThreadRef dataclass
docs.text:
A thread in any scope: thread_id as the client sees it, and the scope it lives in.

scope is the agent id or ScopedConversationStore scope, None for an unscoped store.

docs.title: InboundQueue
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol

A durable queue of messages per thread: reports, questions, answers and steering.

Its own protocol, so a ConversationStore gains no method. Keyed like one, by the owner each method resolves from its request, and addressed by ThreadRef, so a child in one scope reaches its parent in another.

Delivery is at least once. pending reads without removing; a reader acks the ids it has handed on with ack, so a message read by a process that then died is read again, and ack removes exactly those ids and no others. Ids are allocated at insert and seen at commit, so one can become visible behind a higher id already read: pending(after=n) used as a cursor can miss it. A reader that must see every message calls pending without after and acks what it read.

One run holds a thread's inbox at a time. take claims it for a run, under a lease each call renews, and marks and returns the messages that run has not taken yet, so a run sees each message once. A run that holds no claim, because another run's lease is live, takes nothing. release drops the claim and hands the run's unacked messages on; a run that died without releasing is taken over once its lease lapses, and the next holder takes what the dead run took and never acked. pending lists every unacked message, taken or not.

docs.text:
enqueue(
    thread: ThreadRef,
    kind: InboundKind,
    body: Any,

    sender: ThreadRef | None = None,

Append a message to thread's queue and return its id.

pending(

The thread's unacknowledged messages with ids above after, oldest first.

take(

Claim or renew thread's inbox for run_id; its messages not yet taken by it.

Oldest first, each marked as taken by run_id. [] while another run's claim is live.

One message waiting in a thread's inbound queue, id its place in the queue.

body is opaque JSON the store never reads; sender is the thread it came from, if any; taken_by is the run that took it and has not acked or released it, if any.

docs.title: InboundKind
docs.text:
Bases: StrEnum

What an inbound message carries to a thread: a child's report or question, or input.

docs.title: ModelInboundQueue
docs.text:
Bases: ABC

Abstract base for a model-backed (or any sync) inbound queue.

Provides the async wrapping and per-request owner scoping, as ModelConversationStore does; a subclass implements _enqueue, _pending, _ack, _take and _release against its own model, and must filter each by the resolved owner_id. allow_anonymous is off by default: a headless run's owner is always a user.

docs.title: Reference implementations
docs.text: The opt-in django_spec_agents.contrib.store app. Add it to INSTALLED_APPS and run migrate; the base package ships no model, so projects that don't opt in get no migration.

docs.title: DefaultConversationStore
docs.text:
Bases: ModelConversationStore

A ready-to-use model-backed store over StoredConversation.

Cross-device, per-user history with a cheap thread list. Add "django_spec_agents.contrib.store" to INSTALLED_APPS, run migrate, and pass an instance to your transport's conversation_store=. For a bespoke schema, subclass ModelConversationStore instead.

Every query filters by the owner_id the base resolves. A title is derived from the first user message at first save and then left alone except by a rename; the preview re-derives on every save.

Saving also reconciles which attachments the thread refers to, and deleting it drops the ones nothing else refers to, so an attachment's lifetime is tied to the conversations quoting it. An upload that was never sent belongs to no conversation, and the agent_store_prune_attachments command collects those instead.

It is an UnlinkableConversationStore: unlink_parent writes NULL to the thread's parent columns and its lineage, and leaves its place in the list alone, as a rename does.

docs.title: check_identifiers
docs.text:
check_identifiers(*, thread_id: str) -> None

Raise IdentifierTooLongError for a thread_id its column cannot hold.

It reads the column width and writes nothing, so a transport can refuse the id before it starts a run; preflight_identifiers calls it.

docs.title: DefaultAttachmentStore
docs.text:
Bases: ModelAttachmentStore

A ready-to-use model-backed store over StoredAttachment.

Bytes live in Django Storage (filesystem by default, S3 or GCS through STORAGES), metadata in a row. Add "django_spec_agents.contrib.store" to INSTALLED_APPS, run migrate, and pass an instance to your transport's attachment_store=. For a bespoke schema, subclass ModelAttachmentStore instead.

Every query filters by the owner_id the base resolves, so one user's id never reaches another's file, and the public attachment_id is an opaque UUID kept separate from the storage filename.

Uploads are deduplicated by content hash, within one owner: the same file sent into five threads is written to storage once and pointed at five times, while still getting a row of its own each time so it keeps the name the composer showed. The blob goes when the last row pointing at it does.

docs.title: DefaultStepStore
docs.text:
A durable, owner-scoped StepStore over the reference models.

The database equivalent of the harness's own SqliteStepStore / FileStepStore. It structurally satisfies pydantic-ai-harness's StepStore protocol — that protocol is upstream's, not this package's — while partitioning every row by the resolved owner, so one user can never read or resume another's runs even by guessing a run_id. The owner is entirely ours; no harness record carries one.

Built per request, unlike a ConversationStore singleton whose methods each take a request: the protocol's methods carry none, so the request is bound at construction. Owner resolution runs inside each sync_to_async hop, because it may create a session row for the anonymous bucket and must stay off the event loop.

An anonymous request degrades rather than crashing. With no owner and allow_anonymous off, every write no-ops and every read returns empty: the capability's hooks fire mid-run, so refusing by raising would abort the run, and an anonymous visitor has no durable identity to resume under anyway. Pair the store with an authenticated mount for it to persist.

Add "django_spec_agents.contrib.store" to INSTALLED_APPS and run migrate for the backing tables. Requires the django-spec-agents[harness] extra.

docs.title: check_identifiers
docs.text:
check_identifiers(
    *,
    run_id: str | None = None,
    conversation_id: str | None = None,
    parent_run_id: str | None = None,
    tool_call_id: str | None = None,
) -> None

Raise IdentifierTooLongError for an id a column of this store cannot hold.

Each id is checked against every model that keeps it. It resolves no owner and writes nothing, so a transport can refuse the id before it starts a run; preflight_identifiers calls it.

docs.title: list_runs async
docs.text:
list_runs(
    *, parent_run_id: str | None = None, conversation_id: str | None = None
) -> list[RunRecord]

The owner's runs by started_at, oldest first — a contract, not a default.

StepStore.list_runs documents ascending order and tells callers they may take the most recent run with [-1], so answering newest-first would quietly hand upstream's own idiom the wrong run. Presenting recent runs first is a reading order, and belongs where the list is rendered.

docs.title: DefaultMemoryStore
docs.text:
A durable, owner-scoped MemoryStore over the reference models.

The database equivalent of the harness's own SqliteMemoryStore / FileStore. It structurally satisfies pydantic-ai-harness's MemoryStore protocol — that protocol is upstream's, not this package's — while partitioning every row by the resolved owner, so one user's memory can never be read or overwritten by another even when the namespace handed to the capability is wrong. Attach it with::

Memory(DefaultMemoryStore(request), namespace=lambda ctx: memory_namespace(request))

Built per request, like DefaultStepStore and for the same reason: the protocol's methods carry no request, so it is bound at construction. Owner resolution runs inside each sync_to_async hop, because it may create a session row for the anonymous bucket and must stay off the event loop.

The path's namespace is not trusted as the boundary. The harness composes the key as <namespace>/<agent_name>/<file>.md from a resolver the host supplies, and a / inside a resolved namespace is accepted — it simply opens further path segments. So a resolver reading anything user-controlled could otherwise address another scope. Filtering every query on the server-resolved owner_id makes that harmless, and memory_namespace keeps the namespace valid in the first place.

Stored content cannot close the fence it is injected inside. The harness wraps injected memory in <memory> markers and is explicit in its own README that this "is not a hard prompt-injection boundary"; below harness 0.60, which escapes the tag itself, a note containing the closing tag ends the block early and everything after it reads as the user's own turn, durably, on every future run. Every write here escapes the angle brackets of both tags, so the stored bytes are safe for every consumer — the injection, read_memory, search_memory and an app-side read alike. Doing it on write rather than read is also what keeps write_memory's old_text replacement working: the model edits against the same escaped text it was shown.

A per-owner ceiling, which the capability does not have. Its max_memory_size bounds one file and its injection budget bounds what is read; nothing upstream caps how many files a namespace accumulates or how large they grow in total. max_files and max_total_chars do, at the write.

An anonymous request degrades rather than crashing. With no owner and allow_anonymous off, every write no-ops and every read returns empty: the capability's hooks fire mid-run, so refusing by raising would abort the run, and an anonymous visitor has no durable identity worth remembering under. Note the asymmetry with the other stores — the memory tools are model-facing, so a no-op write still reports success to the model. Pair the store with an authenticated mount for memory to persist.

Add "django_spec_agents.contrib.store" to INSTALLED_APPS and run migrate for the backing tables. Requires the django-spec-agents[harness] extra.

docs.title: purge staticmethod
docs.text:
purge(owner_id: str) -> int

Delete every memory row for one owner, returning how many files went.

Not part of MemoryStore, and it has to be here because composing the protocol cannot express it: list_paths then delete needs the current version of each path, so a purge becomes an unbounded read-then-delete loop that a concurrent write_memory can lose to. Memory is durable personal data written about a user, so an erasure request has to be able to reach it in one statement.

Deliberately not wired to a post_delete signal on the user model: whether deleting an account erases its memory is a product policy, and a library's job here is to make the operation possible.

Synchronous — call it from a management command, an admin action, or an async caller through sync_to_async.

docs.title: DefaultRunStore
docs.text:
A durable, owner-scoped run store over the reference models.

It is a ResumableRunStore and a WatchableRunStore.

One instance serves every request, like DefaultConversationStore: each method resolves the owner from its request inside the sync_to_async hop, and refuses an anonymous request unless allow_anonymous buckets it by browser session.

log_retention is how long a run's log outlives the run, a day by default; prune deletes the logs past it. A run that never finished (its owner died) counts from its last write, and a run under a live lease is never pruned; the host schedules agent_store_prune_run_logs to run it.

wait polls the log with one indexed query per tick, pausing poll_interval[0] seconds after the first and doubling up to poll_interval[1] while nothing changes; every call starts from the shortest pause. clock supplies "now" and exists for tests.

docs.text:
Bases: ModelInboundQueue

A durable, owner-scoped inbound queue over StoredInboundMessage.

A thread's queue is its rows under (owner_id, scope, thread_id), an absent scope stored as NULL and kept apart from ""; ack deletes exactly the ids it is given. A run's claim on the queue is a StoredInboxClaim row. clock supplies "now" and exists for tests.

docs.text:
The owner's child sessions from the parent columns and a run store.

A scoped store's scope:thread_id is un-keyed at its first :.

docs.title: DefaultSpendStore
docs.text:
A pydantic-ai-harness BatchSpendStore over the reference models, so every worker on one database enforces one budget.

The Django-model counterpart of the harness's PostgresSpendStore, for PostgreSQL and for SQLite with one process or "transaction_mode": "IMMEDIATE". Built once and shared: it holds no request and scopes nothing, since a budget's scope already names the partition in each key. Every window of a response is applied in one transaction, so all of them count or none does, and a SpendEntry.token already applied to a window within dedup_retain is not counted again. A window past its horizon reads as zero and restarts at the next write.

Horizons are measured on clock, the application's clock (timezone.now unless given), not the database's, so workers whose clocks disagree disagree on when a window rolls over. A read and the increment after it are separate statements, so concurrent runs can each find a budget unspent and pass it together, as with every harness store. Every sweep_every entries this instance writes, it deletes the expired rows.

SQLite refuses a second writer's lock upgrade at once (database is locked), so concurrent workers on SQLite need OPTIONS = {"transaction_mode": "IMMEDIATE"}, which Django 5.1 added; below it they can fail a write. One ASGI process is unaffected.

Add "django_spec_agents.contrib.store" to INSTALLED_APPS and run migrate for the backing tables. Requires the django-spec-agents[harness] extra.

docs.title: Attachment lifecycle
docs.text: Contrib-level, not part of either protocol. See Storage for the semantics and the management commands.

docs.title: reconcile_conversation_attachments
docs.text:
reconcile_conversation_attachments(
    conversation: StoredConversation, messages: Iterable[Any]
) -> None

Point conversation at exactly the attachments its messages quote.

The resolver behind attachment lifecycle, needing no wire or client change: the web component already augments each user message with an attachments array of the refs the composer uploaded, and that undeclared field survives into the stored message list. Reading it here turns an id in some JSON into a relation the database can enforce a lifecycle on.

Reconciled rather than appended, so a message dropped on a re-save drops its reference too and the relation always describes the conversation as it stands.

Owner-scoped, which is the load-bearing part: an id resolves only against the attachments of the conversation's own owner, so a guessed or copied id links nothing — the rule that makes AttachmentStore.open return None across owners.

The parse is total. A message that is not a mapping, an attachments field of the wrong type, an entry with no usable id, an id resolving to an attachment since deleted: all degrade to "no reference" in silence. This runs inside a conversation save, where an exception would lose the user's message.

docs.title: strip_inline_binary_parts
docs.text:
strip_inline_binary_parts(messages: Any) -> tuple[Any, bool]

Rebuild messages without any inline file bytes, and say if it changed.

A transport that inlines an attachment for the model serialises the file into the message list as base64, which persisted turns a 2.6 MB PDF into roughly 3.5 MB of text in one row, shipped to the browser on every load.

The edit is structural: the list is walked as plain JSON and only the offending parts are dropped. Nothing is round-tripped through a message type, because validating and re-dumping is what would silently discard the fields this must not lose — every message's id, and the non-standard attachments array that both renders the chips and drives attachment reconciliation.

A message whose parts were all bytes keeps its place with an empty content list, since dropping it would take its id too.

Returns:

Name Type Description Any

The rebuilt messages and whether anything was removed, so a caller can

bool

leave untouched rows untouched. A non-list messages is handed back

unchanged tuple[Any, bool]

the column is JSON, and a row written by something other than

tuple[Any, bool]

this store is left alone.

docs.title: AttachmentDeletion dataclass
docs.text:
What one attachment deletion pass removed.

Three counts rather than one, because deduplication pulls them apart: deleting one of two rows sharing a file removes a row and no blob, so a command reporting only rows would claim space it did not reclaim.

bytes_freed is summed from the declared size of the rows whose blob went, not from a fresh stat of the backend, so it estimates what a remote store gives back rather than measuring it.

docs.title: Policy
docs.text: Audit, the destructive-tool gate and the tool-failure policy all ride the Pydantic-AI capability seam. The first two are off by default; the third is on. See Policy for the narrative.

Bases: Protocol

An implementation may drop, sample or forward events. The package ships NullAuditLogger and LoggingAuditLogger; a project passes its own to its transport's audit_logger=.

docs.title: AuditEvent dataclass
docs.text:
A single tool invocation as seen by the audit logger.

Arguments are stored as a string, typically JSON, to keep records cheap to serialize and to discourage retaining sensitive raw values.

One run-level record rides this shape: a client disconnecting mid-run is recorded as tool_name="agent.run", success=False and an error starting "cancelled:", so a sink can tell cancelled runs apart without widening the AuditLogger protocol.

docs.title: AuditCapability
docs.text:
Bases: AbstractCapability[Any]

Records every tool execution to an AuditLogger sink.

A Pydantic-AI capability on the tool-execution hooks, so it records every tool the agent runs: registry tools, the MCP and spec bridges, attachment and skill tools alike.

One record per execution, describing the tool's own execution, whatever other capabilities sort ahead of it and on every supported pydantic-ai. That is everything composed through AgentConfig.capabilities unless its own ordering places it inside audit. A capability that sorts after audit is the exception, below.

  • arguments_repr holds the arguments the tool received, after every other capability's before_tool_execute has rewritten them.
  • success and error describe what the tool did. error is Type: message of the exception the tool raised, before any capability converts it (as ToolFailurePolicy does) or recovers from it with an on_tool_execute_error that returns a value. A recovered failure is still recorded as the failure: recovering is a decision about the run, not about the tool. On an ordinary call the exceptions pydantic-ai routes past every error hook are recorded as they arrive: a tool's own ToolFailed as the ToolFailedError pydantic-ai converts it into, with the same message, and ModelRetry as ToolRetryError. From a code-mode sandbox, whose nested tool manager converts neither, they are recorded as raised: ToolFailed: <message> and ModelRetry: <message>. A ToolFailed keeps its own message either way; its cause and context are never read. A ModelRetry on an ordinary call with the tool's retry budget spent is different: pydantic-ai raises UnexpectedModelBehavior in its place, which does reach the error hooks, and that is what is recorded.
  • result_size is the length of the tool's own result, before any after_tool_execute rewrites it.
  • duration_ms spans the tool alone: from the last moment audit sees before the tool runs, which is after every other capability's before_tool_execute, to the first moment it sees the outcome, which is before every other capability's on_tool_execute_error or after_tool_execute. Other capabilities' hooks are not in it.

A call that never runs the tool produces no record. That is a call stopped before audit's before_tool_execute, by any exception, and one whose outcome is what pydantic-ai treats as not executed: SkipToolExecution, CallDeferred or ApprovalRequired, from wherever it is raised. So a veto such as pydantic-ai-harness's guardrails and tool-call judge raise, a destructive call the ToolGuard holds for approval, a call a tool or a toolset such as pydantic-ai's approval_required() defers for approval, and a call deferred to external execution are not executions. A call held for approval is recorded when it is resumed and runs, like any other; a call deferred to external execution never runs in this process, so it has no record here.

How it gets the tool's own record. pydantic-ai runs every capability's before_tool_execute, on_tool_execute_error and after_tool_execute inside the wrap_tool_execute chain, so no wrapper position sees the raw outcome. Audit is pinned innermost, which makes its before_tool_execute the last to run and its on_tool_execute_error and after_tool_execute the first, and observes the tool from all four hooks. Its wrapper is the only one that writes the record, once, as it exits, preferring what the hooks captured over what it saw itself. The wrapper encloses every hook, and for what sorts ahead of audit the captures are what keep the record the tool's.

A capability that sorts after audit runs between audit and the tool. One does when it is innermost and passed to a single run, since pydantic-ai sorts those after the agent's own capabilities whatever build_agent did; when it is composed by hand after audit in the innermost tier; and wherever it is composed, when its own ordering places it inside audit, as an innermost CapabilityOrdering with wrapped_by=[AuditCapability] does. What such a capability does can reach the record, through any of its hooks, and the record is then not the tool's own. These are measured examples, not a list of the only ways:

  • Through its before_tool_execute, on_tool_execute_error and after_tool_execute: a record misses its argument rewrite, records a ModelRetry its before_tool_execute raises as a failure though the tool never ran, records its recovery as a success and an exception it raises in place of the tool's, records a ModelRetry its after_tool_execute raises as a failure though the tool succeeded, measures its result rewrite, and times its hooks with the tool.
  • Through its wrap_tool_execute, when the tool raised ModelRetry or ToolFailed, which pydantic-ai routes past every error and result hook, audit's included: a record carries its rewrite of the message, as pydantic-ai-harness's result_guard does, records its recovery as a success, and records an exception it raises in their place. If it runs the tool again, the record describes the later run alone and the failed run has none; with that rerun refused ahead of audit, the record pairs the first run's arguments with the refusal. Run again after a failure audit's error hook saw, or after a success, the tool gets one record, of its first run. Reruns it makes concurrently share one record, which can pair one run's arguments with another's result.

A SkipToolExecution veto from it is still not recorded. Everything composed through AgentConfig.capabilities is unaffected unless its own ordering places it inside audit: build_agent appends audit after all of it, so audit sorts last among the innermost capabilities there. pydantic-ai-harness's tool guardrail and tool-call judge are innermost, so passed to a single run they sort after audit like any other.

Recording is non-raising. A sink that throws is caught and logged to the django_pydantic_agent.audit Python logger, so a broken audit backend costs audit records rather than the run. Audit's own error hook re-raises what it is handed, and the exception the run sees is never changed by it.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default logger AuditLogger

The sink each AuditEvent is recorded to.

required ip_address str | None

Fallback client IP, used only when the run's deps carry no ip_address. Per-run deps come first because a constructor argument is per-agent: taking the IP from it alone forces a fresh agent per request, and building once anyway fails silently, with every record carrying the IP of whoever arrived first.

None organization_id str | None

Org scope stamped onto every event, for a multi-tenant host.

None

docs.title: get_ordering
docs.text:
get_ordering() -> CapabilityOrdering

Pin audit as an innermost capability.

pydantic-ai runs before_tool_execute hooks outermost first and on_tool_execute_error / after_tool_execute hooks innermost first, so innermost is the one position whose hooks sit directly either side of the tool: after every other capability's argument rewrite and veto, and before any other capability converts, recovers or rewrites the outcome, unless a capability sorts after audit even so (see the class). Declared here rather than left to list order at the build_agent call site, since pydantic-ai sorts by these constraints.

docs.title: wrap_tool_execute async
docs.text:
wrap_tool_execute(
    ctx: RunContext[Any],
    *,
    call: ToolCallPart,
    tool_def: ToolDefinition,
    args: dict[str, Any],
    handler: WrapToolExecuteHandler,
) -> Any

Write the call's one record on the way out, and hand the result back as is.

This wrapper sees every capability's hooks around the tool. The hooks below have recorded the tool's side first where they could, and settle keeps the first account it is given, so what is written is the tool's whenever nothing sorts between audit and the tool (see the class). A call whose before_tool_execute never ran here never reached the tool, and is not recorded.

Every entry starts a fresh, unreached execution, because pydantic-ai lets an outer wrapper call its handler more than once and each call runs the tool again. before_tool_execute runs again inside each entry and says so itself, unless a capability ahead of audit stops that entry first; an entry stopped that way is not recorded, whatever an earlier entry, or an outer call of a nested run, reached.

The reset on the way out puts back what the context held before. Code mode awaits a nested call inline, in run_code's own task, when the nested tool is marked sequential or the run is, so that call's wrapper sets the variable in the context run_code's own hooks read. Without the reset they would settle the nested call's execution and leave run_code's to its wrapper, whose record then describes another capability's rewrite of the result and times its hooks. test_a_code_mode_call_keeps_its_own_record_around_inline_nested_calls fails without it. Coverage cannot see it go missing, since the line runs either way.

docs.text:
before_tool_execute(
    ctx: RunContext[Any],
    *,
    call: ToolCallPart,
    tool_def: ToolDefinition,
    args: dict[str, Any],

Note that the call reached the tool, with the arguments it gets.

Innermost, so this runs after every other capability's before_tool_execute, and nothing else stands between it and the tool, unless a capability sorts after audit (see the class). It runs inside the wrapper, so the execution is the wrapper's own for this call.

docs.title: on_tool_execute_error async
docs.text:
on_tool_execute_error(
    ctx: RunContext[Any],
    *,
    call: ToolCallPart,
    tool_def: ToolDefinition,
    args: Any,
    error: Exception,
) -> Any

Keep the tool's own exception, then pass it on unchanged.

Innermost, so this is the first error hook to run, before any other capability converts or recovers, unless one sorts after audit (see the class). Re-raising is what keeps the chain going: the next capability's hook is handed the same exception.

docs.text:
after_tool_execute(
    ctx: RunContext[Any],
    *,
    call: ToolCallPart,
    tool_def: ToolDefinition,
    args: dict[str, Any],

Keep the tool's own result, then pass it on unchanged.

Innermost, so this is the first result hook to run, before any other capability rewrites the result, unless one sorts after audit (see the class). After a recovery it is handed the recovered value instead, which settle ignores: the error hook settled the call first.

docs.text: Discards every event. The default when no audit logger is configured.

Successful invocations log at INFO; failures log at WARNING with the error message included.

docs.title: ToolGuardConfig dataclass
docs.text:
Resolved policy for the server-side tool-approval gate.

Turns the ToolGuard capability on and tunes which tools it flips to require human approval. Off by default, so the gate never surprises a project that has not opted in.

When enabled, a tool is gated if it is destructive or its name is in require_approval; exempt overrides both. A tool counts as destructive when it is a registry @tool(destructive=True), or when its definition says so — a bridge's metadata key (set for a tool that lists annotations, unless it is read-only or declares destructiveHint false), an MCP readOnlyHint of False (a ServiceSpec through SpecToolset, among others), or an x-destructive stamp at the root of its parameter schema.

Nothing else is gated. A tool from a source that declares none of those is invisible to the gate however dangerous it is, and require_approval is the only answer for it. Off by default, so on stock settings a server-side destructive tool runs with no approval interrupt at all.

docs.title: enabled class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
enabled: bool = False

Whether the ToolGuard capability is composed into the agent.

docs.title: exempt class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
exempt: frozenset[str] = field(default_factory=frozenset)

Tool names never gated, even if flagged destructive: the escape hatch for a mutation a project has decided is safe to auto-run.

docs.title: require_approval class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
require_approval: frozenset[str] = field(default_factory=frozenset)

Tool names always gated, even if not flagged destructive, for a read tool a project treats as sensitive. exempt wins on a name in both.

docs.title: ToolGuard
docs.text:
Bases: AbstractCapability[Any]

Gates destructive server-side tools behind the AG-UI approval loop.

pydantic-ai supplies the mechanism — a tool whose definition is kind="unapproved" defers to an interrupt the client approves or denies — and this supplies the policy, flipping a plain function tool to unapproved at prepare_tools time when it is destructive. Server-side tools thereby get the confirmation gate the web component already applies to client-registered ones.

Destructiveness is read from every vocabulary a toolset might declare it in, so one hook covers every tool the agent sees wherever it came from:

  • Registry @tool(destructive=True), collected at construction: the flag lives on the spec and never reaches pydantic-ai, which sees a bare callable, so the capability reads it directly.
  • Bridged MCP tools, through the DESTRUCTIVE_METADATA_KEY the bridge stamps into ToolDefinition.metadata. The bridge marks a tool unless its readOnlyHint is true or its destructiveHint is false, as MCP reads the pair, so a mutation registered with annotations={"destructiveHint": False} is not gated. A tool listed with no annotations is not marked.
  • MCP tool annotations — metadata["annotations"], read by the bridge's rule: annotations that say something mark the tool unless readOnlyHint is true or destructiveHint is false, and a field that is None is unsaid, as are annotations with nothing said. A toolset that speaks MCP's own vocabulary rather than this package's key declares a mutation this way, SpecToolset over a ServiceSpec and a remote MCP server among them. Reading it gates a spec attached in process the way the bridge's key gates the same spec over MCP, so a transport swap cannot silently remove the gate.
  • The x-destructive schema stamp at the root of parameters_json_schema, which is what build_input_schema writes, so a project deriving a schema with the package's own helper and attaching the tool through toolsets= is gated by it too.
  • Project overrides: require_approval force-gates a name, exempt un-gates one, and exempt wins.
  • A tool that gates itself, marked with SELF_GATED_METADATA_KEY, raises its own approval with a card built from the call: it is gated whatever exempt says, and never flipped, since a flip would defer it before its card exists.

A hint has to say something. Annotations that say nothing, an absent stamp or metadata of another shape entirely leave the tool alone — silence is not a claim, and require_approval is the answer for a tool whose source declares nothing. Annotations that say anything are read by MCP's defaults, as the bridge reads them.

Only kind="function" tools are flipped — an external tool is already gated client-side, and an output tool is not executed.

The guard touches only prepare_tools, so it is orthogonal to AuditCapability and audit still records the tool when an approved call finally runs.

docs.title: requires_approval
docs.text:
requires_approval(tool_def: ToolDefinition) -> bool

Whether tool_def is gated, by the guard's precedence, whatever its kind.

A tool that gates itself is always gated. Otherwise exempt wins, then require_approval, then a registry @tool(destructive=True), then a mutation the definition declares in any of the vocabularies above. prepare_tools flips a function tool on this answer unless it gates itself; a caller recording whether a parked call is destructive, or pre-approving a routine's tools, asks the same question.

docs.title: ApprovalReviewerConfig dataclass

A second model that may approve a gated call in the person's place.

build_agent composes a ReviewedApprovals from it, which needs the [harness] extra. The reviewer answers question about each call waiting for approval: no runs the call, marked reviewer:<model>; yes, unsure or a failed review leaves it for the person, as without a reviewer. It never denies a call.

tools names the tools it reviews, or 'all' for every approval request, those a ToolGuardrail or ToolCallJudge raises and tools added later included. Under either, the tools in NEVER_AUTO_APPROVED are never reviewed.

docs.title: GrantedApprovals
docs.text:
Bases: AbstractCapability[Any]

Approves a fixed grant of tool names in the run, marked answered_by.

A routine's firing spec can pass preapproved_exempt(routine) with answered_by="routine:<id>": the guard still gates each call, and this answers it, so the call runs in the same run with the mark on its result and its audit record. A call of any other tool, an external call, and a tool in NEVER_AUTO_APPROVED are left to the next answerer, and then to the person. It sorts before ReviewedApprovals, so a granted call costs no review.

docs.title: ToolFailureConfig dataclass
docs.text:
Resolved policy for what an unhandled tool exception does to a run.

Tunes the ToolFailurePolicy capability. On by default, because without it one raising tool ends the whole run, discarding the answer the model had assembled and every other tool result in the turn.

The two flags default opposite ways because they answer different questions. Whether the run survives is reliability; whether the exception's text reaches the model is disclosure, since a message can carry a query, a path or a credential, and whatever the model sees also reaches whatever renders the transcript. The policy never redacts the operator's copy, whichever way include_detail is set: the full exception goes to the audit logger, and to the Python logger whenever the policy converts it. A capability that sorts after audit can still change what audit records; the AuditCapability states that exception.

docs.title: enabled class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
enabled: bool = True

Whether the ToolFailurePolicy capability is composed into the agent. Set False to restore the fail-the-run behaviour.

docs.title: include_detail class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
include_detail: bool = False

Whether the model-facing failure message carries the exception type and text. An exception message is written for an operator, not for a model or the browser that renders its answer.

docs.title: reraise class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
reraise: tuple[type[BaseException], ...] | None = None

Exception types that pass through untouched, ending the run as they would without the policy.

None means the built-in set: an authorization refusal, in each flavour this package's stack raises it — django.core.exceptions' PermissionDenied, and django_service_specs' NotPermitted and PrincipalUnavailable when the kernel is installed. Pass a tuple to replace that set wholesale, or () to convert every exception. Replacing means re-listing each of those classes your project can raise to keep denials exempt, and it is how a project whose own stack raises another refusal class keeps that one exempt too.

A spent tool retry budget. Add UnexpectedModelBehavior (from pydantic_ai.exceptions) to end the run when a tool's own ModelRetry has no retries left, rather than converting it into a failed result. It ends the run for every UnexpectedModelBehavior a tool raises, including a sub-agent's exhausted budget the tool propagates, and __cause__ cannot tell the two apart.

Why a denial is not a tool failure. A converted denial leaves the run alive and the model free to call the same tool on the next row, while a failed result stays distinguishable from a "not found" one — so a sweep over ids turns a permission boundary into an existence oracle inside a single turn. A ToolFailed spends no retry budget, so nothing bounds the sweep but run-level UsageLimits. Refusing to run is the answer to a denied call, not a fault to route around.

docs.title: ToolFailurePolicy
docs.text:
Bases: AbstractCapability[Any]

Turns an unhandled tool exception into a failed result the model can read.

Without it, a tool that raises takes the run down: the transport emits RUN_ERROR, the turn ends, and everything the model produced is discarded along with every other tool result in the round. One broken integration costs the whole answer.

It hangs off on_tool_execute_error, which is a correctness point rather than a stylistic one: pydantic-ai does not call that hook for control-flow exceptions (SkipToolExecution / CallDeferred / ApprovalRequired), retry signals or failure signals. The approval interrupt the tool guard depends on therefore passes through untouched, and so does a ModelRetry while the tool has retries left, where a hand-rolled except Exception around the handler would swallow them and quietly disable the gate. The policy neither spends nor grants retries; what it changes is the end of a tool's own budget, below.

The re-raise is pydantic_ai.exceptions.ToolFailed, so the model sees a result marked failed rather than one reading as success. (Precisely, a private subclass of it: pydantic-ai's control flow treats it as a ToolFailed, and a trace records the subclass's name as the exception type.) A failed result spends no retry budget, so bound a persistently broken tool with run-level UsageLimits rather than expecting this to stop the model calling it.

Nothing is swallowed. An exception this converts is logged with its traceback to the django_pydantic_agent.failure logger first, and an AuditCapability in the same chain still records the failure against the tool that caused it. What changes is only who the failure stops. That logger hears only about what this converts: not a call another capability recovered or answered for, not a refusal passing through, and not an exception pydantic-ai never hands to an error hook, such as a tool's own ToolFailed, or its ModelRetry while it has retries left.

It converts last. Pinned outermost, and placed first by build_agent, so its on_tool_execute_error is the last of every capability's to run (pydantic-ai runs that hook innermost first). Every other capability's error hook is handed the exception the tool raised, never this policy's redacted copy: a step recorder such as harness's StepPersistence logs the tool's failure, and a capability that recovers answers before anything is converted. What an earlier hook raised in the exception's place is that capability's answer, and passes through when it is one pydantic-ai gives the model itself: a ToolFailed already carries its own message for the model, and a ModelRetry spends the tool's retry budget. Once that is spent the run ends with UnexpectedModelBehavior, which pydantic-ai raises after every error hook has run, so this never sees it.

A tool's own ModelRetry with no retries left is converted. While the tool has retries left pydantic-ai never hands its ModelRetry to an error hook. Once they are spent it raises UnexpectedModelBehavior in its place from inside the call, which does reach the error hooks, so this logs it and converts it into a failed result like any other exception, where without the policy the run would end. A capability's ModelRetry is different: pydantic-ai checks its budget outside the error hooks, so it still ends the run when the budget is spent. The default carries a cost, since the tool keeps executing on later calls and its side effects repeat, bounded by the model taking the failed result's "do not retry" (with include_detail off) or by pydantic-ai's default request limit. Naming UnexpectedModelBehavior in ToolFailureConfig.reraise ends the run instead, and ends it for a sub-agent's exhausted budget a tool propagates too.

An authorization refusal is exempt and ends the run as it would without the policy — see ToolFailureConfig.reraise, which is also how a project exempts more, or nothing at all.

docs.title: get_ordering
docs.text:
get_ordering() -> CapabilityOrdering

Pin the policy as an outermost capability.

pydantic-ai runs on_tool_execute_error hooks innermost first, so the outermost one runs last: whatever else is composed sees the tool's exception before this converts it. build_agent also places it first in its list, which keeps it last among other outermost capabilities, since list order breaks ties within a tier.

docs.title: LoopDetectionConfig dataclass
docs.text:
pydantic-ai-harness's DetectLoops, as build_agent composes it (the [harness] extra).

action="nudge" tells the model which loop it is in and lets the run carry on. action="error" ends the run with LoopDetectedError, which a child session reports as failed, its text the loop's description. Each threshold is how many repeats report a loop, None turning that check off; window is how many recent tool calls the call checks read. stream_checks keeps the checks for a response that repeats itself as it streams.

docs.title: SpendLimitsConfig dataclass
docs.text:
pydantic-ai-harness's SpendLimits, as build_agent composes it (the [harness] extra).

Each response's price is added to every budget's counter, and once a counter is spent the next model request is refused with SpendLimitExceeded, a UsageLimitExceeded: the run ends as a usage limit ends it, which a child session reports as budget. store is the harness BatchSpendStore the counters live in, Any because the harness is optional; DefaultSpendStore keeps them in the database, so every worker shares them. price prices a response before the genai-prices registry does, None falling through to it, for a self-hosted model or a negotiated rate.

docs.title: SpendBudget dataclass
docs.text:
One ceiling a SpendLimitsConfig enforces.

usd and tokens are the ceilings, either, both or neither (a budget with neither only counts). window is the period the counter covers: one run, one conversation, a UTC day or month, or the total for all time. per_user counts each acting user (ctx.deps.user) apart, every run with no authenticated user sharing one anonymous counter; otherwise the whole mount shares one. warn_at is the fraction past which the harness reports a warning, never a stop. name tells budgets on one window apart.

docs.title: Registry
docs.text: Server-side tools and their derived schemas. See Tools for the narrative.

docs.title: ToolRegistry
docs.text:
An ordered, named collection of server-side tools.

State lives on the instance — a transport holds one, tests build a fresh one per scenario. Each tool's JSON Schema is derived once at registration, with the tool's own ToolSpec.schema_strategy when it sets one and the registry's schema_strategy otherwise (see build_input_schema), and either sync or async callables can be dispatched.

The strategy shapes ToolBinding.input_schema only. The schema the agent offers the model for a registry tool is pydantic-ai's own, whichever is set.

docs.text:

Register spec and return its binding.

Raises:

when spec.name is already registered, or its schema_strategy is not a SchemaStrategy.

docs.text:

Return the binding for name or raise KeyError.

docs.title: call
docs.text:
call(name: str, arguments: dict[str, Any], *, ctx: Any = None) -> Any

Dispatch a sync call to the registered tool.

arguments is the model's payload and nothing else. A tool declaring a leading ctx: RunContext[...] gets it from ctx here, the way pydantic-ai would supply it from the run; passing one to a tool that takes none is harmless.

Refuses coroutine functions to avoid silently returning an un-awaited coroutine. Use acall for async tools.
