docs.title: tool
docs.text:
tool(
    registry: ToolRegistry,
    *,
    name: str | None = None,
    description: str | None = None,
    destructive: bool = False,
    category: ToolCategory = ToolCategory.OTHER,
    confirm: str | None = None,
    summary: str | None = None,
    schema_strategy: SchemaStrategy | None = None,
) -> Callable[[F], F]

Register the decorated callable on registry as a tool.

name defaults to the function's name and description to the first paragraph of its docstring. confirm is the confirmation prompt for a destructive tool and summary a short display label; both reach the client as the matching x-* schema key. schema_strategy overrides the registry's for this tool's schema; None keeps the registry's.

docs.title: ToolSpec dataclass
docs.text:
Canonical declaration of a server-side tool.

Bundles the callable with the metadata the registry needs to expose it to a Pydantic-AI agent and to a frontend.

docs.title: name instance-attribute
docs.text:
name: str

Stable identifier exposed to the agent, unique within a ToolRegistry.

docs.title: fn instance-attribute
docs.text:
fn: Callable[..., Any]

The callable implementing the tool. Its parameters must be typed; the registry derives a JSON Schema from the signature.

docs.title: description instance-attribute
docs.text:
description: str

Summary shown to the agent. Most clients display the first line.

docs.title: destructive class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
destructive: bool = False

Whether calling this tool may mutate state. Stamped as x-destructive, and an enabled ToolGuard gates it server-side.

docs.title: category class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
category: ToolCategory = ToolCategory.OTHER

Coarse capability grouping, stamped as x-category.

docs.title: confirm class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
confirm: str | None = None

A confirmation prompt for a destructive tool, stamped as x-confirm, shown instead of a generic "Run ?".

docs.title: summary class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
summary: str | None = None

A short label, stamped as x-summary, shown on the tool-call card instead of the raw tool name.

docs.title: schema_strategy class-attribute instance-attribute
docs.text:
schema_strategy: SchemaStrategy | None = None

How this tool's ToolBinding.input_schema is derived. None takes the registering ToolRegistry's strategy; a value overrides it for this tool alone, so one registry can hold tools of both strategies.

docs.title: ToolBinding dataclass
docs.text:
A registered tool plus the JSON Schema derived from its signature.

The schema is computed once at registration and carried alongside the spec, so a tool listing does not re-introspect on every request.

docs.title: build_input_schema
docs.text:
build_input_schema(
    fn: Callable[..., Any],
    *,
    destructive: bool = False,
    category: ToolCategory = ToolCategory.OTHER,
    confirm: str | None = None,
    summary: str | None = None,
    schema_strategy: SchemaStrategy = SchemaStrategy.HAND_BUILT,
) -> dict[str, Any]

Derive a JSON Schema object from fn's parameters.

schema_strategy picks the derivation. The default, SchemaStrategy.HAND_BUILT, covers str, int, float, bool, list[T], dict[str, Any] and X | None unions, and reads Annotated[T, ...] as T plus what its metadata maps to: a Field's description, title and examples, and the bounds of a Field or of annotated_types metadata. A string or forward reference nested in an annotation is resolved in the globals the top level is evaluated in. Anything richer, or a nested reference that does not resolve, falls back to an empty fragment, imposing no type constraint but staying wire-valid; so does a bound that is not an int or float (a Decimal, a date), and examples that do not serialise to JSON. An annotation that does not evaluate at the top level raises NameError under either strategy, from inspect.signature.

SchemaStrategy.PYDANTIC builds a pydantic model over the same parameters and returns its JSON Schema, so it covers whatever pydantic does, keyed by parameter name rather than a Field alias, and raises where pydantic does: on a type it cannot schematise, an unresolvable reference (NameError), or a parameter pydantic would not hold as a field (TypeError).

destructive / category / confirm / summary are stamped at the schema root as the matching x-* extension keys, which AG-UI passes through verbatim to the client.

A leading ctx: RunContext[...] parameter is not an argument and is left out. Pydantic-AI fills it from the run — it is how a tool reaches the acting user — so advertising it would ask the model to invent a value for something it cannot supply.

Raises:

Type Description ValueError

when schema_strategy is not a SchemaStrategy.

docs.title: ToolCategory
docs.text:
Bases: str, Enum

Coarse grouping for a tool, surfaced to the agent and the UI.

Advisory metadata: it lets a frontend group tools, a system prompt reason about capability classes, and a project apply category-wide policy. It does not gate execution; that is the destructive flag's job.

docs.title: SchemaStrategy
docs.text:
Bases: str, Enum

How build_input_schema derives a tool's JSON Schema from its signature.

HAND_BUILT is the default and the package's own mapping: a flat schema with no titles, X | None as nullable, and an unrecognised type as an empty fragment. PYDANTIC hands the parameters to pydantic and returns its JSON Schema: titles on every property, X | None as anyOf, defaults, and $defs for nested models and enums.

docs.title: Schema and metadata keys
docs.text:
The x-* keys are JSON-Schema extensions that reach the client on a tool's schema. DESTRUCTIVE_METADATA_KEY is different: it rides pydantic-ai's tool metadata and is read server-side by the tool guard, which needs destructiveness for tools whose flag doesn't come from the @tool registry.

Each lives in its own module under django_spec_agents.types and is importable from the package root.

docs.title: x_destructive_key
docs.text:
x-destructive: this tool mutates.

One of four JSON-Schema extensions stamped at the schema root, which is what carries them to the client: AG-UI has no native concept for any of them and passes unknown keys through verbatim. Read client-side to gate execution behind a confirmation, and server-side by ToolGuard for a tool whose schema is the only place its author said so.

docs.title: X_DESTRUCTIVE_KEY module-attribute
docs.text: X_DESTRUCTIVE_KEY = 'x-destructive'

docs.title: x_category_key
docs.text:
x-category: the tool's category, stamped at the schema root.

Lets a frontend group or filter tools without a side channel.

docs.title: X_CATEGORY_KEY module-attribute
docs.text: X_CATEGORY_KEY = 'x-category'

docs.title: x_confirm_key
docs.text:
x-confirm: a confirmation prompt, stamped at the schema root.

Shown instead of a generic "Run ?".

docs.title: X_CONFIRM_KEY module-attribute
docs.text: X_CONFIRM_KEY = 'x-confirm'

docs.title: x_summary_key
docs.text:
x-summary: a short label, stamped at the schema root.

Shown on the tool-call card instead of the raw tool name.

docs.title: X_SUMMARY_KEY module-attribute
docs.text: X_SUMMARY_KEY = 'x-summary'

docs.title: destructive_metadata_key
docs.text:
The "this tool mutates" signal on ToolDefinition.metadata.

The same signal as x-destructive, but on metadata rather than the schema, because metadata is the channel a bridge controls where the schema belongs to the tool's author: ToolGuard reads it at prepare_tools time for tools whose destructiveness the @tool registry does not know, such as a bridged MCP tool whose readOnlyHint and destructiveHint the bridge maps onto this key. It lives in process only and is never stored, so its value follows the package's name.

docs.title: DESTRUCTIVE_METADATA_KEY module-attribute
docs.text: DESTRUCTIVE_METADATA_KEY = 'django_spec_agents.destructive'

docs.title: self_gated_metadata_key
docs.text:
The "this tool asks for approval itself" signal on ToolDefinition.metadata.

A tool marked with it raises ApprovalRequired from its own body, carrying a card built from the call, so ToolGuard and ChildLineage never flip it to unapproved: that would defer the call before the body runs, and the card would never be built. The guard's requires_approval still answers True for it, whatever exempt says. It lives in process only and is never stored, so its value follows the package's name.

docs.title: SELF_GATED_METADATA_KEY module-attribute
docs.text: SELF_GATED_METADATA_KEY = 'django_spec_agents.self_gated'

docs.title: Routines
docs.text: The routine model, its policy, the schedule vocabulary and the functions over them. See Routines for the narrative. Everything here but run_agent_spec imports from django_spec_agents.routines.

docs.title: AbstractRoutine
docs.text:
Bases: Model

A stored prompt for one agent, its schedule and its principal, the user who created it.

The consumer subclasses it with its tenant relation and returns its policy from routine_policy(). next_fire_at is None while the routine is disabled.

The stored schedule, read through parse_schedule.

The IANA zone the schedule's wall times are read in.

The granted tools, each with the destructive flag pinned when it was granted.

The policy every read, write and firing goes through; None fails the system check.

The queue and spec run_due_routines fires this model with; None leaves it unswept.

docs.title: thread_waits classmethod
docs.text:
thread_waits(thread_id: str, principal: Any) -> bool

Whether the last firing's thread still waits on a person; the host reads its run store.

Return True while principal's thread thread_id is parked on an approval or a question, and the sweep skips the next firing rather than start another beside it. The default, False, never skips, so a host without a run store fires on schedule.

docs.title: RoutinePolicy
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol, Generic[RoutineT]

Who sees which routines, who may write them, and whether one may fire: the consumer's.

docs.title: visible
docs.text:
visible(request: HttpRequest) -> Iterable[RoutineT]

Every routine the caller may see, disabled ones too.

docs.title: can_write
docs.text:
can_write(request: HttpRequest, routine: RoutineT) -> bool

Whether the caller may save routine, a new unsaved one or an existing row.

docs.title: can_run
docs.text:
can_run(principal: AbstractBaseUser, routine: RoutineT) -> bool

Whether routine may fire now as principal, its creator; asked with no request.

docs.title: new_routine
docs.text:
new_routine(request: HttpRequest) -> RoutineT

An unsaved routine carrying the scope (tenant) a create by the caller writes to.

docs.title: RoutineDraft dataclass
docs.text:
What a create or an update writes to a routine.

preapproved_tools names the tools to grant; the write pins each new name's destructive flag through the agent's guard, and keeps the flag already pinned for a name it held.

docs.title: WeeklySchedule dataclass
docs.text:
Fire on each of weekdays (0 is Monday, 6 is Sunday) at the local wall time at.

at is a naive time to the minute, read in the routine's timezone. A time a DST change skips fires at the same instant shifted by the gap, and a time it repeats fires once, at its first occurrence. Raises InvalidRoutineError for no weekday, a weekday outside 0 to 6, an aware at, or one with seconds.

docs.title: IntervalSchedule dataclass
docs.text:
Fire every every_hours hours of elapsed time, whatever the timezone's DST changes.

Raises InvalidRoutineError for an interval shorter than MIN_ROUTINE_INTERVAL or longer than MAX_ROUTINE_INTERVAL.

docs.title: PreapprovedTool dataclass
docs.text:
A tool a routine's firings may call without parking, and whether it was gated when granted.

destructive is the guard's requires_approval answer at grant time, kept as it was: a tool granted while ungated and gated later is not covered, and its call parks.

docs.title: next_fire_at
docs.text:
next_fire_at(schedule: Schedule, timezone: ZoneInfo, after: datetime) -> datetime

The first firing of schedule strictly after the aware after, in UTC.

A weekly schedule reads its wall time in timezone: a time a DST change skips fires shifted by the gap, and a repeated time fires at its first occurrence only. An interval adds elapsed hours to after, so pass the firing just claimed, not the sweep's clock, or every late sweep pushes the cadence later. Raises ValueError for a naive after.

docs.title: parse_schedule
docs.text:
parse_schedule(data: object) -> Schedule

Read a stored or submitted schedule; raises InvalidRoutineError outside the vocabulary.

The vocabulary is closed: {"kind": "weekly", "weekdays": [0, ...], "at": "HH:MM"} or {"kind": "interval", "every_hours": N}, and no other key. There are no cron strings.

docs.title: schedule_to_json
docs.text:
schedule_to_json(schedule: Schedule) -> dict[str, Any]

schedule as the JSON a routine stores; parse_schedule reads it back to an equal one.

docs.title: create_routine
docs.text:
create_routine(
    policy: RoutinePolicy[RoutineT],
    request: HttpRequest,
    draft: RoutineDraft,
    *,
    guard: ToolGuard,
    tool_defs: Iterable[ToolDefinition],
) -> RoutineT

Create a routine from draft in the scope policy.new_routine gives, run as the caller.

The caller is the principal and created_by, and must be authenticated. Each granted tool is pinned through guard against tool_defs, the definitions the agent offers. Raises InvalidRoutineError for a broken rule, an unknown tool, or a caller who already holds MAX_ROUTINES_PER_USER routines, and RoutineWriteRefusedError when the policy refuses.

docs.title: update_routine
docs.text:
update_routine(
    policy: RoutinePolicy[RoutineT],
    request: HttpRequest,
    routine: RoutineT,
    draft: RoutineDraft,
    *,
    guard: ToolGuard,
    tool_defs: Iterable[ToolDefinition],
) -> RoutineT

Replace routine's fields with draft's, if can_write admits it; the principal stays.

Every granted name must be a tool in tool_defs. While the agent stays the same, a tool the routine already granted keeps the flag pinned when it was granted, so an edit never re-approves a tool declared destructive since; a new name, or every name when the agent changes, is pinned now. next_fire_at moves only when the schedule, the timezone or enabled changes. can_write is asked of the row as stored and of the result; a refusal leaves routine as it was. Raises InvalidRoutineError for a broken rule or an unknown tool, and RoutineWriteRefusedError when the policy refuses.

docs.title: pause_routine
docs.text:
pause_routine(
    policy: RoutinePolicy[RoutineT], request: HttpRequest, routine: RoutineT
) -> RoutineT

Disable routine, if can_write admits it, keeping its prompt, schedule and grant.

next_fire_at clears, so the sweep skips it until an update enables it again. can_write is asked of the row as stored and of the result; a refusal leaves routine as it was and raises RoutineWriteRefusedError.

docs.title: list_routines
docs.text:
list_routines(policy: RoutinePolicy[RoutineT], request: HttpRequest) -> list[RoutineT]

The routines the caller may see whose principal is the caller, disabled ones too.

A routine the policy shows the caller but that runs as someone else, a teammate's, is left out; an anonymous caller has none.

docs.title: authoring_toolset
docs.text:
authoring_toolset(
    policy: RoutinePolicy[Any], request: HttpRequest, *, agent_id: str, guard: ToolGuard
) -> FunctionToolset[Any]

The routine tools for a run on the agent agent_id, as the user request carries.

list_routines lists the caller's own routines. create_routine, update_routine and pause_routine always ask first, whatever guard exempts or requires: each is marked with SELF_GATED_METADATA_KEY and raises ApprovalRequired with an x-confirm card that names the routine's principal, prompt, schedule, timezone and every pre-approved tool, a destructive one named as such. GrantedApprovals and ReviewedApprovals leave them to the person (NEVER_AUTO_APPROVED); a project's own HandleDeferredToolCalls must too. An approval that edits the arguments writes nothing: the model is told to call again, so the edited routine gets a card of its own. A routine's principal is always the caller, its agent always agent_id, and an update or a pause reaches only a routine whose principal is the caller; every write still goes through the policy's can_write. Each granted name is pinned through guard against the run's own tools, client tools and these four left out. Compose it into a browser run only: a routine's firing hides these tools, and a headless run has nobody to show the card to.

docs.title: ROUTINE_AUTHORING_TOOLS module-attribute
docs.text:
ROUTINE_AUTHORING_TOOLS: frozenset[str] = frozenset(
    {"create_routine", "update_routine", "pause_routine", "list_routines"}
)

The tools authoring_toolset offers, which a routine's firing never sees.

docs.title: due_routines
docs.text:
due_routines(
    model: type[RoutineT],
    sweep: RoutineSweep,
    *,
    now: datetime | None = None,
    limit: int = 100,
) -> SweepResult

Fire every enabled routine of model whose next_fire_at has come, at most limit of them.

The due rows are claimed in one query with select_for_update(skip_locked=True), so a second sweep running at the same time passes over them, and each is moved to its next firing in the same transaction that enqueues it: a sweep run twice fires once. The queue sends what was enqueued when that transaction commits. Run it on a database that honours skip_locked, such as PostgreSQL; SQLite ignores the lock.

Each claimed routine, in this order:

  • its last firing lapsed (its worker died, or its principal or spec went away): the routine is paused, enabled off and paused_reason naming the run, and last_run_id is cleared so the routine fires again once turned back on;
  • it is later than its grace (sweep.grace, by default one schedule period): it is skipped, logged and counted as missed, so downtime runs a missed firing at most once;
  • its last firing is still pending, or the model's thread_waits says its thread still waits on a person: it is skipped;
  • the policy's can_run refuses its principal: it is paused with the reason;
  • otherwise the spec sweep.spec_name is enqueued as the principal with {"routine_id": pk, "thread_id": <a fresh uuid hex>}; the firing spec runs into that thread, which becomes last_thread_id, and the run id the queue returns last_run_id.

However late the sweep, next_fire_at moves to the first firing after now, stepped from the one claimed. A routine whose handling raises is rolled back, logged and left for the next sweep, and the others go on.

docs.title: RoutineSweep dataclass
docs.text:
What run_due_routines sweeps a routine model with: the queue, the spec it enqueues.

spec_name is the name the queue's registry holds the firing spec under. grace is how late a missed firing may still run; None is one schedule period, read at the missed firing.

docs.title: SweepResult dataclass
docs.text:
What one sweep did with each routine it claimed, by primary key.

fired were enqueued; missed were past their grace and skipped; busy were skipped because the last firing is still queued or running, or its thread still waits; paused were turned off; failed raised, were left as they were for the next sweep, and were logged.

docs.title: pin_preapproved_tools
docs.text:
pin_preapproved_tools(
    guard: ToolGuard, tool_defs: Iterable[ToolDefinition], names: Iterable[str]
) -> tuple[PreapprovedTool, ...]

Grant names, each pinned to guard.requires_approval of its definition as it is now.

Raises InvalidRoutineError for a name none of tool_defs carries, so a typo is never recorded as a grant.

docs.title: preapproved_exempt
docs.text:
preapproved_exempt(routine: AbstractRoutine) -> frozenset[str]

The names a firing's guard exempts: the granted tools that were gated when granted.

A tool granted while ungated is left out, so if it is declared destructive later its call parks rather than running on a grant that never named it as destructive.

docs.title: run_agent_spec
docs.text: Needs the [specs] extra, so it is imported from its module, django_spec_agents.routines.run_agent_spec, never from the package.

docs.title: run_agent_spec
docs.text:
run_agent_spec(
    model: type[AbstractRoutine], runner: HeadlessRunner, *, timeout: float
) -> ServiceSpec

The kernel spec a routine's firing runs: model's routine, to its first stop.

Register it in the queue's registry under the RoutineSweep's spec_name. It takes the sweep's {"routine_id", "thread_id"} and runs the routine's prompt on its agent, as its principal, into that thread, within timeout seconds. It presents the RunStop: completed, waiting when a gated call parked the thread, timed_out or error, so a parked firing ends SUCCEEDED with waiting and the thread's approval card takes it from there.

Its permission check refuses a routine that does not exist, a caller who is not the routine's principal, and a routine the model's policy can_run refuses, at enqueue and again on the worker, so a routine disabled in between lapses its firing.

The run gets GrantedApprovals over preapproved_exempt, marked routine:<pk>: a pre-approved tool that was gated when granted runs without parking, its result marked, and the kernel's own authorization still runs on the call. Any other gated call parks. Its first request's metadata carries the grant under ROUTINE_GRANT_KEY, and the routine-authoring tools, ROUTINE_AUTHORING_TOOLS, are not offered.

It declares atomic=False, so no transaction spans the run, and idempotent=False, so a worker that dies mid-run is not run again: the queue reports the firing lapsed.

The optional hook a SkillPolicy adds to keep the names its code-registered skills hold from being taken by a stored one.

A policy that defines reserved_names has create_skill, update_skill and every write through them, the skill tools and an editor endpoint alike, refuse a stored skill named like a reserved one. A policy without it reserves nothing.

docs.text:

The optional hook a SkillPolicy adds to scan user-authored skills, with pydantic-ai-harness's ArtifactScanner or one of its shape.

A policy with a scanner attribute has create_skill, update_skill and import_skill_md refuse a draft whose description or body the scanner flags, with InvalidSkillError naming the field, and has a flagged stored row left out of what StoredSkills offers a run and what the list_skills tool lists. A policy without it, or whose scanner is None, scans nothing.

docs.title: SkillScoping
docs.text:
Bases: Protocol, Generic[SkillT]

The optional hook a SkillPolicy adds to say whether a skill is the caller's own or one shared with them.

A policy that defines scope lets a transport label each skill it shows: the django-ag-ui skill editor, from 0.91.0, carries it as the entry's scope key. scope returns "personal" for a skill in the caller's own scope and "shared" for one another scope holds (a tenant's or a company's). A policy without the method labels nothing, and a transport leaves the key out. It is a separate protocol because a Protocol has no optional members: adding scope to SkillPolicy would break every policy written before it.

docs.title: create_skill
docs.text:
create_skill(
    policy: SkillPolicy[SkillT], request: HttpRequest, draft: SkillDraft
) -> SkillT

Create a skill from draft in the scope policy.new_skill gives, if can_write admits it.

Raises InvalidSkillError for a broken rule, SkillLimitError when the caller already sees MAX_VISIBLE_SKILLS enabled skills, and SkillWriteRefusedError when the policy refuses. A name the policy reserves through ReservedSkillNames, and a description or body its SkillScanning scanner flags, are an InvalidSkillError.

docs.title: update_skill
docs.text:
update_skill(
    policy: SkillPolicy[SkillT], request: HttpRequest, skill: SkillT, draft: SkillDraft
) -> SkillT

Replace skill's name, description, body and flags with draft's, if can_write admits it.

can_write is asked twice, of the row as stored and of the result, so a policy can refuse both touching a skill and a change to it. Raises InvalidSkillError for a broken rule and SkillWriteRefusedError when the policy refuses; a refused update leaves both the row and skill as they were. A rename to a name the policy reserves through ReservedSkillNames is an InvalidSkillError; a skill keeping a name reserved since it was stored is not. So is a description or body the policy's SkillScanning scanner flags; the stored row is not scanned.

docs.title: Specs as tools
docs.text: Expose services and selectors declared as specs as a Pydantic-AI toolset, so a plain pydantic_ai.Agent can call them as tools — no MCP server and no AG-UI bridge in the path. A spec is anything django-service-specs compiles: one of its own ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec, or a value its kernel_spec compiles to one.

docs.title: What this is
docs.text:
A single thin adapter, SpecToolset, that turns a name -> spec mapping into agent tools. Every call runs on the kernel, on the compiled spec, so a spec is served the same way whichever library declared it:

  • dispatch, the kernel's, authorizes the call and executes the service or selector: the class-level check of the spec's permissions before anything is called, the object-level one on the resolved target, and validation, instance resolution and the output-selector re-fetch around them. Authorization is part of the dispatch, so no adapter can skip it;
  • the run's call_context carries the request the run arrived on, if any. Where it carries none, and no call_seeds override returns one, a selector or provider declaring request or view is handed None, while a permission check reads the principal and, where it declares arguments, the call's arguments;
  • spec_caller_input_schema, the kernel's, derives each tool's parameter schema from the compiled spec: the argument set dispatch checks, less what the server fills, requiring what dispatch refuses the caller for leaving out; and spec_output_schema its return_schema, projected for the audience;
  • paginate_output, the kernel's, slices a list selector into the page the tool returns, the same shaper the MCP transport uses;
  • present_for_audience, the kernel's, renders the result through the spec's presenter and applies the field markings.

The result is that an agent driving these tools sees exactly what an HTTP client would: the same validation errors, the same permission checks (class-level before anything is called, and object-level on the resolved row), the same rendered payloads — without the network hop, and without standing up an MCP server.

docs.title: How it compares
docs.text: If you already run a django-spec-mcp server, MCPToolset from this package's [mcp] extra exposes its tools to Pydantic-AI through the in-process MCP surface. SpecToolset is for the case where you want the specs as tools without any MCP layer: the [specs] extra installs it on django-service-specs and pydantic-ai-slim alone, and the toolset imports nothing from Django REST Framework.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• Quickstart — wire a toolset to an agent.
  • Shared spec registry — declare your specs once when more than one transport exposes them.
  • Reference — the public API.

docs.title: Hide plumbing from the model
docs.text:
An output declared for your API is handed to the model verbatim when the same spec becomes a tool. Everything in it is equally visible, so records get referred to by primary key, a status reads as IN_STOCK rather than "In stock", and internal fields get narrated as if they were content.

The marking travels to both halves of what the model sees. The payload is projected as it is rendered, and the tool's return_schema is generated from the same declaration — so a hidden field is absent from the schema as well as from the result, and a handle carries its description in both. A schema still advertising a field the render drops would be worse than no schema at all: the model asks for it, gets nothing back, and is told nothing about why.

docs.title: Mark the fields
docs.text:
The marking is FieldMarking, from django-service-specs, declared on the output field it marks. On the kernel's DataclassPresenter it goes in the field's annotation, so the dataclass that declares the output declares its audience too:

from dataclasses import dataclass
from typing import Annotated

from django.db import models
from django_service_specs import DataclassPresenter, FieldMarking


class WidgetStatus(models.TextChoices):
    IN_STOCK = "IN_STOCK", "In stock"
    SOLD_OUT = "SOLD_OUT", "Sold out"


@dataclass
class WidgetOut:
    id: Annotated[int, FieldMarking.handle("Widget handle.")]
    name: Annotated[str, FieldMarking.label()]
    price: Annotated[str, FieldMarking.hidden()]
    status: WidgetStatus


presenter = DataclassPresenter(WidgetOut)

A presenter of your own carries the same marking on each OutputField its output() declares, as marking=.

Nothing changes at the toolset. A tool rendering through that presenter returns:

{"items": [{"id": 1, "name": "Sprocket", "status": "In stock"}], "page": 1, ...}

(the pagination envelope is the list-tool wrapper; the projection lands on the rows inside it, never on the envelope's own keys, which belong to no presenter).

price is gone. status reads as a person would say it: a field with choices is rendered for the agent as its display, which the kernel takes from a Django Choices enum's label. id is untouched — a handle is another tool's input, so its value is never re-spelled.

The derived instructions gain one line, and only when some tool in the toolset actually returns a handle:

Some tools return opaque identifier fields, described as such in the tool's output. Pass them to other tools that ask for one; refer to records by their name in anything you say, never by the identifier.

A handle that declares no description of its own is described in the output schema with the field-level half of the same advice. Both sentences are yours to reword, or drop, through conventions=: handles and handle_field_description.

docs.title: One tool that needs what its siblings hide
docs.text:
The presenter is the declaration and stays authoritative. The exception is a tool whose whole job is handing back something the others drop — a lookup returning the price a list view hides. That tool gets a presenter of its own, declaring the field without the marking, on its own spec:

from dataclasses import dataclass, replace


@dataclass
class WidgetPriceOut:
    id: Annotated[int, FieldMarking.handle("Widget handle.")]
    name: Annotated[str, FieldMarking.label()]
    price: str


registry.register(
    "lookup_widget",
    replace(specs.lookup_widget, presenter=DataclassPresenter(WidgetPriceOut)),
)

The marking is part of the spec's output declaration, so SpecToolset projects it whether it is handed the registry or registry.specs(), and so does an MCP server registering the same spec — which is the reason it lives there rather than in either constructor. FieldMarking's axis is audience, not transport: an in-process toolset and an MCP server want the same thing as each other and something different from a browser, so a field hidden from one agent caller and visible to another is a bug you find in a transcript rather than in a test.

Two fields left claiming FieldMarking.label() raises ImproperlyConfigured when the toolset is built (SpecToolset tool 'list_widgets': Output: both 'id' and 'name' are marked FieldMarking.label()...): a record has one name. The refusal is the kernel's, from the spec's output declaration; the toolset prefixes it with the tool, since the kernel names only the fields.

docs.title: What it costs
docs.text: Nothing per call. The markings are pure in the presenter's output declaration, like the tool schemas, so SpecToolset resolves them once at construction and reuses them.

docs.title: Other callers are unaffected
docs.text: A marking applies only for a caller that names an agent audience, as the kernel's FieldMarking documents. Any other caller of the same spec, a browser among them, is rendered the full output, which is the point: one declaration, whichever consumer is reading.

docs.title: Running from a worker
docs.text:
Every worked example in these docs is HTTP-shaped, down to deps=AgentDeps(user=request.user). The larger surface for a lot of projects is the other one: a Celery task, a management command, a scheduled job — an agent run with nobody waiting on it.

There is no headless mode to switch on, and this page is not describing one. The same SpecToolset runs either way; a spec dispatched from a worker takes exactly the path it takes behind a view, because that path was never an HTTP one to begin with. What actually differs is two things: there is no request, and there is more load. Everything below follows from one of those.

docs.title: The smallest run
docs.text:
Agent.run_sync works today and needs nothing from this package:

tasks.py
from celery import shared_task
from django.contrib.auth import get_user_model
from pydantic_ai import Agent

from django_spec_agents import AgentDeps
from django_spec_agents.spec_tools import SpecToolset

toolset = SpecToolset({"list_orders": list_orders_spec})
agent = Agent("anthropic:claude-opus-4-8", deps_type=AgentDeps, toolsets=[toolset])


@shared_task
def summarise_account(user_id: int) -> str:
    user = get_user_model().objects.get(pk=user_id)
    result = agent.run_sync(
        "Summarise this account's open orders.",
        deps=AgentDeps(user=user),
    )
    return result.output

Build the toolset and the agent once, at module scope. Both are reusable across runs — the toolset resolves its specs, validates its declarations and derives each tool's schema in the constructor, and repeating that per task is pure waste. Nothing per-request is closed over in either, which is what makes that safe.

docs.title: The acting user is the whole authorization story
docs.text:
AgentDeps.user is not a convenience. It is the identity every permission_class, extend_queryset and scoping provider resolves against, and off HTTP it is the only thing that carries it.

Resolve it server-side, from something you trust: a task argument that is a primary key you put there, a row you already own. Never from the model's own output, and never from text the model was given — a run that can talk its way into a different user has no authorization boundary at all.

The run's request is not an identity

A request in the run's call_context is there so a callable or scoping provider reading request.META finds something plausible. Nothing downstream re-derives the acting user from it. Passing an authenticated request authorizes nothing, and leaning on it would put a second, invisible identity in the call.

docs.title: Nobody is anonymous by accident
docs.text: A view refuses an unauthenticated caller before the agent is reached. A worker has no such gate, so a task whose user_id is None runs with user=None and whatever the spec's permissions make of that. Decide it at the top of the task, where the answer is obvious, rather than in a permission class three layers down.

docs.title: Concurrency: the one setting a worker genuinely needs
docs.text:
Every tool call goes through sync_to_async, which defaults thread_sensitive=True — and asgiref's single_thread_executor is a class attribute, so that is one thread for the whole process, shared by every toolset instance and every concurrent run in it.

Pydantic-AI runs function tools in parallel within a segment. Four 0.30s tool calls under one model step therefore take about 1.2s rather than 0.3s. In a chat turn calling one tool this is invisible. In a fan-out it is the ceiling.

from concurrent.futures import ThreadPoolExecutor

toolset = SpecToolset(
    SPECS,
    thread_sensitive=False,
    executor=ThreadPoolExecutor(max_workers=8),
)

Read this before flipping it

thread_sensitive=True is what keeps Django's thread-local database connections coherent. Setting it False moves dispatch onto a pool, and each of those threads opens and owns its own connection. That is fine — and it is what you want — provided you have accounted for it:

  • Your database can take max_workers more connections per worker process, or you front it with a pooler.
  • Nothing in your specs relies on being in the caller's transaction. An outer atomic() block in the task does not wrap work that ran on another thread.
  • You are not inside pytest.mark.django_db without transaction=True, where the test's wrapping transaction is invisible to other threads. That holds under the default too: see a test whose tool writes.

executor= is only consulted when thread_sensitive is False — that is asgiref's rule, not this package's. Setting it alone does nothing, silently.

docs.title: Reading the logs afterwards
docs.text:
Nobody is watching a background run, so the log line is the whole record. Every tool call logs at DEBUG (WARNING for a permission denial, which is otherwise traceless — the run loop absorbs it into a message) on the django_spec_agents.spec_tools logger, and carries correlation fields in extra:

Field run_id, conversation_id which run this line belongs to run_step, tool_call_id where in that run run_input_tokens, run_output_tokens, run_requests, run_tool_calls the run's usage so far

Concurrent runs interleave, and without these the lines are indistinguishable. The usage fields are cumulative for the run rather than attributable to the call — a tool call spends no tokens itself — which is exactly what makes them useful here: they say where the budget stood when a long run went wrong. They ride on the timing line; the run_id / conversation_id / run_step / tool_call_id four are on every line the package emits, including the WARNINGs a misbehaving call produces (a dispatch timeout, a result over its byte ceiling, a file described rather than returned over it).

settings.py
LOGGING = {
    "version": 1,
    "loggers": {
        "django_spec_agents.spec_tools": {"level": "DEBUG", "handlers": ["json"]},
    },
}

Bounding the run is Agent.run's job, not the toolset's. Pass UsageLimits there. A toolset can only refuse the next tool call, which is the wrong instrument and a second place for the limit to live.

The limits are still readable from a tool call, though, and one thing is worth doing with them: ctx.usage_limits reaches an enforce_result_bytes override, so a project can taper how much a call is allowed to return as the run consumes its budget. That is shaping a result, not enforcing a limit — the run still stops where Agent.run says it does.

docs.title: Bounding what comes back
docs.text:
A model reading a 40,000-row selector is a cost and latency problem before it is a correctness one, and in a fan-out it is multiplied by every concurrent run.

  • max_page_size= caps what one list call can return, however large a limit the model asks for. The clamp is reported back in the envelope, so the model is told it received less than it asked for rather than silently truncated.
  • max_result_bytes= (and tool_max_result_bytes= per tool) bounds the serialized payload, answering with a refusal the model can act on; a file result over it is described to the model rather than attached or refused.
  • dispatch_timeout= bounds how long a call blocks the run. It does not stop the work — the thread runs to completion; the run stops waiting.

docs.title: Changing the pipeline
docs.text:
Five overridable methods cover a tool call end to end. The front half — call_seeds and translate_exception — is documented under SpecToolset; the back half is shape_page, render_output and enforce_result_bytes. All five receive the live RunContext, which is the point: a run's typed deps are usually what needs to reach them.

The one worth knowing about before you need it is render_output. By default a result is rendered through the spec's presenter and projected for the agent audience. If a background job feeds one spec's output into the next, project the handles away and the next step has nothing to key on. Presenting with the kernel's present(spec, result) instead is the opt-out — and passing projection=None is not it, since that means "derive one from the spec".

docs.title: Testing it
docs.text:
The run loop is where the interesting failures live, and it needs a model. django_spec_agents.testing ships the three doubles this package's own suite uses — no provider, no network, no key. The module imports pydantic-ai alone, so it works on an install without the [specs] extra too:

from pydantic_ai import Agent

from django_spec_agents import AgentDeps
from django_spec_agents.spec_tools import SpecToolset
from django_spec_agents.testing import tool_calling_model


async def test_the_task_calls_the_tool():
    toolset = SpecToolset({"list_orders": list_orders_spec})
    agent = Agent(tool_calling_model("list_orders"), deps_type=AgentDeps, toolsets=[toolset])

    result = await agent.run("go", deps=AgentDeps(user=user))

    assert result.output == "done"

Test the task as a whole this way rather than calling call_tool directly. Asserting on call_tool answers does the tool work; only a run answers whether the tools execute in-process, whether a ModelRetry is fed back for another attempt, and whether the toolset's instructions reached the model.

If your worker code is sync, drive it with agent.run_sync inside django_db(transaction=True) — the same shape production uses.

docs.title: A test whose tool writes needs transaction=True
docs.text:
A plain pytest.mark.django_db test runs inside one transaction on its own connection and rolls it back at the end. Under the default thread_sensitive=True too, a tool call made by await agent.run(...) in an async test, or by agent.run_sync(...) in a sync one, runs on asgiref's shared thread. That thread has a connection of its own, in autocommit, and the test's transaction does not reach it:

  • A write that succeeds commits. It survives the test's rollback and lands on whichever later test counts rows, which then fails for a reason nowhere near itself. The next transaction=True test truncates every table at teardown, so the evidence is gone by the end of the session.
  • The tool cannot see the test's uncommitted rows. On PostgreSQL a write pointing at one fails its foreign key with IntegrityError, and a read answers as though the rows were never made.
  • On SQLite the test's lock answers first. Once the test has written anything, every tool write fails, whatever it points at: with database is locked after the timeout when TEST["NAME"] makes the test database a file, and at once with database table is locked on Django's default in-memory one, where a read of a table the test wrote raises the same error.
  • The async ORM runs on that thread too. Rows an async test makes with acreate, aget_or_create and the rest are made on the shared thread, outside the test's transaction. They commit and outlive the test, and the connection that made them stays open, so PostgreSQL reports the test database as "being accessed by other users" when the session drops it.

A test whose tool writes, or reads rows the test made, uses pytest.mark.django_db(transaction=True): its rows are committed, every connection sees them, and the tables are truncated afterwards. A test asserting only a refusal that reads nothing the test created can stay on the plain marker, provided it makes its rows with the sync ORM, in a fixture for an async test. Arguments the Validator rejects are such a refusal, and so is a permission check reading a field of the principal, such as is_staff; user.has_perm(...) is not, since it reads the permission tables.

docs.title: Progress, when there is no browser
docs.text: AgentDeps.progress takes a ProgressReporter, and a spec that reports progress calls it wherever it runs. This package never constructs one: picking a sink would be picking a transport it does not own. Off HTTP, the useful sinks are the ones a worker already has — a task-state update, a row, a log line.

docs.title: Queuing a headless run
docs.text:
A transport's HeadlessRunner runs an agent with no browser. By default the run's owner is a task in the process that started it, so a restart of that process ends the run. A host with a task queue can move the owner to a worker instead: it fills a FiringQueue and registers run_headless, a kernel spec whose body is the runner's run_to_first_stop, in the registry the worker reads. A host that claims the thread before it enqueues, so the caller learns the run at once, puts the claimed id in the firing's run_id, and the worker's run adopts that claim rather than taking a new one. A firing's answers, a tool_call_id to its answer's text, resume a thread parked on a question: the runner resumes its stored history with them and sends no new prompt. The spec passes run_id and answers only when the firing carries them. Its inbox_mark, an optional integer, is the thread's inbox mark taken at enqueue: the spec does not pass it to the runner, a worker that wakes the thread reads it from the firing, so mail enqueued before pickup still wakes the thread.

spec_tasks.py
from datetime import timedelta

from django_service_specs import SpecRegistry
from django_spec_agents.headless.run_headless import run_headless
from django_spec_agents.headless.types.firing_state import FiringState
from django_spec_tasks import TaskBinding, enqueue, state_of

registry = SpecRegistry()
registry.register("run_headless", run_headless(runner, permissions=[IsMember()]))
binding = TaskBinding(
    name="agents", registry=registry, backend=backend, lease=timedelta(minutes=20)
)

_LAPSED = {"ABANDONED", "AUTHORIZATION_LAPSED", "SPEC_UNAVAILABLE"}


class SpecTasksQueue:
    def enqueue(self, spec_name, params, *, actor):
        return enqueue(binding, spec_name, params, actor=actor)

    def state(self, run_id):
        state = state_of(binding, run_id)
        if state is None:
            return None
        if state in {"PENDING", "RUNNING"}:
            return FiringState.PENDING
        return FiringState.LAPSED if state in _LAPSED else FiringState.FINISHED

runner is the transport's HeadlessRunner, IsMember your own PermissionCheck (the worker checks it again before the run), and backend is django-spec-tasks' Celery or Django Tasks backend. The binding's lease must outlast the longest timeout a headless run is given, or the worker is refused its terminal write for a run still going.

The spec declares atomic=False, so no transaction spans the agent run and what the run wrote before a crash stands, and idempotent=False: a worker that dies mid-run is not run again, which would be a second paid run. Its thread's lease lapses instead, so the thread reads failed with reason interrupted, and the queue reports the firing lapsed. A queued run carries no capabilities, since they cannot cross a queue as JSON; the runner composes what the mount declares.

docs.title: 1. Have some specs
docs.text:
SpecToolset works with the ServiceSpec and SelectorSpec objects you declare on django-service-specs, the kernel, with no DRF in them (see a spec declared on the kernel). A read selector and a write service, their input and output declared as dataclasses:

from dataclasses import dataclass

from django_service_specs import (
    DataclassPresenter,
    DataclassValidator,
    SelectorKind,
    SelectorSpec,
    ServiceSpec,
    Unrestricted,
)


@dataclass
class OrderOut:
    id: int
    status: str


@dataclass
class OrderIn:
    status: str


def list_orders(*, user):
    """List the current user's orders."""
    return Order.objects.filter(owner=user)


list_orders_spec = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=list_orders,
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(OrderOut),
    permissions=[Unrestricted()],
)


def create_order(*, data: OrderIn, user):
    """Create an order for the current user."""
    return Order.objects.create(owner=user, status=data.status)


create_order_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=create_order,
    validator=DataclassValidator(OrderIn),
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(OrderOut),
    permissions=[Unrestricted()],
)

docs.title: 2. Build the toolset
docs.text:
from django_spec_agents.spec_tools import SpecToolset

toolset = SpecToolset(
    {
        "list_orders": list_orders_spec,
        "create_order": create_order_spec,
    }
)

Each key is the tool name. The description comes from the selector/service docstring, the parameter schema from the selector's reads or the service's Validator and target lookup (see What a tool asks the model for), the return_schema from its presenter's output, and the readOnlyHint annotation from the spec kind (selectors read, services mutate). List selectors additionally accept page and limit tool args, plus ordering where the selector's filter_set declares one.

docs.title: 3. Run an agent
docs.text:
The acting user flows through RunContext.deps. The default AgentDeps carries it:

from pydantic_ai import Agent
from django_spec_agents import AgentDeps

agent = Agent("anthropic:claude-opus-4-8", deps_type=AgentDeps, toolsets=[toolset])

result = await agent.run(
    "show me my last 5 orders, newest first",
    deps=AgentDeps(user=request.user),
)

No request in sight?

request.user is the HTTP shape. A Celery task, a management command or a scheduled job resolves the acting user itself and passes it the same way — see Running from a worker, which also covers the one setting a fan-out genuinely needs.

For that request the model can call list_orders with {"limit": 5, "ordering": ["-created"]} and the toolset enforces permissions, runs the selector as request.user, hands ordering to the selector's filter_set, slices the result, and renders it through its presenter.

docs.title: Every list result is a page
docs.text:
A list selector answers with the pagination envelope, never a bare array:

{
    "items": [{"id": 12, "amount": "48.00"}, ...],
    "page": 1,
    "totalPages": 4,
    "hasNext": True,
}

limit defaults to 100 rows and page to 1, so a tool over a large table returns its first hundred rows and says so. That is the point: a bare slice would leave a model asking for a collection with 50 of 51 rows and nothing in the answer telling it more existed. hasNext closes that gap — the model can ask for page: 2, or narrow the request with a filter, instead of answering from a page it took for the whole set.

A service whose result is a list -- a LIST output re-read, a many=True call, a returns_many=True return -- is not paged, but it is not a bare array either: the model is handed its rows under items, as {"items": [...]}, and its return_schema is an object with that one required property holding the array. The value decides, so any list or tuple a tool returns is wrapped the same way, a presenter-less service's and a render_output override's included. A model reads a list's rows at one path whether the tool pages or not, and django-spec-mcp serves the same spec in the same shape, so a list reads the same through SpecToolset and the MCP bridge.

Because the toolset takes page and limit out of a list tool's call to serve the page, a list selector taking a parameter of either name is refused with ImproperlyConfigured when the SpecToolset is built: the parameter would never receive what the model sent, and one with a default would quietly run on it. Rename the parameter. A retrieve selector's page is not paginated and reaches it.

max_page_size caps limit and advertises itself as JSON-Schema maximum on it. A call naming no limit is served the smaller of 100 and the ceiling, and that is the default both the limit description and the toolset's instructions state, so with the toolset below the model reads "Defaults to 25" beside maximum: 25. A ceiling above 100 raises what a call may ask for, not what it gets by asking for nothing: the stated default stays 100.

toolset = SpecToolset(specs, max_page_size=25)

The same envelope is what the tool's return_schema describes, generated from the same spec — so, as the default shape_page serves it, the schema and the payload cannot disagree about it.

docs.title: How many rows match: include_total
docs.text:
A model asked "how many orders are open" can read only totalPages off the envelope above and multiply, or page through every row and count. Turn on include_total and every list tool the toolset serves says it outright, beside the rows:

toolset = SpecToolset(specs, include_total=True)

{
    "items": [{"id": 12, "amount": "48.00"}, ...],
    "page": 1,
    "totalPages": 4,
    "hasNext": True,
    "total": 352,
}

total is how many rows the selector matched across every page, after its filters and before the slice. It costs no query: the toolset already counts the rows to clamp page against the last one, and the flag hands that count on. With it on, the tool's return_schema lists total as required and the limit description names it, so a model knows a one-row page answers "how many", and so do the pagination line of the derived instructions and the sentence on each read-shaping parameter that lists the envelope's keys. With it off, the default, the envelope, both schemas and the instructions are exactly as above. SpecCapability takes the same keyword.

The flag is toolset-wide, and so is what it advertises: the return schema, the limit description, and the envelope the pagination line, each read-shaping parameter's sentence and its render retry name (the {envelope} placeholder) are written from it when the toolset is built, never from a shape_page override. For total on some tools only, leave the flag off and override shape_page to return a counting page for those tools, reading the call's tool name off ctx.tool_name. The recipe below does exactly that, and an empty entry in its LIST_AGGREGATES adds total alone. Nothing advertised then claims a key a page lacks. The reverse, the flag on and an override dropping total from some tools, leaves those tools' limit description and the pagination line, which the model reads on every turn, promising a key that never comes.

include_total never governs tools bridged through [mcp]: the MCP server's own choice does, because the bridged payload and the bridged schema both come from the server, so whether they carry total is its decision.

docs.title: Aggregates beside the total: a shape_page override
docs.text:
The toolset ships the count and no other figure, because which sums a list owes its reader is the project's to declare. A model asked "how much is outstanding" otherwise pages through every invoice and adds the balances itself, slowly and not always correctly; the database does it in one query. Declare the aggregates per tool and write them into the envelope from shape_page:

import dataclasses
from typing import Any

from django.db.models import Aggregate, QuerySet, Sum
from django_service_specs import OutputPage

from django_spec_agents.spec_tools import SpecToolset

# Keyed by tool name. A list tool with no entry is served the default page;
# an empty entry adds ``total`` alone.
LIST_AGGREGATES: dict[str, dict[str, Aggregate]] = {
    "list_invoices": {"amount_total": Sum("amount")},
    "list_customers": {},
}


@dataclasses.dataclass(frozen=True)
class AggregatedPage(OutputPage):
    """A page whose envelope also carries the count and the declared aggregates."""

    aggregates: dict[str, Any] = dataclasses.field(default_factory=dict)

    def envelope(self, rendered: Any) -> dict[str, Any]:
        return {**super().envelope(rendered), "total": self.total, **self.aggregates}


class AggregatedSpecToolset(SpecToolset):
    def shape_page(self, rows, *, ctx, page, limit, max_page_size):
        shaped = super().shape_page(
            rows, ctx=ctx, page=page, limit=limit, max_page_size=max_page_size
        )
        declared = LIST_AGGREGATES.get(ctx.tool_name or "")
        if declared is None or not isinstance(rows, QuerySet):
            return shaped
        # Over ``rows``, the filtered queryset before its slice: the same set
        # ``total`` counts. An empty list sums to ``None``, reported as 0, and an
        # empty entry aggregates nothing, which Django answers without a query.
        aggregates = {name: value or 0 for name, value in rows.aggregate(**declared).items()}
        return AggregatedPage(
            items=shaped.items,
            page=shaped.page,
            limit=shaped.limit,
            total=shaped.total,
            aggregates=aggregates,
        )

Called with limit: 20, list_invoices then answers {"items": [...], "page": 1, "totalPages": 3, "hasNext": true, "total": 41, "amount_total": 10428}, and list_customers its page with total beside it. Unlike total, the aggregates are a query of their own, one per call of a tool that declares any. With the flag off, the return_schema and the limit description still describe the default envelope: true of what is sent, but silent about the new keys, which name themselves in the payload. A project sending return schemas to the model states them in the tool's metadata["json_schema"]["output"] fragment. The merge is shallow, so that fragment replaces properties and required whole: restate the envelope's keys, items with its row schema, beside total and the aggregates, or the schema loses them.

docs.title: The output schema
docs.text:
Each tool definition carries a return_schema derived from the spec's presenter output, projected the same way the payload is: a field marked hidden is absent from both, and a marked handle carries its description in both. It is the kernel's spec_output_schema.

A spec's metadata["json_schema"] is merged over both schemas, keyed by phase: {"input": {...}} over the parameter schema and {"output": {...}} over the return_schema. The merge is shallow, so a key the fragment names is the fragment's whole, and an output fragment never makes a return_schema for a spec with none. A fragment that is not keyed by phase is refused when the toolset is built, naming the tool.

It is populated but not sent by default, because a return schema costs context on every turn of every run and only your model and your outputs say whether that trade is worth it. Pydantic-AI owns the opt-in, at either scope:

agent = Agent(model, toolsets=[SpecToolset(specs).include_return_schemas()])

A spec with no presenter gets None rather than a guessed shape.

A spec declaring shapes= requires no field of a row, at any depth, where the kernel's schema requires each one its presenter always renders. The relaxation is the kernel's own spec_output_schema, which the toolset advertises as it is. A shape drives the presenter, and a fields selection there leaves keys out, so no key is present under every value the model may send. The affordances each row carries stays required, since dispatch writes it whatever the shapes, as do the four keys of a list tool's page.

A return_schema admits null, with the root type ["object", "null"], where the spec says dispatch may hand the model None, as the kernel's can_present_nothing answers it for every route that states an output schema:

  • a retrieve selector declaring allow_none=True, when nothing matches;
  • a service whose output_selector_spec re-reads through a selector, because dispatch materializes the re-read with .first(), and a re-read that filters out the row it wrote finds none;
  • a service with nothing to re-read that declares ServiceSpec(allow_none=True), since dispatch then presents the service's own return, a None included.

A many=True or returns_many=True service declaring allow_none=True may return None too, but a list result is an object (below), so the model is handed {"items": []} and its return_schema admits no null.

A None the spec does not declare is still handed to the model. A service with nothing to re-read and no allow_none=True that returns None is presented as None, against a return_schema whose root is "object" and does not admit null. ServiceSpec(allow_none=True) is the declaration that admits it, so declare it on any such service that can return nothing.

allow_none on a service's nested output_selector_spec is not read, because dispatch does not read it, and a list result is never null, only empty. A service whose output_selector_spec declares LIST presents a list whether or not it has a selector to re-read through: with none, dispatch presents the service's own return as the list, and a return that is not a set of rows, such as the one row a create returns, raises ImproperlyConfigured out of the run. Return the rows, or declare RETRIEVE to present one.

docs.title: A file result
docs.text:
A spec presenting its result through the kernel's FilePresenter produces a FileResult, and the toolset reads it to the model the way read_attachment reads an attachment, under the toolset's attachment_inline config. Pass it the AttachmentInlineConfig read_attachment is given, so one config governs both; without one the defaults apply. SpecCapability and build_spec_capability take the same keyword:

from django_spec_agents import AttachmentInlineConfig
from django_spec_agents.spec_tools import SpecToolset

inline = AttachmentInlineConfig(max_bytes=1024 * 1024)
toolset = SpecToolset(specs, attachment_inline=inline, max_result_bytes=256_000)

Below, the limit is the smaller of the config's max_bytes and the tool's max_result_bytes, or the config's alone when the tool has no ceiling:

The file What the model gets Textual (text/*, JSON, XML, JavaScript, YAML, SVG), valid UTF-8, within the limit Its text. A type in media_types (PDF, PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP) within the limit The bytes, attached to the tool result as file content for that turn, beside a one-line note. A file over the limit A one-line note giving its name, type and size, and the limit it is over: the config's, or the tool's ceiling on one result. Anything else: another type, undecodable "text" A one-line note giving its name, type and size.

A file over the limit is read no further than the limit, and one of a type the model cannot read is closed without being read. Unlike read_attachment, the note does not ask the model to call the tool again for a later turn: calling a service again runs it again.

A file spec has no return_schema, since a file has no JSON shape. One the kernel's file_output refuses, such as a LIST selector presenting a file per row, is refused when the toolset is built, naming the tool.

max_result_bytes measures a file by its bytes: a text file by its UTF-8 length, an attached one by its bytes plus the note, never by the repr of the bytes. A file over it is described, a success, never refused with the advice to narrow the request that a list over it gets: a file has nothing to narrow, and a smaller file never fares worse than a larger one. That holds for a FileResult a render_output override returns unrendered too. Handing the user a download of the file is not the toolset's to do.

docs.title: What a tool asks the model for
docs.text:
A tool's parameter schema is the model's only account of what to send, and the kernel reflects nothing off a callable's signature: every argument is one the spec declares. So the schema is the kernel's spec_caller_input_schema of the compiled spec: the argument set dispatch checks, less the kernel's server_owned_keys for the toolset's seeds, with a parameter a provider may fill offered and not required:

  • A name the toolset fills is not advertised. That is the dispatcher's own pool seeds (request, user, progress and the rest), every name registered in pool_seeds, and the keys a kwargs= provider returns when its return annotation is a TypedDict, less any it may decline with UNSET (below). The annotation is read by the kernel's provider_keys, the reader dispatch's own contract is stated in, so this toolset and django-spec-mcp read a provider the same way.
  • A namesake is still advertised. A key a spec's kwargs= provider returns that is named like a Validator field does not fill the field: unless input_data fills it, the field stays the caller's, advertised and required as the Validator says, and validated into data, while the provider's value goes to the service keyword of that name. A target selector's kwargs= key named like a Validator field or a spec reads name reaches only the selector, and the field or read stays the caller's. The same holds for a many spec's row fields, offered in each row.
  • An input field the spec's Validator requires and no call can send is refused when the toolset is built, with ImproperlyConfigured naming the tool and the field, under either unknown_arguments policy. A Validator says so as its unsendable attribute, a collection of field names: a field it fills itself under a name dispatch seeds, so it declares no parameter for it, the tool does not advertise it, and the model's value would be refused or dropped. Rename the field or make it optional. A Validator that does not answer unsendable names none, and a spec compiled partial is left alone. A field named like one of your own pool_seeds, such as tenant, is a parameter, so it is the model's to send and is not refused.
  • A read declared required=True is required, and one with a default or none stays optional.
  • A kwargs= provider without a TypedDict return annotation may fill any read, a plain dict or a lambda included, so no read its values reach is required of the model, one declared required=True included: the tool advertises each and the kernel checks it on the pool the call assembles instead, handing the model back a read neither of them filled. So may a provider whose return annotation does not resolve, or that has none. A provider that only reads, and fills nothing, says so by returning an empty TypedDict declared at module level, and the reads beside it keep their required; under from __future__ import annotations one declared inside a function does not resolve. Only the return annotation is read for the keys, so a parameter typed with a name imported only under TYPE_CHECKING changes nothing, and a TypedDict value that does not resolve makes only its own key one the provider may decline, so that key stays advertised and the others are still filled. Annotate the provider to have the rest required:
from typing import TypedDict


class ProjectScope(TypedDict):
    ceiling: int


def scope(project_pk) -> ProjectScope:
    # ceiling is filled here, so the model is never asked for it. project_pk is
    # a read the tool declares, handed to the provider by name.
    return {"ceiling": ceiling_for(project_pk)}


list_spec = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=priced_under,
    reads=Parameters.of(
        Parameter("project_pk", "integer", required=True),
        Parameter("ceiling", "integer", required=True),
    ),
    kwargs=scope,
    permissions=[Unrestricted()],
)
  • A key whose value admits UnsetType is not one the toolset fills. A provider may decline a key by returning the kernel's UNSET for it, which drops the key from the pool and lets the model's value through, so ceiling: int | UnsetType keeps ceiling advertised for the model to send, and optional, since the provider may fill it instead. The provider's other keys are still not asked for. It is the key's own value that has to admit UNSET, as a union member: regions: list[str | UnsetType] always comes back as a list, so regions is filled. A generic TypedDict is read with what binds its type parameters, so -> Scope[str | UnsetType] declines Scope's tenant: T as the written-out tenant: str | UnsetType does. If the provider declines the key and the model has not sent it either, the kernel refuses the call before the selector runs, and the model is handed back ceiling: This field is required. to send it on its next turn, as it is when an untyped provider leaves a parameter unfilled. Where the selector can run without the value, give the read a default.
  • A service's input_data= provider relaxes its Validator's fields the same way, and those fields only. input_data is merged over the model's arguments before the Validator runs, so a Validator field beside one that returns no TypedDict is advertised and optional, any of them being what it may fill; beside a typed one only the keys whose value admits UnsetType are, and the keys it always fills are not advertised at all. A field nobody filled is handed back to the model as a retry naming it, owner: This field is required., which the kernel raises before the Validator runs, so a Validator's own wording for a missing field does not reach the model there. A lookup parameter beside it stays required: a provider's values reach its own seat only. All of this is for a service that is not many. A many service's Validator fields are each row's, so its rows are neither relaxed nor stripped: the schema keeps listing them as the kernel advertises them, the top level relaxes nothing and the list stays required, though a row a provider fills is served without the field.
  • A name only a call_seeds override fills is not a read. An override is code the schema cannot read, so leave the name out of reads=: the callable takes it by name from the pool, as it takes user. Declared as a read, it is the model's to send, and a seed of that name is refused at the call with ImproperlyConfigured: the seed would replace whatever the model sent, so a model that asks for one project would be served another's rows. Where the value is the same for every run, register it as a pool seed instead, which the schema does read.

A service tool also advertises its target lookup: the reads of its collection_selector_spec or its instance_selector_spec, whichever the service declares, beside the Validator's fields. A rename tool whose instance selector reads pk asks for pk as well as the new title, and requires it. A lookup parameter and a Validator field sharing a name are two declarations of one argument, and the toolset refuses the spec when it is built with ImproperlyConfigured naming the tool and the parameter, rather than advertising one of them. Rename one of the two.

A call that leaves out a required argument is handed back, the tool's own or its target lookup's, as ModelRetry naming each one left out, as in Missing required argument(s): `pk`., so the model corrects the call on its next turn. A required Validator field is checked by the Validator once the call runs, so a service call missing both pk and a field is told about pk first, and about the field on the turn after. A name a provider may fill is not checked before the call, since only the pool the call assembles can say whether it arrived, and the kernel checks that pool: a read nothing filled comes back as a retry naming it too, ceiling: This field is required.

docs.title: Custom identity
docs.text:
If your project carries identity on a richer deps object, hand the toolset a get_user extractor instead of using AgentDeps:

toolset = SpecToolset(specs, get_user=lambda ctx: ctx.deps.principal.user)

docs.title: Project pool seeds
docs.text:
Over HTTP a service reads its tenant, locale or clock off request. Off HTTP there is no request carrying any of that, and the kernel's PoolSeeds is the channel for it. Hand the registry to the toolset as pool_seeds=:

from django_service_specs import DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS

seeds = DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS.extend(tenant=lambda user: user.profile.tenant)
toolset = SpecToolset(specs, pool_seeds=seeds)

Every dispatch the toolset makes is handed the registry. A service, a selector or an affordance's condition that declares tenant therefore receives the resolver's value, as it would from the kernel's dispatch(pool_seeds=seeds) called directly. The per-step check that leaves out an unavailable operation asks its conditions against the same seeds, so a step's catalog and the call's own refusal answer alike.

A registered name is reserved the way user and request are:

  • The model cannot supply it. An argument of that name is not passed on and is not refused as unknown either, so the callable always sees the resolver's value.
  • A read cannot declare it. A read with that name in a spec's reads= raises ImproperlyConfigured when the toolset is built, as one named user does. The kernel refuses an argument that meets a seed, so an accepted read would offer the model an argument every call is then refused for.
  • No schema advertises it. A selector or target lookup declaring the seed as a parameter does not offer it to the model, so the model is not asked for a value the call would ignore. See What a tool asks the model for.

A top-level Validator field named like a registered seed is the exception to the first point: the model sends it and it is validated into data, while the service parameter of that name stays the seed's. A Validator declaring parameters(self, *, call_context=None) is read as it declares itself to the call. A field the tool's schema offers that the call's declaration drops is answered by the seed, and the model's value is dropped rather than refused as unknown (under REJECT; IGNORE drops an unknown argument silently). A field declared only to the call is the model's to send.

The registry applies to the whole toolset. A seed is ambient to the deployment, and what varies with the acting user belongs in the resolver, which declares user to receive it. What varies with the run or the tool being called is the per-call form.

docs.title: Per-call seeds and the run's context
docs.text:
Two things reach every call beside its arguments, and neither is a request the toolset builds.

The run's context is AgentDeps.call_context, a plain dict the code starting the run fills. Each call is handed its own copy, built through the kernel's build_call_context with the run's dict as its base: the tool's name under action, "agent" under transport, and request, view and format set to None where the run put none. action and transport replace any entry of the same name the run put there, so a callable reading call_context["transport"] == "agent" knows an agent's tool call made it even when the run carries the HTTP request it arrived on. The run's entries reach every call as the same objects, so put the request the run arrived on there, under request:

deps = AgentDeps(user=request.user)
deps.call_context["request"] = request
result = await agent.run(prompt, deps=deps)

A callable declaring request is then handed that request, and a permission check declaring call_context reads it there. The toolset builds no request and no view of its own, so a selector or provider declaring request or view receives None unless the run puts one here or a call_seeds override returns one. A value it would read off a view's captures or a request's query string it takes by name instead, as one of the spec's reads. What a call writes to its copy does not reach the next call, nor the run's dict, so two calls the model makes at once never see each other's action.

Which transport a callable reads. call_context["transport"] is "agent" on every call this toolset makes, and django_spec_agents.spec_tools exports the same string as AGENT_TRANSPORT. A callable written for several transports compares the plain string and imports nothing; one written for agents alone may import the name. The kernel lists no transports: each package owns its value, and this one's is "agent". The key is stamped on every context a callable can see, the call's and the listing's conditions' alike, so a tool listed on call_context["transport"] == "agent" is not refused at its call on another value, and a check, a Validator's validate, the service, the selector and the presenter of one call read the same value.

What a tool's schema reads. The schema is built once, when the toolset is constructed, with no run in hand. A Validator declaring parameters(self, *, call_context=None) is asked there with what build_call_context(AGENT_TRANSPORT) returns: transport is "agent", and request, view, format and action are None. It says "a call through this transport", never "this caller". So:

  • A field declared to the "agent" transport is offered, and required if it says so, and a call sending it is served. One declared only to another transport is not offered, and under REJECT a call sending it is refused as unknown (under IGNORE its value is dropped).
  • A field keyed on the run, on its request or any other entry of deps.call_context, stays unoffered. A call sending it is still served, since the call reads its own declaration, but the model is not told about it, so a required one fails every call the model makes from the schema. Leave such a field optional, or fill it from an input_data= provider, which can read a per-call seed; a seed alone fills the service's parameter of its name, not the Validator's field, so a call leaving the field out is still refused. A schema per run would ask every Validator again on every model step.
  • A Validator declaring call_context handles None, from the construction checks, and guards request: reading call_context["request"].user raises when the toolset is built. The error raised there is the Validator's own, and a note on it names the tool. A field it declares only with no request is offered and then, under REJECT, refused as unknown in a run that carries one, unless a registered seed carries its name, which answers it.
  • A clash only this declaration shows, such as a field sharing a target lookup's read or named for a seat of the dispatcher, is refused when the toolset is built, with ImproperlyConfigured naming the tool.

What you can override here is the run's call_context entries, which become the call's, and the per-call seeds call_seeds returns, request and view among them. A seed replaces what a callable declaring request or view is handed; the context's own request and view entries stay the run's. What you cannot is action and transport: the toolset writes them last, so a run's own entry of either never reaches a callable.

A service reads its actor from user, not from request.user. A service declaring request is handed it the same way, so a run that put no request in its context, such as a worker's or a test's started with AgentDeps(user=...) alone, hands the service request=None. A service that records who acted from request.user then records no one, or raises reading user off None. The principal reaches every callable on every route as user: here it is deps.user, or what get_user returns. Declare user and record the actor from it. Putting a request in the context to supply one would carry a second identity that the permission checks never see.

Per-call seeds come from call_seeds, asked once per call with the live RunContext and the tool's name, and once per conditioned tool when the catalog is listed. Each value is a resolver, as for PoolSeeds.extend:

class TenantToolset(SpecToolset):
    def call_seeds(self, *, ctx, tool_name):
        tenant = ctx.deps.tenant
        return {"tenant": lambda: tenant}

A name the mount's pool_seeds registers already is refused with ValueError at the call, and request or view returned here replace the call's own. A read or parameter tool_server_arguments binds or withholds for the tool is refused at the call too, with ImproperlyConfigured naming the tool, as the same seed on the mount is when the toolset is built; a bound Validator field of that name is not, and takes the bound value while the service parameter takes the seed.

docs.title: What a permission check sees
docs.text:
Every call is authorized by the spec's permissions, the kernel's PermissionChecks, inside the kernel's dispatch: has_permission before anything is called and has_object_permission on the resolved row. Each is asked with the call's principal, the acting identity: deps.user, or whatever get_user returns. The request a run arrived on never contributes an identity.
