A check reading more of the call than its principal names it, as the kernel's PermissionCheck documents: a keyword arguments is handed the call's arguments, as a read-only mapping, a keyword call_context is handed the run's context, with the tool's name under action, and a keyword named after a registered pool seed is handed that seed's value.

docs.title: The tool catalog is not permission-filtered
docs.text:
get_tools advertises every spec to every run, except a tool whose operation condition is unmet at that step. A tool whose permissions will deny this caller is still listed — the denial happens on the call. That is deliberate: a permission whose answer depends on the arguments has none to read at listing time and would hide a tool the caller can actually use, the listing runs once per model step so a database-backed check would cost a query per spec per step, and a model that cannot see a tool cannot ask about it. A listing carries a name, a description and an input schema; no row data.

If a deployment does want a narrower catalog, override is_tool_listed:

from asgiref.sync import sync_to_async


class OpsOnlyToolset(SpecToolset):
    async def is_tool_listed(self, name, ctx):
        if name != "suspend_account":
            return True
        # Django refuses ORM access on the event loop, so anything that
        # queries has to go through a thread — as dispatch itself does.
        return await sync_to_async(ctx.deps.user.groups.filter(name="ops").exists)()

Hiding a tool is a disclosure decision, never an authorization one: the call is gated by the spec's permissions whatever this returns.

docs.title: An operation that is unavailable right now is left out
docs.text:
A spec's Affordance answered without a row, a callable when such as lambda: Period.current().is_open (see below), is asked on every model step, and a tool whose condition is unmet is left out of that step's catalog. The arguments against filtering by permission do not apply to it. The condition reads only the seeds (the user, the request and any registered seed), never an argument, so it cannot hide a tool the caller could have invoked with other arguments. Only the specs declaring one are asked, and a toolset declaring none pays nothing. And the model can still tell the user about the missing tool, because the instructions for that step end by naming each tool left out with its reason:

- These operations exist but cannot be performed right now, so they are not among your tools. If the user asks for one, say it is unavailable at the moment and give the reason listed for it, rather than guessing why:
  - `post_invoice`: The books are closed.

The rest of the instructions are derived from the tools that step offers, so no line describes a tool it lacks. An instructions= override replaces those conventions but not this list, which is appended after the override: which tools a given step lacks is not something an override written in advance can say. The heading is the unavailable_heading field of conventions=, and setting it to None drops the heading and the list, with an override or without one.

A few things follow from how it is asked:

  • An is_tool_listed override cannot put the tool back. The omission is applied beside it rather than inside the default, so an override returning True does not need to call super() to keep it.
  • Conditions run where a dispatch runs, in a thread under the toolset's thread_sensitive and executor, so one that queries is fine. The connection it opens is closed after it, as a dispatch's is.
  • A condition is asked with the seeds its call would register, so one reading request sees the request the run arrived on when the catalog is listed as at the call, None for a run that arrived on none, and one reading a name a call_seeds override returns is asked with the seed returned for its own tool. That listing call carries no arguments, and its context's action is the tool's name.
  • A condition on the row (an ORM expression) is never asked here. There is no row when the catalog is listed, so the call answers it for its own row.
  • get_tools and get_instructions each ask once per step. A shared answer would need a key scoping it to one run, and the run context has none that is safe: run_id can be supplied by the caller and is reused when a failed run is retried. A condition that flips between the two reads can leave one step's catalog and instructions disagreeing about one tool.

None of this changes the call. The kernel's dispatch enforces every affordance whatever was listed, a call against a listing that went stale is refused as below, and a model calling a tool that was left out gets pydantic-ai's unknown-tool retry, which names the tools that do exist.

docs.title: Changing what the model is told
docs.text:
Every line of the instructions block, the heading of the unavailable list included, is a field of AgentConventions, and so are three sentences outside it: the description a handle field gets when it declares none, the sentence scoping a paged tool's read-shaping parameters, and the retry for a missing argument. conventions= changes them one line at a time. Each field defaults to the toolset's own wording, so AgentConventions() changes nothing, and leaving conventions= unset is the same as passing it.

Nothing else the toolset writes is a field. The descriptions of the arguments it adds, such as limit and page, stay fixed, and so do its other retries: a limit or page that is not a positive integer, an ordering the tool does not take, a service asking for more input, and the opening of a render retry, whose closing scope sentence is the one part that is a field.

from django_spec_agents.spec_tools import AgentConventions, SpecToolset

toolset = SpecToolset(
    specs,
    conventions=AgentConventions(
        # {envelope} is the page as this toolset writes it, `total` included under
        # include_total; {page_size} is the page an omitted `limit` is served.
        pagination=(
            "- Collections come back one page at a time, as {envelope}, "
            "{page_size} items unless you pass `limit`. Ask for the next `page` while "
            "`hasNext` is true."
        ),
        handles=None,  # this audience never sees identifiers, so say nothing about them
    ),
)

A field changes what a line says, never whether it appears. The toolset still decides that: the pagination line above is still absent from a toolset with no list tool, and the block is still re-derived on each step an unmet condition leaves a tool out, so an overridden line goes with the tool it describes. None drops a line wherever it would have been said.

Field Where it lands Said when Placeholders base instructions, first always none pagination instructions some tool returns a page {envelope}, {page_size} ordering instructions some tool advertises a sort argument {names} handles instructions some tool's output marks a handle none read_shaping instructions some tool declares a read-shaping parameter {names} read_shaping_on_pages instructions, after read_shaping that tool also returns a page {envelope} unavailable_heading instructions, last, above the tools left out a condition left a tool out this step none handle_field_description a handle field's output schema the field declares no description of its own none query_param_on_pages a read-shaping parameter's description, and the render retry the tool returns a page {envelope} missing_arguments the retry for a call missing an argument a required read or lookup parameter is left out {names}

A few rules follow from what each field is:

  • Every field is a str.format template, placeholders or not, so a literal brace is written twice everywhere. {names} is each name in backticks, joined with , (sorted, except ordering's, which follow the tools).
  • {envelope} is the page the default shape_page returns, with total when the toolset is built with include_total and without it otherwise. It follows the flag, not a shape_page override: an override that adds total with the flag off does not change it. In pagination it is the page written as an object, {"items": [...], "page": 1, "totalPages": N, "hasNext": true|false}, with "total": T last under the flag; in the two read-shaping fields it is the keys, `items`, `page`, `totalPages`, `hasNext`, and `total` last. Text without it is said exactly as written, flag or not.
  • A typo fails at startup. A placeholder the field does not accept, an unbalanced brace, or a format spec its value cannot take raises ImproperlyConfigured naming the field when the AgentConventions is built.
  • None on read_shaping drops read_shaping_on_pages too, because that sentence continues it; None on unavailable_heading drops the list beneath it. To drop a line, use None, not "", which leaves a blank line. missing_arguments cannot be None, empty or only whitespace: it is the retry's whole text.
  • missing_arguments covers the check made before the spec's Validator runs. A field the Validator requires is still reported in the Validator's own words, and a parameter a provider may fill and did not in the kernel's (ceiling: This field is required.), since only the pool it assembles can say the value never arrived.

Some lines state facts about behaviour, and an override owns keeping them true. pagination and query_param_on_pages name the page envelope's keys, and base says which failures come back as a retry and which as a failed call. The toolset goes on behaving as the defaults describe whatever the text says, so a rewording that drops or contradicts one of those facts tells the model something false. For the envelope the toolset keeps it true for you: write {envelope} where your text names the page, and it follows include_total.

conventions= and instructions=. instructions= replaces the whole derived block, so changing one of its lines (base through read_shaping_on_pages) beside it would be ignored, and the toolset refuses the pair with ImproperlyConfigured naming the fields. The other four land outside the block and apply either way, unavailable_heading included, since the list of unavailable operations is appended after an override too. Prefer conventions= where it can say what you need: an override is a copy of the block, so it keeps advising about pagination on a step with no list tool, and it misses every correction a later release makes to the wording.

SpecCapability takes the same keyword, and SpecCapability.from_toolset keeps the conventions of the toolset it wraps. They reach this toolset's tools only: the MCP transport, django-spec-mcp, writes its own schemas and retries, so a model reading the same specs over MCP is told what that transport is configured to say.

docs.title: Unexpected arguments
docs.text:
By default the toolset rejects tool args outside a spec's declared input set — a key the model invented — surfacing them as a ModelRetry so the model self-corrects. A filter_set's filters are declared names, so a key outside them and the selector's parameters is refused like any other. A selector taking a bare **kwargs declares no name, so every key sent to it is refused. Pass unknown_arguments= to change this:

from django_service_specs import UnknownArguments

# silently drop unexpected keys instead of rejecting them
toolset = SpecToolset(specs, unknown_arguments=UnknownArguments.IGNORE)

IGNORE drops a key no parameter declares. The tool's schema says which: under REJECT it closes the argument set with additionalProperties: false, at the top and on each row of a list input, and under IGNORE it states nothing, since a key outside the set is dropped and the call served. Under either policy the key never reaches the callable: the kernel hands a callable only what its spec declares. One exception is known: a selector taking **kwargs beside a filter_set also receives the FilterSet's values in its catch-all. REJECT and IGNORE are the two the toolset accepts. PASSTHROUGH raises ImproperlyConfigured when the toolset is built, because a tool call is one flat object and has no other channel to carry an undeclared name to the callable; to hand one over, declare it, as a reads entry or a Validator field.

docs.title: A list as input
docs.text:
A ServiceSpec declaring many=True becomes a tool that takes its list as one named argument. Its input validates as a JSON array, and a model's tool arguments are always a JSON object, so the array travels under the argument the spec's many_argument names, items unless it names another:

@dataclass
class WidgetIn:
    name: str
    price: str


def create_widgets(*, data: list[WidgetIn], user):
    """Create several widgets in one call."""
    return [Widget.objects.create(owner=user, name=w.name, price=w.price) for w in data]


create_widgets_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=create_widgets,
    validator=DataclassValidator(WidgetIn),
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(WidgetOut),
    many=True,
    many_argument="widgets",  # optional; the default is "items"
    permissions=[Unrestricted()],
)

The model sends {"widgets": [{...}, {...}]} and the service receives the list, exactly as it would from a bare array body. The tool's parameter schema says so: an object with that one required property, an array of the item schema, carrying the spec's many_min_length and many_max_length as minItems / maxItems, and, under the default REJECT, additionalProperties: false. A read the spec declares is advertised beside it. Each item is read by what input_data= fills, since it is merged over every row: a field it is annotated to fill is not in the item schema, and one it may fill, or any field beside a provider whose return names no TypedDict, is offered and not required.

The list's name may not be a pool seed's: a seed fills its name on every call, so no call could send the list. A many spec whose many_argument is a seed the mount registers, or request or view, which each call registers, is refused with ImproperlyConfigured naming the tool when the toolset is built.

What the model is told when a call is wrong:

  • An invalid item comes back as a ModelRetry naming the argument, then the invalid item's index, then the field, as widgets[1].price: ..., the same rendering every validation error gets, so the model corrects that one item.
  • Any other argument sent beside the list is held to the toolset's unknown_arguments, as any undeclared key is: under REJECT it comes back as note: Unknown argument., and under IGNORE it is dropped, since the service receives only the list and the argument would have nowhere to go.

A many spec may name the set its rows edit with a collection_selector_spec (django-service-specs 0.33.0). The selector's reads are its lookup, advertised beside the list and required as the selector declares them; a call sends them at the top level, and the service receives the resolved set as collection:

add_widgets = ServiceSpec(
    service=add_widgets,  # (*, data, user, collection)
    validator=widget_input,
    many=True,
    collection_selector_spec=SelectorSpec(
        selector=owned_widgets,
        kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
        reads=Parameters.of(Parameter("owner_id", "integer", required=True)),
    ),
)

The model sends {"owner_id": 7, "items": [...]}, and a call leaving out owner_id is asked for it. A lookup the selector takes but does not declare in reads is not advertised. An instance_selector_spec on a many spec is still refused by the kernel.

Any other argument a tool needs beside its list rules out many=True. Name the list as a field of the Validator's input instead, and loop over it:

@dataclass
class BulkWidgetIn:
    items: list[WidgetIn]
    dry_run: bool = False

The model sends {"items": [...], "dry_run": true}, and an invalid item comes back placing its errors at its index, as items[1].price: ....

docs.title: Ordering
docs.text:
The filter_set owns ordering. Declare a django-filter OrderingFilter named ordering on the selector's FilterSet and you are done:

import django_filters


class OrderFilterSet(django_filters.FilterSet):
    ordering = django_filters.OrderingFilter(
        fields=(("created_at", "created"), ("total_cents", "total")),
    )

    class Meta:
        model = Order
        fields = ["status"]

The kernel lists that filter in the tool's input schema as an array of its public choices, each a const under the label OrderingFilter gives it: {"type": "array", "items": {"type": "string", "anyOf": [{"const": "created", "title": "Created"}, {"const": "-created", "title": "Created (descending)"}, ...]}}, as OrderingFilter takes a list of sort keys, so the model is told exactly what it may sort by, in the words the FilterSet uses. A single key is sent as a one-element list, ["-created"]; one sent as a bare string is handed back as ordering: Expected an array. for the model to correct, rather than read as one key. At call time the value is handed to the FilterSet as filter data: it validates the choice, applies its own param_map, and a value outside the choices comes back as a ModelRetry. The toolset contributes nothing and takes nothing away.

One vocabulary, one declaration site, and the same ordering your HTTP views already serve.

The filter's name is yours to pick — an OrderingFilter declared as sorting is found and used the same way. What the schema advertises is what the model may send, under whatever it is called.

docs.title: A list selector with no filter_set
docs.text:
A selector that takes its own sort argument works too: declare it as a read, and it is advertised like any other, and handed to the callable to apply.

def list_orders(*, user, ordering: str):
    """List the acting user's orders."""
    return Order.objects.filter(customer=user).order_by(ordering)


list_orders_spec = SelectorSpec(
    kind=SelectorKind.LIST,
    selector=list_orders,
    reads=Parameters.of(Parameter("ordering", "string", default="-created_at")),
    presenter=DataclassPresenter(OrderOut),
    permissions=[Unrestricted()],
)

Prefer the FilterSet where there is one: it validates the value against a published set of choices before anything reaches the ORM, while a bare parameter is only as safe as what the selector does with it.

docs.title: Migrating from ordering_fields
docs.text:
SpecToolset(specs, ordering_fields=[...]) and its per-tool tool_ordering_fields form do not exist; passing either raises TypeError at construction. Move the names onto an OrderingFilter as (orm_path, public_name) pairs — the FilterSet at the top of this section is exactly ordering_fields=["created_at", "total_cents"] rewritten — and drop the argument.

The vocabularies are not the same, and that is the point of the move: the knob's values were raw ORM paths, applied with queryset.order_by itself, while a FilterSet's choices are public names it maps through its own param_map. Picking public names is the migration's one decision — they are what the model sees, so give them the words a reader would use.

docs.title: Read-shaping parameters
docs.text:
page / limit are built in for list selectors and ordering comes from the filter_set, but a spec can declare its own parameters that shape what it returns, as shapes= on the spec. The toolset advertises each as a tool argument, and the kernel hands what the model sent to the spec's presenter, as the call's PresentationContext.shapes, and to a callable that declares shapes. That is for a presenter that selects fields or switches between a summary and a detail rendering. A null is read as left out, and a declared default is applied when the model leaves one out, as the tool's schema advertises.

Declared on the spec, never on the toolset

A shape is the spec's to declare, so every transport and every mount reads the same answer; SpecToolset takes no channel declarations of its own, and passing query_params= or tool_query_params= is a TypeError. For a value the model may not choose, see arguments the server supplies.

You don't need this for filter_set

A SelectorSpec.filter_set's fields are already generated into the tool's input schema and flow through as ordinary arguments, which the kernel's dispatch hands the FilterSet as its filter_data. So the model can filter a list selector with no shape declared at all, and the same goes for ordering.

from dataclasses import replace

from django_service_specs import Parameter, Parameters, SpecRegistry

from django_spec_agents.spec_tools import SpecToolset

# A parameter several tools read is one declaration, in each spec's shapes.
FIELDS = Parameter("fields", "string", help="Comma-separated fields to return.")

registry = SpecRegistry()
registry.register(
    "list_orders",
    replace(
        list_orders_spec,
        shapes=Parameters.of(FIELDS, Parameter("detail", "string", default="summary")),
    ),
)
toolset = SpecToolset(registry)

A declared shape is one of the call's arguments, so unknown_arguments never flags it; a declared default is applied when the model leaves it out or sends it as null, unless it accepts null as a value. A shape cannot be named page, limit or ordering, which the toolset's own pagination and ordering arguments take.

docs.title: One read the selector and the presenter both need
docs.text:
A shape reaches the presenter and a read reaches the callable, and the kernel refuses one name declared as both. An argument that drives the selector's eager loading and the presenter's field selection, as django-restql's query does, can be declared once as a shape, and any callable then reads the call's shape values by declaring shapes, which the kernel hands it as a read-only mapping (empty on a spec declaring none). The name is the kernel's: a read, shape or many list named shapes is refused when the spec is declared, and a Validator field of that name when the toolset is built, so name it for what it holds.

def list_projects(shapes: Mapping[str, Any]) -> QuerySet[Project]:
    return Project.objects.prefetch_related(*relations_named_in(shapes.get("query", "")))

A shape the model leaves out, with no default declared, is absent from the mapping, so read an optional one with get.

A value that must be a read, because the argument also fills a parameter of the selector's own, is declared once as a read instead: the selector takes it by name and writes it to the call's context, which the presenter is handed on every row of the page the toolset presents.

def list_projects(query: str, call_context: dict) -> QuerySet[Project]:
    call_context["query"] = query
    return Project.objects.prefetch_related(*relations_named_in(query))


class ProjectPresenter(Presenter):
    def presented(self, value, context):
        return select_fields(self.present(value), context.call_context["query"])

A read is not a shape, so such a spec's return_schema still lists each field its presenter always renders as required, which a selection may leave out. A shape the selector reads through shapes keeps the relaxed schema.

A presenter that needs the whole page, to batch a lookup over its rows, overrides the kernel's Presenter.presented_rows(values, context). The toolset slices a list before it renders, so it is called once per page served, with exactly that page's rows.

docs.title: On a list tool, a parameter shapes each row
docs.text:
Every list tool returns a page, {"items": [...], "page": 1, "totalPages": N, "hasNext": ...}, but the presenter that reads a shape renders one row at a time and never sees the envelope. So a selection written against the documented shape, fields=items, asks each row for an items field it does not have. The toolset tells the model this in two places:

  • each read-shaping parameter on a list tool has "On a paged result it applies to each item in items, never to the page envelope (items, page, totalPages, hasNext)." appended to its description, or as its description when it declares none, with `total` last in the list under include_total; a retrieve tool's parameter is left as declared;
  • the read-shaping line of the instructions the toolset derives says the same, "On a tool that returns a page, they apply to each item in items, never to the page itself.", when some list tool declares a read-shaping parameter.

An instructions= override replaces the derived block, and this line with it: an override written before this sentence existed does not gain it, so add the advice to your own text if your tools page and take a selection. Changing the lines you need with conventions= instead keeps this one, and both sentences are fields there (read_shaping_on_pages and query_param_on_pages).

docs.title: A selection the presenter rejects
docs.text:
A read-shaping parameter is the one argument used while the result is rendered rather than while the call runs, so it is the one that can fail after the work is done. When the presenter raises the kernel's ServiceValidationError or InvalidArguments while rendering, and the model supplied a value for at least one of the tool's read-shaping parameters, the model gets a retry naming the argument:

`fields` was rejected while rendering the result: Unknown field `items`. On a
paged result it applies to each item in `items`, never to the page envelope
(`items`, `page`, `totalPages`, `hasNext`).

What follows the colon is the presenter's own message, verbatim. The toolset never reads a parameter's value, so this works the same for any grammar a presenter parses. The last sentence is there only on a list tool. With several parameters supplied, all of them are named, since the presenter does not say which one it refused. exception_map= / translate_exception sees the error first, as on the dispatch path.

The same error stays loud, and ends the run, when nothing the model sent shaped the render: no read-shaping value supplied, an explicit null, or a value that came from a declared default. A retry cannot fix a presenter that fails on its own or a default that is wrong, and would hide the bug behind the retry budget. Only those two refusals are converted; an AttributeError in a presenter is a bug whatever the model sent.

Use strict selection on tools an agent calls

This only works if the presenter says no. Make a name it does not know raise ServiceValidationError, and the model corrects itself in one retry. A tolerant selection, one that drops fields it cannot find, turns the same mistake into a page of empty rows, "items": [{}, {}], which is a successful result as far as anything downstream can tell. The toolset cannot tell that apart from a real answer without knowing the parameter's grammar, so it does not try.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
The toolset maps the kernel's failure kinds onto the Pydantic-AI model loop:

Outcome What the agent sees ServiceValidationError (bad input), or the kernel's InvalidArguments (an argument of the wrong shape, or a Validator's refusal of its value) ModelRetry with the field errors, one field: message line each — the model self-corrects. The arguments' shape is checked before the permission check, so a malformed call is handed back before it is authorized A read-shaping value the presenter rejects while rendering ModelRetry naming the argument — see A selection the presenter rejects ActionUnavailable (an Affordance condition not met) ToolFailed with the reason followed by the rule's code — The books are closed. (code: books_closed); see below AdditionalInputRequired (the service wants one more input) ModelRetry with the service's message, ending in the names to supply (Call this tool again, additionally supplying: `confirmed`.) — see the warning below ServiceError (business rule) ToolFailed with the rule's own message — a failed result the model reads and reports Unresolved instance: a read's or a write's instance selector that finds no row, or raises DoesNotExist or Django's Http404 (as get_object_or_404 does) ToolFailed("not found"), unless the spec sets allow_none=True, when the tool returns None. A list selector's Http404, usually from a parent it looked up, is ToolFailed("not found") whatever allow_none says; a list that finds no rows returns [], and a DoesNotExist escaping a list selector is an error, not a not-found A dispatch past dispatch_timeout ToolFailed — abandoned, with the sentence telling the model to narrow and call again A rendered result over max_result_bytes ToolFailed — refused rather than truncated, since a partial payload looks complete. A file is described instead: see A file result Unexpected argument (default REJECT) ModelRetry naming the unknown key, in the kernel's words: note: Unknown argument. A required argument left out: a required read, or a service's target lookup such as pk ModelRetry naming each such parameter left out; a missing Validator field is reported by the Validator when the call runs — see What a tool asks the model for An invalid item in a many=True list ModelRetry with the errors keyed under the list's argument, then the item's index — see A list as input An argument sent beside a many=True list As any undeclared key: ModelRetry naming it under REJECT, dropped under IGNORE Non-integer page / limit ModelRetry — naming what is accepted An ordering sent to a list tool that advertises no sort at all ModelRetry — saying the tool has none, rather than letting it fall through as an unknown key A limit over max_page_size, or a page past the last one Clamped, not refused — the envelope reports the page and totalPages actually served, so the clamp is visible rather than silent An OrderingFilter's ordering sent as one string rather than a list ModelRetry — ordering: Expected an array., as the schema advertises an array An ordering outside a filter_set's OrderingFilter choices ModelRetry — the FilterSet rejects it, which arrives as the InvalidArguments row above A FilterSet param_map target that isn't a real column Django's FieldError propagates — an author's error the model cannot correct by picking a different sort, and one that can't be checked at construction without a queryset A denied permission check (class-level has_permission or object-level has_object_permission), raised as the kernel's NotPermitted, Django's own PermissionDenied raised bare by a service, or a deactivated principal (PrincipalUnavailable, refused before any check) The refusal is raised, logged at WARNING naming the tool, and aborts the run — see the caveat below Another library's permission or validation exception, raised by a spec Neither of the above: the exception escapes the call unchanged. A spec library raising one translates it into the kernel's refusals

A confirmation raised as AdditionalInputRequired is not a gate

The retry for AdditionalInputRequired goes to the model, so the model can answer it: a spec that raises AdditionalInputRequired("Confirm to proceed.", schema={"confirmed": ...}) gets its first call back as a retry, and the model may re-send the same call with confirmed=true and run the mutation. No person is asked at any point.

Treat that confirmation as a prompt for missing input, not as a security boundary. An operation that needs a human decision has to be gated by an approval mechanism outside the spec: pydantic-ai's deferred-tool approval, or this package's ToolGuard. ToolGuard is off by default, and a tool named in its exempt list stays ungated even when it is also in require_approval. Every tool built from a mutating spec carries readOnlyHint: False in its annotations metadata (only a SelectorSpec reads True), so an approval policy keyed on that annotation covers them.

A tool-failure policy does not change the last row

"Aborts the run" is what a plain pydantic_ai.Agent does: nothing catches the exception, so it propagates out of agent.run. A tool-failure policy normally converts an escaping exception into a failed-tool result and lets the run continue — but this package's exempts an authorization refusal from exactly that, by default, and django-ag-ui inherits the exemption. So a denial aborts the run under those hosts too.

That exemption is deliberate and worth knowing rather than working around: converting a denial would leave the run alive with the model free to try the next row, and a refusal a model can tell apart from a missing row turns a permission boundary into an existence oracle over rows the acting user cannot read — inside one turn, spending no retry budget.

The denial itself is unaffected on every host: nothing is dispatched and no data is rendered.

Your own exception has to be a ServiceError

Every row above is matched by type. A service that raises its own error class gets none of this unless that class derives from the kernel's ServiceError:

from django_service_specs import ServiceError


class BookingError(ServiceError):  # not Exception
    """Something the booking rules refuse."""

Deriving from Exception is the ordinary thing to reach for, and the failure is silent in a way worth spelling out, because it is not confined to the agent. The same exception escapes an HTTP view as a 500 for what is plainly a 409, escapes MCP as a protocol error, and aborts an agent run rather than settling the call as failed. Nothing warns — not at declaration, not at mount, not at dispatch.

Two separate projects made this exact mistake and neither test suite could see it, because every write test asserted a path that succeeds. If a project genuinely cannot change its exception's base class, exception_map= is the other door: it takes the type and returns what the model should be told.

docs.title: A refused affordance names its code
docs.text:
The kernel's dispatch raises ActionUnavailable when one of a spec's Affordance conditions is not met, with the affordance's reason as the message and its code as an attribute. ToolFailed carries a message and nothing else, and that message is also what a transport forwards as the tool result, so the toolset puts both into it — the reason first, then the code, labelled:

from django_service_specs import Affordance, DataclassValidator, ServiceSpec, Unrestricted


def post_invoice(*, data, user):
    """Post an invoice to the current period."""
    ...


post_invoice_spec = ServiceSpec(
    service=post_invoice,
    validator=DataclassValidator(InvoiceIn),
    permissions=[Unrestricted()],
    affordances=[
        Affordance(
            code="books_closed",
            reason="The books are closed.",
            when=lambda: Period.current().is_open,
        ),
    ],
)

While the period is closed the tool is left out of the catalog, so a run reaches this refusal only through a listing that went stale: the step was offered the tool, and the period closed before the call arrived. A condition on the row is refused the same way, and it is never asked when the catalog is listed. The failed tool result's content, which is what the model reads and what a transport streams, is:

The books are closed. (code: books_closed)

The code is the part that connects the refusal to what the model may already have read. A selector naming the same spec in its own affordances (affordances={"post_invoice": post_invoice_spec}) answers it on each row it renders, under affordances.post_invoice, as {"available": false, "code": "books_closed", "reason": "The books are closed."} — and the reason is a sentence a project may reword while the code stays put. The conventions block get_instructions returns tells the model a refusal may end this way. A ServiceError or ServiceConflict raised by hand has no code and keeps its message exactly as written.

The suffix is written for the model and for a person reading a tool card, not for a program. It is meant to read the same on every agent transport serving these specs, and its wording is not an interface. A program that branches on the code reads .code off the exception instead: the ActionUnavailable is the ToolFailed's __cause__, and translate_exception receives it before the toolset's own handling runs. A handler returned from there, or registered in exception_map for ActionUnavailable or any class above it, replaces the sentence along with the rest of the default.

docs.title: Why the failed rows raise instead of returning
docs.text:
Every ToolFailed row above is raised rather than returned as a {"error": "..."} dict. The model reads the same sentence either way, so the choice is not about what it sees — it is about what everything else sees. Pydantic-AI marks an ordinary return outcome="success" on the resulting ToolReturnPart; only a raised ToolFailed marks it "failed". Returning the dict would make a refusal indistinguishable from an answer to a log, an audit record, or a transport streaming the call to a browser, all of which would have nothing but the payload's wording to go on.

ToolFailed keeps the two properties a returned dict would have: it spends none of the tool's retry budget, and it does not end the run. It also prepends no correction instructions, which ModelRetry does — right for a bad argument, and wrong for a conflict the model cannot argue with.

If a failure is one your project would rather express as an ordinary result, exception_map still takes a handler that returns a value, and a returned value is still marked "success".

Each ModelRetry row consumes one unit of the tool's retry budget: after max_retries failed attempts (default 1, pydantic-ai's function-tool default) the run aborts with UnexpectedModelBehavior. Raise it for models that need more attempts to converge:

toolset = SpecToolset(specs, max_retries=3)

docs.title: Reference
docs.text: django_spec_agents.spec_tools exports four symbols: SpecToolset, SpecCapability, AgentConventions and the string AGENT_TRANSPORT. A django-service-specs spec declares what it reads as Parameters in its reads and shapes, documented with the kernel. The deps a run passes are the package's one AgentDeps, and the doubles for driving a toolset through a real run loop are in django_spec_agents.testing.

docs.title: SpecToolset
docs.text:
Bases: AbstractToolset[Any]

Exposes specs as a Pydantic-AI toolset.

A spec is anything django-service-specs' kernel_spec compiles: a django-service-specs ServiceSpec or SelectorSpec, or a declaration that compiles to one. Every read of it is the compiled spec's. Build it from a name -> spec mapping and hand it to an Agent:

toolset = SpecToolset({
    "list_orders": orders_selector_spec,   # SelectorSpec -> read-only tool
    "create_order": create_order_spec,     # ServiceSpec  -> mutation tool
})
agent = Agent(model, deps_type=AgentDeps, toolsets=[toolset])

Each key becomes one tool: the description is the spec's selector/service docstring, the parameter schema is the kernel's spec_caller_input_schema (with a list selector's page / limit args merged in), the return_schema comes from the same spec's projected output path, and the readOnlyHint annotation is derived from the spec kind (selectors read, services mutate).

The parameter schema asks for what a call needs and nothing the toolset fills. A selector parameter named after a pool seed or a key a typed kwargs= provider returns is not advertised; every other selector parameter without a default is required, except one the provider may fill, which stays advertised but optional: any parameter, beside a provider whose return annotation does not name a TypedDict, and a key the provider may decline with UNSET, both as the kernel's provider_keys reads the annotation. A key the spec's own kwargs= provider returns that is named like a Validator field, or a key a target selector's kwargs= provider returns that is named like a Validator field or a read, is a namesake, not a fill: the field or read stays advertised unless input_data fills it, and the provider's value reaches only its own seat (the service keyword, or the selector). A name a call_seeds override fills is invisible here, so it has to be declared (see call_seeds). A single-item service also advertises its target lookup -- the parameters of its collection_selector_spec, or failing that its instance_selector_spec, such as a pk -- beside its input's fields, the input's property winning a shared name, and less every key the kernel's server_owned_keys names, which dispatch fills itself and which leaves a namesake out. A call leaving out a required selector parameter is handed back as ModelRetry naming each one left out, before anything runs. A required input field is the Validator's to report, once the call is dispatched, so a call missing both hears about the field on its next turn.

A list selector's result is a page, always. It comes back as {"items": [...], "page": 1, "totalPages": N, "hasNext": bool} — never a bare list — with at most DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE rows unless max_page_size lowers it, which is what the page and limit arguments every list tool advertises promise. hasNext is what tells a model asking for a collection that more rows exist than it was shown.

Every other list result is an object too: the rows a service presents -- a LIST output re-read, a many call, a returns_many return -- come back as {"items": [...]}, with no page around them, under a return schema saying so. items is the key a page holds its rows under, so a model reads a list's rows at one path whether the tool pages or not, and django-spec-mcp serves the same spec in the same shape. A list that presents nothing, a many or returns_many service declaring allow_none returning None, is {"items": []}.

Filtering needs no declaration here, and ordering belongs to the filter_set. A SelectorSpec.filter_set's fields are already generated into the tool's input schema and flow through as ordinary params, which the kernel hands the FilterSet as filter_data. That includes ordering: a FilterSet carrying an OrderingFilter named ordering advertises the argument itself — the kernel derives the filter's public choices into the schema, each a const under its label — and the toolset keeps its hands off the value, which the FilterSet validates and applies through its own param_map.

A many=True service takes its list as one named argument. Its input validates as a JSON array and a model's arguments are always an object, so the list travels under the argument ServiceSpec.many_argument names -- items unless the spec names another -- and nothing may be sent beside it but the spec's own reads. An invalid item comes back as a ModelRetry keyed under that argument and then by the item's index. The result is the rendered list under items, advertised so.

What a tool reads off HTTP is the spec's to declare, in its reads, where every transport and every mount reads the same answer; the toolset reads them off the compiled spec, so a spec arriving in a SpecRegistry and the same spec in a bare mapping are served alike. A read no callable takes is one of the compiled spec's shapes: it is advertised as a tool argument and dispatched as one, and the kernel hands what the caller sent to the presenter, on PresentationContext.shapes, and to any callable declaring shapes, so a field selection is the presenter's to read, with no toolset awareness of how it parses one. A read a callable does take, by name or through **kwargs, is that callable's argument: advertised as a plain one, and handed its declared default when the model leaves it out. A read standing for a URL route capture (parent_pk) is an argument of the spec, which a selector, a service or a kwargs= provider takes by its name. A null sent under a read that cannot be null is the model declining it, and its default answers. A value the model may not choose is not a read at all but tool_server_arguments, which keeps it from the model rather than defaulting it.

For anything the keywords below do not cover, call_seeds and translate_exception are overridable and both receive the live RunContext, which is how per-run typed deps reach dispatch; the run's AgentDeps.call_context is copied into every call's context.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default specs SpecSource

The name -> spec mapping to expose, one tool per key. A SpecRegistry is accepted anywhere the mapping is — the shared declaration site for a project exposing the same specs over more than one transport, so the agent reads the source MCP and the HTTP views read. The registry and registry.specs() build the same tools: the toolset reads every spec's reads and its output projection off the compiled spec, which either carries. A filtered view is itself a registry, so several toolsets can be projected from one declaration with no shared state (SpecToolset(registry.by_tag("read"), id="reads")). Only the names come from it; everything else here is transport-specific, which the registry deliberately carries none of.

required id str

Identifies this toolset, and keys a wrapping SpecCapability's defer_loading catalog entry — so give each projection of one registry its own.

'spec-tools' instructions str | None

Replaces the conventions block get_instructions derives from the specs. None derives it. What it does not replace is the per-step list of operations that are unavailable right now, which is appended after it whenever an operation condition leaves one out of the catalog, unless conventions sets unavailable_heading to None, which drops that list with or without an override: the override replaces conventions, and which operations are offered on a given step is state no override written in advance could have described.

Refused beside a conventions= that changes a line only the derived block says, because the override would ignore it without a word. The fields that land elsewhere -- unavailable_heading, handle_field_description, query_param_on_pages and missing_arguments -- apply with or without it.

None conventions AgentConventions | None

The wording the model is told, one line per field -- an AgentConventions. None is AgentConventions(), the default wording. A field changes what its line says and never whether it appears, which the toolset still decides per step; None on a field drops its line. Unlike instructions=, an override of one line leaves every other line derived, conditional and current.

None get_user UserExtractor | None

Reads the acting identity off the run context. Defaults to ctx.deps.user (the AgentDeps shape).

None get_progress ProgressExtractor | None

Reads the run's ProgressReporter sink off the run context, for a spec that reports progress. Defaults to ctx.deps.progress, tolerating a deps type without the field.

None unknown_arguments UnknownArguments

What to do with a tool arg outside the spec's declared input set — a key the model invented. UnknownArguments.REJECT (the default) surfaces it as a ModelRetry so the model self-corrects, and IGNORE drops it. Under either, the key never reaches the callable, which the kernel hands only what its spec declares. A filter_set's filters are declared names, so a key outside them and the selector's parameters is refused like any other; a selector taking a bare **kwargs declares no name, so every key sent to it is refused. PASSTHROUGH raises ImproperlyConfigured here: a tool call has no channel that carries an undeclared name through to the callable, and the kernel's dispatch refuses it on every call.

REJECT tool_server_arguments Mapping[str, ServerArguments] | None

Values the server supplies for a tool's arguments, and names it keeps from the model, keyed by tool name -- a django-service-specs ServerArguments per tool. Each name is one the tool's spec declares: a selector or target-lookup parameter, or one of its reads. A name in values is bound: the call carries the server's value whatever the model sent, it satisfies a required parameter, and every reader of the call sees it, as one of the call's arguments. A withheld name is absent, so its declared default, or the callable's own, answers. Neither is advertised: both leave the tool's properties and required, and the instructions name neither. What the model sends under one is dropped before the call is checked, never refused, and logged at WARNING with the tool and the names, never the values. Checked when the toolset is built: a name the tool does not expose is refused with ValueError, and a binding check_server_arguments refuses -- an undeclared name, a seed or provider's name, a withheld name no call could do without, a bound value its parameter refuses -- with ImproperlyConfigured naming the tool. A seed call_seeds returns under a bound or withheld read or parameter is refused the same way, at the call, since the mount's check cannot see it (test_a_call_seed_under_a_bound_or_withheld_name_is_refused_at_the_call); a Validator field of that name still takes the bound value, and the service parameter the seed. Static, like the tool definitions: build a toolset per scope, as a run scoped to one project builds one with that project bound.

None max_retries int

Each tool's retry budget: how many times a ModelRetry is fed back to the model before the run aborts with UnexpectedModelBehavior. The default matches pydantic-ai's own function-tool default.

1 max_result_bytes int | None

Ceiling on a rendered result, measured on the encoded payload because what is being protected is the model's context window. Over it the call fails with a model-readable ToolFailed — never truncates, because a partial payload looks complete. A file is the exception: over it, the file is described in a one-line note, a success, never refused; see render_output.

None tool_max_result_bytes Mapping[str, int | None] | None

max_result_bytes per tool. An explicit None opts that tool out; an absent key inherits the default.

None attachment_inline AttachmentInlineConfig | None

The AttachmentInlineConfig a file result is read with, the one read_attachment is given: which binary types are attached and the largest file returned rather than described. None is AttachmentInlineConfig(). See render_output.

None max_page_size int | None

Clamps a list tool's limit and advertises the ceiling as JSON-Schema maximum. It lowers the default page size only when it is below DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE: an omitted limit is served min(DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE, max_page_size), and that is the default the limit description and the instructions state. A ceiling above it raises what a call may ask for, not what it gets by asking for nothing. Unset, a list tool still returns at most DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE rows per page — the unbounded read is the one that hurts, and it is what a model produces by not thinking about pagination.

None include_total bool

Adds total, how many rows the list matched across every page, to each list tool's page beside totalPages and hasNext, and advertises it in the tool's return schema and its limit description, and in what {envelope} renders: the pagination line of the derived instructions, the sentence on each read-shaping parameter and its render retry. Off by default. It costs no query: the count is the one taken before the slice. The flag is toolset-wide, and what is advertised follows it rather than any shape_page override. A project that wants total on some tools only leaves it off and has an override return a counting page for those tools, so nothing advertised claims a key a page lacks; turning it on and dropping total from some tools would.

False thread_sensitive bool

Whether every dispatch shares one thread. True (the default, and asgiref's) is what keeps Django's thread-local database connections coherent, and is why it is not flipped for you.

The cost is that concurrent tool calls serialise, process-wide. asgiref's single_thread_executor is a class attribute, so it is one thread shared by every toolset instance and every concurrent run in the process -- not one per toolset. Pydantic-AI genuinely runs function tools in parallel within a segment, so four 0.30s calls under one model step take ~1.2s rather than ~0.3s. That is invisible in a chat turn calling one tool and severe in a fan-out.

Set False only when you know the dispatched work is safe off the main thread -- typically because each call opens and closes its own connection, or you pass an executor you control.

True executor ThreadPoolExecutor | None

A ThreadPoolExecutor to run dispatch on, instead of asgiref's shared single thread. Only consulted when thread_sensitive is False, which is asgiref's own rule.

None dispatch_timeout float | None

Seconds bounding one call, so the model gets an answer instead of a hang. It does not stop the work: the dispatch runs in a sync_to_async thread and asyncio cannot interrupt a thread parked in a database driver's socket read, so the query runs to completion regardless. Pair it with a database statement timeout.

None require_permissions bool

Refuse to construct a toolset containing a spec declaring no permissions, whose permissions compiles to None. Over HTTP that may mean inherit from a view; here there is nothing to inherit from, so it means ungated. An empty list is a declaration that anyone may call, and is neither refused nor warned about. False downgrades the refusal to an UnguardedSpecWarning while migrating.

True descriptions Mapping[str, str] | None

Overrides spec.description per tool — the docstring an API developer reads is rarely the sentence a model needs. A tool left with no description anywhere gets an UndescribedToolWarning.

None exception_map Mapping[type[BaseException], ExceptionHandler] | None

Maps an exception type to a handler returning the tool's result (or raising ModelRetry). Matched along the MRO, most specific first, and consulted before the built-in arms, so a project can override those too.

None pool_seeds PoolSeeds

The project's own always-available pool seeds -- a PoolSeeds registry of names such as a tenant, a locale or a clock, which over HTTP hang off request and off it have no channel. Handed to every dispatch this toolset makes, so a service, a selector or an affordance's condition declaring one receives it as it would from the kernel's dispatch(pool_seeds=) called directly; and to the per-step check that leaves out an operation whose condition is unmet, so the catalog and the instructions are decided against the same seeds the call is refused with. A registered name is also reserved: the model cannot supply it where the seed fills a parameter, so an argument of that name is dropped where the spec declares such a parameter and refused as unknown under REJECT where the spec declares the name nowhere, no tool's input schema advertises it, and a read the spec declares under it, in any seat, is refused here with ImproperlyConfigured. A Validator field of the name is the one exception, and the model's to send: it is validated into data, while the service's parameter of the name still receives the seed's value. Toolset-wide, with no per-tool or per-call form: a seed is ambient to the deployment, and what varies per call belongs in its resolver, which declares user / request to receive them.

DEFAULT_POOL_SEEDS

Raises:

Type Description ImproperlyConfigured

unknown_arguments is neither REJECT nor IGNORE, a spec declares no permissions and require_permissions is set, a spec reads a registered pool seed's name, a many spec's list is named after a registered pool seed or request / view, a selector takes a parameter that a list tool's page / limit takes out of the call before it runs (a spec's own read of an input's name is not one: it is where the input comes from, and is served as the input), a shape takes the name page, limit or ordering, tool_server_arguments names something django-service-specs' check_server_arguments refuses for the tool's spec, instructions= is given beside a conventions= that changes a line of the block it replaces, a spec's Validator names a required field no call can send, or the kernel or a spec's own library refuses a spec while the toolset compiles it, reads its input schema or projects its output -- a malformed metadata["json_schema"] fragment, or two output fields marked FieldMarking.label(). The refusing message is prefixed SpecToolset tool '<name>':.

TypeError

A value in specs is not one kernel_spec compiles -- a registry's entry rather than its spec, say, or a declaration of several specs, whose variants each take their own name. The kernel's message, prefixed with the tool's name.

ValueError

A tool name is outside ^[a-zA-Z0-9_-]{1,64}$, or a per-tool mapping, tool_server_arguments included, names a tool this toolset does not expose.

docs.title: specs property
docs.text:
specs: Mapping[str, Spec]

The resolved name -> spec mapping this toolset exposes.

The synchronous answer to "what tools are these?", for a caller composing this toolset at configuration time — a name-dedup pass, a tool catalog — with no run in sight, since get_tools is async and needs a RunContext. Read-only (a MappingProxyType), so enumerating it cannot add a tool that skipped the constructor's permission and description checks.

docs.title: get_tools async
docs.text:
get_tools(ctx: RunContext[Any]) -> dict[str, ToolsetTool[Any]]

The tool catalog this run is offered, one entry per listed spec.

The catalog is not permission-filtered, by design. Every tool is advertised to every run and the spec's permissions gate the call: a denied tool is one the model can see and cannot use. Filtering by default would be worse in three ways — a permission whose answer depends on the arguments has none to read at listing time and would deny a tool the caller can in fact invoke; get_tools runs once per model step, so a DB-backed check becomes a query per spec per step; and a tool the model never sees is one it cannot ask about, which is how a run ends in a guess instead of a denial. Nothing row-level is exposed either way — a listing carries a name, a description and an input schema.

An operation whose condition is unmet right now is left out, and that is not the same decision. A spec's Affordance answered without a row -- a callable when, "the books are open" -- is asked each step, and a tool it fails is omitted until it holds again. Each of the three arguments above has an answer here. Such a condition reads only the seeds -- the user, the request, a registered seed -- and never an argument, so it cannot hide a tool the caller could in fact invoke: whatever the model would send, the call would be refused. Only the specs declaring one are asked, so a toolset that declares none pays nothing, not even a thread hop. And the model can still ask about what it cannot see, because get_instructions names every tool left out this way together with its reason, which is what it needs to tell the user why rather than guess.

A condition on the row (an ORM expression) is never asked here: there is no row at listing time, and it goes on being answered per object at the call. A condition that raises aborts the step, as it would the call -- one that cannot be answered is not a no.

The omission is applied beside is_tool_listed, not inside it, so an override of that seam -- which is free to return True -- cannot switch it off by not calling super(). Neither is an authorization decision: the call enforces every affordance whatever this listed, and a model calling a name left out gets pydantic-ai's unknown-tool retry.

This and get_instructions each ask the conditions for themselves, once per step apiece, rather than sharing one answer. The run context carries no key that could safely scope a shared answer to one run and one step: run_id may be supplied by the caller and is reused when a failed run is retried under it, and a context built by hand has none. A memo keyed on it could hand one run's -- one user's -- answer to another, where asking twice costs a second evaluation of conditions that read only seeds. The price is that a condition flipping between the two reads can leave one step's catalog and its instructions disagreeing about one tool; the call's own enforcement is authoritative either way.

Override is_tool_listed when a deployment does want a narrower catalog.

docs.title: is_tool_listed async
docs.text:
is_tool_listed(name: str, ctx: RunContext[Any]) -> bool

Whether name belongs in this run's catalog. True by default.

The seam for a deployment that wants a per-run catalog — hiding a staff-only tool from a non-staff run, or scoping the catalog to a tenant read off ctx.deps. Hiding a tool is a disclosure decision, never an authorization one: the call is gated by spec.permissions whatever this returns, so an override that wrongly returns True grants nothing.

Not consulted for a tool an unmet operation condition already left out of this step's catalog, and returning True does not put one back: that omission is applied by get_tools itself, so an override need not call super() to keep it.

async because get_tools is, and it is called once per tool per model step. An override that queries the database must wrap that work in asgiref.sync.sync_to_async — Django refuses ORM access on the event loop, exactly as call_tool has to for dispatch.

docs.title: get_instructions async
docs.text:
get_instructions(ctx: RunContext[Any]) -> str | None

Teach the model this toolset's conventions.

The per-tool descriptions and parameter schemas say what each tool is, but not how the family behaves: that list tools accept page / limit / ordering, that a business failure comes back as a readable failed result (a final answer, not a reason to retry) while a bad argument comes back as a retry request, and that a permission error is final. Pydantic-AI appends the block to the system prompt each turn, for a toolset attached directly or wrapped by a capability.

Per step, when an operation condition leaves a tool out. The block is then derived from the tools this step offers, so no line advises about one it does not, and it ends by naming each tool left out with its reason: the model sees neither the tool nor, otherwise, any sign it exists, and a user asking for it would get a guess where a sentence was available. The conditions are asked here and in get_tools separately -- see that method for why, and for what it costs. With an instructions override, the override stands in for the derived block and the unavailable tools are still appended after it, because an override replaces the conventions and cannot have described which operations a given step would lack. unavailable_heading=None in the conventions drops that list either way, override or not.

A toolset declaring no such condition is untouched by any of this: it asks nothing, and returns the same string every step.

Each line is worded by the toolset's conventions, which change what a line says and never whether it appears.

Returns:

Type Description str | None

The instructions override when one was given, else a block

str | None

derived from the specs — each line conditional on something in this

str | None

toolset being able to act on it, so the prompt carries no advice that

str | None

cannot fire — followed in either case by the operations unavailable

str | None

this step, when there are any and unavailable_heading is not

str | None

None. None when conventions dropped

str | None

every line that would have been said and nothing is unavailable.

docs.title: call_seeds
docs.text:
call_seeds(*, ctx: RunContext[Any], tool_name: str) -> Mapping[str, Callable[..., Any]]

The seeds one call registers beside the mount's pool_seeds, by name.

Each value is a resolver, as for PoolSeeds' extend: called once per call, with whatever it declares of the kernel's base pool (user, progress). The default returns none. Override it for a value that depends on the run or on the tool being called, which pool_seeds=, toolset-wide, cannot carry: a tenant read off ctx.deps, or the role a permission check reads for this operation.

Called in the dispatch thread, before the call's arguments are checked, so a name a seed fills is never asked of the model (test_a_seed_the_hook_returns_reaches_the_call_and_is_not_asked_of_the_model), and once per conditioned tool when the catalog is listed, so a condition reading a seed it returns is asked with the tool's own (test_a_listing_asks_each_condition_with_its_own_tool_s_seeds).

A read or parameter tool_server_arguments binds or withholds for the tool is refused too, with ImproperlyConfigured naming the tool, as the same seed on the mount's pool_seeds is when the toolset is built. A configuration error rather than a retry: the model cannot act on it, and the seed would otherwise win over the server's value without a trace (test_a_call_seed_under_a_bound_or_withheld_name_is_refused_at_the_call). A bound Validator field of the same name is not a read: it takes the bound value and the service parameter the seed, as on the mount (test_a_bound_validator_field_and_a_call_seed_of_the_same_name_both_reach_the_call).

A name the mount's pool_seeds registers already is refused with ValueError at the call, as PoolSeeds.extend refuses one registered twice (test_a_hook_seed_the_mount_already_registers_is_refused). Returning request or view replaces the one the call carries, which is otherwise the run's call_context entry of that name, None where the run put none: a view returned here is what a permission check or a presenter declaring view reads.

A name a seed fills has to be declared. A selector parameter only a seed fills is, to the tool's schema, a parameter without a default like any other, so it is advertised as required. Leave it out of the spec's reads, as a library compiling a spec does for a parameter it marks as no client input: the name is left out of the schema, so the model is never asked for it, and the seed fills it. Under the default unknown_arguments a call that sends it anyway is handed back as an unexpected argument (test_a_marked_name_sent_to_an_open_selector_is_refused). test_a_name_a_call_seeds_override_fills_is_kept_from_the_model holds the marker, and test_a_name_a_call_seeds_override_fills_is_declared_to_the_toolset a seed the mount registers instead.

docs.title: translate_exception
docs.text:
translate_exception(
    exc: BaseException, *, ctx: RunContext[Any]
) -> ExceptionHandler | None

Return a handler for exc, or None to leave it to the defaults.

The default consults exception_map by walking the exception's MRO, so a handler registered for a base class catches its subclasses and the most specific registration wins. Override for a decision the map cannot express — one that has to read the run's deps.

This runs ahead of every built-in arm, so it is also where a program reads a refusal's code: an ActionUnavailable arrives here with .code intact, before the default renders it into the sentence <reason> (code: <code>). A handler returned for it replaces that sentence along with everything else the default would have done.

docs.title: shape_page
docs.text:
shape_page(
    rows: Any,
    *,
    ctx: RunContext[Any],
    page: int | None,
    limit: int | None,
    max_page_size: int | None,
) -> OutputPage

Slice a list selector's rows into the page this call serves.

Called only for list selectors -- the specs that advertise pagination arguments and return something sliceable. The default is the kernel's shared paginate_output (which counts the rows and clamps both bounds) followed by forcing evaluation, so nothing downstream holds a lazy queryset.

No sorting happens here, and an override should not add any. Ordering belongs to whatever the spec declared it on, which has already applied it to the queryset by the time this runs; an order_by here would replace that sort rather than compose with it.

include_total decides the page here: on, the page returned writes total into its envelope, as the kernel's page does. The return schema, the limit description and the {envelope} the conventions render follow the flag too, but they are written at construction, so an override changes the payload and never what is advertised. An override that builds a page of its own carries what that page's envelope writes (rebuilding the page keeps total only through dataclasses.replace or include_total=shaped.include_total): that is how a project with the flag off adds total, or figures of its own, on the tools it chooses (ctx.tool_name names the call's). Under the flag, an override should keep total on every page, since every tool advertises it.

docs.title: render_output
docs.text:
render_output(
    spec: Spec,
    result: DispatchResult,
    *,
    ctx: RunContext[Any],
    projection: AudienceProjection | None,
    max_bytes: int | None,
) -> Any

Turn a dispatch result into the payload the model reads.

result is the kernel's DispatchResult: for a paged tool, with the page's rows as its value, and the envelope is added after this returns. The default is the kernel's present_for_audience: the spec's presenter, handed each value with the call's PresentationContext -- its seeds, its context and the read-shaping arguments the caller sent, on shapes -- then the output's audience markings, using the projection this toolset resolved once at registration. result.instance (the pre-mutation target), result.data (the validated input) and result.service_result (the flags an upsert's created rides on) are here for an override that wants them.

This is the opt-out of projecting, and the only one. Passing projection=None is not it -- present_for_audience reads None as "derive one from the spec", so the payload is projected anyway. An override that wants the unprojected payload calls the kernel's present(spec, result) directly.

Two cases want that. A chaining pipeline feeding one spec's output into the next needs the handles the next step reads by, and the kernel says so in present_for_audience's own docstring: project them away and the next step has nothing to key on. And an output field declaring choices whose display differs from its value is projected without any marking being declared -- choice_labels is derived from the field itself -- so "we marked nothing, so nothing is projected" is not true, and an override is how a project that means it says so.

A file is read the way read_attachment reads an attachment, with the toolset's attachment_inline config (AttachmentInlineConfig() when none was given). A spec presenting a FileResult (through the kernel's FilePresenter) is answered with its text when its type is textual and it fits; with its bytes attached to the tool result, for that turn, when its type is one of the config's media_types and it fits; and otherwise with a one-line note giving its name, type and size.

It fits under the smaller of two limits: the config's max_bytes and max_bytes here, the tool's max_result_bytes (None when it has none, and then the config's limit alone applies). An attached file fits when its bytes plus the sentence beside them do, as enforce_result_bytes measures it. A file over either limit is a success carrying the note, which names the limit that fired, never a refusal: there is nothing in a file to narrow. A file over the limit is read no further than it, and one of a type the model cannot read is closed unread.

docs.title: enforce_result_bytes
docs.text:
enforce_result_bytes(
    payload: Any, *, ctx: RunContext[Any], max_bytes: int | None, label: str
) -> Any

Return payload, or raise a model-readable refusal when it is over budget.

Measured on the envelope, because the envelope is what is sent. A file is measured by its bytes: a text file by its text's UTF-8 length, an attached one by its bytes plus the note beside them, never by its repr. render_output already described a file that would not fit, so a rendered file reaches this under the ceiling. One an override returned unrendered, a FileResult, is measured by its declared size, or read up to the ceiling when it declares none; over it, the default returns the note render_output would have, as a success, and closes the file, rather than refusing. A note render_output returned is final: it is not measured again, whatever the ceiling, and one naming the ceiling is logged at WARNING. Override to bound on something other than serialized length -- a row count, a per-run running total read off ctx.usage, a taper against ctx.usage_limits as a run gets long -- or to shape the refusal differently.

The default raises ToolFailed; an override is free to return a value instead, and that value becomes the tool's result marked outcome="success". An override delegating to super() sees the refusal as an exception, not as a returned value.

ctx is not merely passed through to an override here: the default reads this run's correlation fields off it and stamps them on the WARNING a fired bound emits, which is the one line saying why a result the model expected came back as a refusal.

docs.title: Subclassing SpecToolset
docs.text:
A project scoping an assistant to what one run may reach subclasses SpecToolset, and these are the parts of it a subclass builds on. They are public.

  • get_tools(ctx) and call_tool(name, tool_args, ctx, tool), pydantic-ai's toolset methods. Override get_tools to narrow the catalog a run is offered and call_tool to wrap a call, each delegating to super(): the run loop offers the model what get_tools returns and dispatches every call through call_tool.
  • specs and id, read-only properties that answer at configuration time, with no run: specs is every tool the toolset was built with, whatever a get_tools override offers a given run.
  • The five seams, each receiving the live RunContext: call_seeds and translate_exception cover the front half of a call, shape_page, render_output and enforce_result_bytes the back half.
  • AgentDeps.call_context, the run's context, of which every call is handed its own copy.

An attribute whose name starts with an underscore is not part of it, and a minor release may rename one.

docs.title: SpecCapability
docs.text:
Bases: AbstractCapability[Any]

A Pydantic-AI capability exposing specs as tools.

SpecToolset is a first-class toolset you can attach directly (Agent(toolsets=[SpecToolset(...)])), and it already exposes the tools and teaches the model its conventions. This wraps one to add the two capability-only knobs, defer_loading and the description its catalog entry is chosen by. It does not re-emit those conventions — Pydantic-AI collects them from the owned toolset — so wrapping and attaching directly yield the same instructions, exactly once.

Construct it the same way as SpecToolset (it forwards the toolset knobs):

agent = Agent(
    model,
    deps_type=AgentDeps,
    capabilities=[SpecCapability({
        "list_orders": orders_selector_spec,   # SelectorSpec -> read-only tool
        "create_order": create_order_spec,     # ServiceSpec  -> mutation tool
    })],
)

or wrap an already-built toolset with from_toolset (the compose path). Either way the exposed tool set and instructions are the toolset's.

Everything else SpecToolset accepts, this accepts, and means there. That is a guarantee rather than a list, enforced name-by-name by the forwarding tests: a knob added to the toolset and forgotten here is not a missing feature but an unreachable one for every consumer composing through a capability. See SpecToolset for what each does; the safety-relevant ones are require_permissions, max_result_bytes, max_page_size and dispatch_timeout.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default specs SpecSource

As SpecToolset, including a SpecRegistry or a filtered view of one, so a project declaring its specs once can project several capabilities from them. Every entry is a django-service-specs spec or a declaration that compiles to one; one that compiles to no spec raises TypeError when the capability is built, as it does for the toolset.

required defer_loading bool

Hide the whole spec toolset and its instructions behind Pydantic-AI's native load_capability tool until the model loads it — progressive disclosure for a large spec map.

False id str

As SpecToolset. It keys defer_loading's catalog entry, so give each capability projected from one registry its own.

'spec-tools' description str | None

One line saying what this capability is for, rendered beside id in defer_loading's catalog. Give one to every deferred capability: Pydantic-AI's loader renders - {id}: {description} when there is one and a bare - {id} when there is not, so several undescribed capabilities leave the model choosing between names alone — the guess-or-load-everything outcome deferring exists to avoid. Not the same knob as descriptions, which relabels individual tools.

None unknown_arguments UnknownArguments

As SpecToolset: REJECT (the default) or IGNORE. PASSTHROUGH raises ImproperlyConfigured when the capability is built, since the toolset it owns is built then.

REJECT

docs.title: from_toolset classmethod
docs.text:
from_toolset(
    toolset: SpecToolset, *, defer_loading: bool = False, description: str | None = None
) -> SpecCapability

Wrap an already-built SpecToolset (the compose path).

The capability adopts the toolset's id, and its tools and instructions are the toolset's own — set an instructions override or conventions on the SpecToolset itself if you need them, so from_toolset(ts) and SpecCapability(specs, …) behave identically. A toolset's conventions are kept because the toolset is: this wraps that instance rather than rebuilding it.

description means what it does on the constructor: the catalog line a deferred capability is chosen by. It has no toolset counterpart to adopt, so pass it here.

docs.title: AgentConventions dataclass
docs.text:
The instructions a toolset gives the model, and three sentences beside them, one field each.

Every field defaults to the sentence the toolset says today, so AgentConventions() changes nothing and AgentConventions(pagination=...) changes exactly one line. Pass it as conventions= to SpecToolset or SpecCapability; leaving that unset is the same as passing AgentConventions().

What is a field: every line of the instructions block, the heading of its unavailable list included; the description of a handle field that declares none; the sentence scoping a paged tool's read-shaping parameters; and the retry for a missing argument. Nothing else is. The descriptions of the arguments the toolset adds, such as limit and page, and its other retries stay fixed.

A field changes what a line says, never whether it appears. The toolset still decides that: the pagination line only when some tool returns a page, the ordering line only when some tool can sort, and so on, re-derived per step when an operation condition leaves a tool out. An override keeps those conditions, which is what instructions= loses by replacing the whole block, and a later release that corrects one default reaches every field you did not override.

None drops the line wherever the toolset would have said it; "" does not, and leaves a blank line where an instructions line was. The one exception is missing_arguments, which is the whole text of a retry and so can be neither dropped nor left blank.

Each field is a str.format template. The placeholders a field accepts are the ones listed on it, and nothing else; anything outside them raises ImproperlyConfigured naming the field when the instance is built, so a typo fails at startup rather than inside a prompt. A literal brace is written twice, {{ or }}, in every field.

Some lines state facts about behaviour, not just advice: pagination names the keys of the page envelope, base says which failures come back as a retry and which as a failed call, and query_param_on_pages lists the envelope's keys again. The toolset keeps behaving as the defaults describe whatever the text says, so an override that rewords one of those owns keeping it true. The envelope is the one fact the toolset keeps true for it: {envelope}, in the three fields that name the page, is the page as the toolset writes it, total included when it is built with include_total. Text without the placeholder is said as written, flag or not, so an override written against an earlier release keeps its words and does not gain total.
